"Mum was nervous about me travelling to Uganda. Even though she’d met the choir and knew the organisation, she was still concerned for my safety. My best friend was coming with me, which helped—but saying goodbye at the airport still felt surreal. Mum was crying, and I am thinking, “Are we really going to Africa right now?” We arrived at night, but even in the darkness, the drive was eye-opening—so many people wandering the streets, animals on the road, and vendors selling almost everything. We were taken to a large red-brick guesthouse where we spent our first night. The staff were incredibly kind, and they cooked the most delicious meal. The next day, we bought some groceries and headed to Suubi Village, where we would be living for the next month. As soon as you drive into Watoto, you are struck by how organised and lush it is compared to the rest of Kampala. After settling into a house, we shared with another 22-year-old from the USA and completing orientation, we were taken to Baby Watoto. For the next month, I helped in the one-to-eighteen-month room—feeding them, playing with them, and reading to them. I was even able to take one of the smallest babies, Grace, to church. She was so light, and being able to worship while holding such a precious little baby is a moment I will never forget. During our time in Uganda, we attended a local cell group, met families from all over the world, and a neighbourhood mum. She was caring for six children in a tiny shack with no electricity, no running water, and just one mattress that the entire family shared. She had recently joined the program and dreamed of opening her own store. Towards the end of my trip, during worship, I felt the Lord say to me, “What are you going to do with the life I have given you?” I thought about my family, my education, my financial resources, and how much money I spend on things I don’t need. This trip made me rethink my priorities. Life is about people — and in the end, the things we chase will fade. When I think about the future now, even though I am young, I know it’s going to look very different."

**Brussels Corner**

**What the first DSA fine means for platform regulation**

[On 5 December, the Commission issued](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_2934) a fine of €120 million to X for breaching its transparency obligations under the Digital Services Act (DSA). These breaches include the misleading design of its “blue checkmark,” insufficient transparency in its advertising repository, and its failure to grant researchers access to public data.

[In response to the fine](https://www.politico.eu/article/x-axes-european-commissions-ad-account-after-e120m-eu-fine/), Elon Musk’s X cut the European Commission off from its advertising control panel. X accuses the Commission of attempting to exploit the platform’s Ad Composer to amplify its post about the fine. In doing so, X’s claim effectively draws attention to an additional design weakness in its Ad Composer, reinforcing concerns about broader systemic risks on the platform. 

The issued fine marks[ only the beginning of DSA enforcement](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/eu-disinfolab_x-fine-dsa-activity-7402680040657743872-nkVR?utm_source=social_share_send&utm_medium=member_desktop_web&rcm=ACoAAFbYDM0BOPzavo8liee3Unqk37nKIhomoVs). X can be expected to appeal and regulators need to hold firm as case law develops. The goal of the DSA is not to collect fines but to compel platforms to change harmful business practices and comply with democratically agreed rules. Effective enforcement also requires addressing [malicious semi-compliance](https://www.disinfo.eu/malicious-semi-compliance-as-platform-approach-to-eu-regulation/) (cases where companies technically follow the law while undermining its purpose) and applying tougher sanctions when necessary. Finally, the evidence for this non-compliance decision relied heavily on the work of civil society and fact-checking communities, whose essential contribution to supporting enforcement should be recognised and sustainably funded.

At the time of writing, the Commission’s full non-compliance decision is still not public. This decision should explain the rationale for the imposed fine and clarify the threshold of evidence required to establish a breach of the DSA.

**Initial steps in EU institutions towards adopting the AgoraEU funding package**

Following the publication of the European Commission’s AgoraEU funding package, part of the Multi-annual Funding Framework, the EU co-legislators (the Council and Parliament) have taken initial steps toward agreeing on their positions.

[The European Parliament](https://oeil.europarl.europa.eu/oeil/en/procedure-file?reference=2025/0550(COD)) has decided that the work will be shared between the Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs Committee (LIBE), which handles a large number of legislative files, and the Culture and Education Committee (CULT), which handles a much smaller number of legislative files. Swedish Greens/EFA MEP Alice Kuhnke (LIBE) and French S&D MEP Emma Rafowicz (CULT) will be the rapporteurs for the proposal, with work expected to begin in early 2026. Meanwhile, [the Council](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15187-2025-INIT/en/pdf) has started more substantive discussions. It has focused on procedural points, including the possible creation of a committee to oversee implementation of the various strands of the programme, even though, to our knowledge, no such committee was ever necessary in the past, as well as on a rather long-winded definition of cultural industries that would exclude those that do not correspond to a very messy definition, which would, inter alia, require recipients to “have the potential to generate innovation and jobs in particular from intellectual property.” Discussions on the CERV+ strand (“Rights, Equality, Citizens and Civil Society,” “Daphne,” and “Democratic Participation and Rule of Law”) appear to have barely touched on activities to uphold democracy.

**The Democracy Shield draft report **

The European Parliament’s draft report on the Democracy Shield is expected to be published next month. Signals of what might or might not be there can be found in the [Parliament’s working document.](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/EUDS-DT-771957_EN.pdf)

According to the working document, the report was supposed to serve as an “early contribution” to the Commission’s communication on EUDS, which was released on 12 November (read our position [here](https://www.disinfo.eu/advocacy/eu-democracy-shield/)). Arriving after the publication of the Commission’s document, the Parliament’s report has already missed the opportunity to influence the Commission’s communication; however, in certain areas, the working document indicates a stronger ambition than the Commission’s document.

The rapporteur, Tomas Tobé, looks favourably on the creation of a new independent EU-level structure dedicated to combating FIMI and appears to have a clearer vision of what such a body could do than the Commission’s less ambitious ideas.

Similarly, the working document devotes a substantial section to cooperation in justice and home affairs and sanctions, whereas the Commission’s communication only briefly mentions this. Whether these stronger ambitions will be reflected in the draft report remains to be seen.

**Is There a Better Way to Shield Our Democracy?**

On 9 December, MEPs from the Greens/EFA, S&D, Renew, and EPP organised an event at the European Parliament on “Election Integrity and Foreign Interference in Romania, Moldova and Poland.” 

Speakers shared insights into the various Foreign and Domestic Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI and DIMI) tactics observed during elections in each country, noting that domestic actors are also used to spread disinformation. 

The discussion made clear that social media is no longer just a space for entertainment but has become a weaponised tool. This dynamic is enabled by engagement-driven algorithms that amplify illegal and polarising content. It was emphasised that known interference tactics can be easily replicated across borders, making this a truly EU-wide challenge. 

The issue is not a lack of legislation but a lack of enforcement, and platforms cannot be assumed to act in good faith. As co-legislators, MEPs have a responsibility to push for stronger action and to ensure the protection of Europe’s electoral integrity.

* **New paper calls for national institutions to build long-term information resilience. **A new discussion paper by International Idea warns that [escalating disinformation and malign influence campaigns are increasingly exploiting weaknesses in national information systems](https://www.idea.int/publications/catalogue/designing-resilience-building-institutions-safeguard-information-ecosystems), eroding public trust, and democratic stability. Current counter-disinformation efforts, the authors argue, remain too fragmented and fail to address the underlying systemic vulnerabilities that make societies susceptible to manipulation. To meet this growing threat, the paper calls for a coordinated, whole-of-society approach and advocates establishing dedicated national institutions focused on long-term information resilience. These bodies would strengthen cross-sector collaboration and provide the sustained capacity needed to protect democracies from evolving information threats.
* **UNESCO launches course to counter climate disinformation. **[UNESCO has launched a new free online course to tackle the surge in climate change disinformation](https://www.framerspace.com/course/climate-change-mil/?cid=66c4d62fd5a7ecdca11b28b3), which continues to undermine public understanding of one of the world’s most urgent threats. The program strengthens Media and Information Literacy (MIL) skills by teaching participants to critically evaluate digital content, recognise misleading narratives, and respond ethically to misinformation. By empowering global citizens to identify and counter climate-related disinformation, the course supports UNESCO’s broader effort to ensure reliable information remains a public good during the climate emergency. 
* **2025 marked a turning point as tech giants normalised digital deception**. A new analysis by [Indicator](https://indicator.media/p/2025-the-year-tech-embraced-fakeness) argues that 2025 was the year major institutions and tech companies openly embraced digital deception, with profound consequences for the public. The shift was symbolised by Mark Zuckerberg’s decision to end Meta’s third-party fact-checking program, an emblem of the broader rollback of moderation and oversight across platforms. This permissive environment enabled the explosive growth of AI-generated “slop,” deepfakes, ragebait marketing, and large-scale digital scams, including among venture-backed startups. The authors contend that these trends reflect a deeper systemic failure: tech giants continue to prioritise engagement and revenue over information integrity. 
* **New ATHENA publication**. [Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference: Case Studies from the ATHENA Project](https://project-athena.eu/new-athena-publication-released/) is the project’s latest publication, edited by Dr. David Wright, including a contribution from EU DisinfoLab. This new volume offers a comprehensive look at how state and non-state actors use FIMI to shape democratic processes worldwide. Drawing on 32 case studies and 20 expert interviews, the book examines who conducts these operations, how they target societies, which channels they exploit, and what countermeasures exist. A key highlight is its detailed analysis of the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used in modern disinformation campaigns, including rapidly advancing deepfake text, image, audio, and video manipulation. 
* **Cambridge Online Trust and Safety Index. **This [article](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adw8154) reveals that a thriving market for on-demand SMS verifications is a key enabler of inauthentic online activity, including bots and coordinated disinformation campaigns. Using the Cambridge Online Trust and Safety Index (COTSI), researchers tracked verification prices across 197 countries and 500 platforms, finding that costs often spike ahead of national elections, particularly on apps like Telegram and WhatsApp. The study suggests that stricter SIM card registration could help disrupt this manipulation economy and reduce the spread of disinformation.
* **Reddit tests verified profiles to address identity and misinformation threats. **[Reddit has launched a limited alpha test of verified profiles](https://redditinc.com/news/testing-verified-profiles-on-reddit), marked with a grey checkmark, that allow individuals and businesses to confirm their identities. The opt-in feature aims to add clarity for users engaging with experts, journalists, and brands and to “ease the burden on moderators who often verify users manually.” As platforms continue to grapple with mis/disinformation, Reddit frames the initiative as “privacy-preserving” and focused on transparency rather than amplification.

**This week’s recommended read**

[Raquel Miguel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/raquel-miguel-serrano-b5658130/), Senior Researcher at EU DisinfoLab, recommends two blog posts warning about the serious implications of introducing advertising into AI-driven chatbots.

Drawing on a recent leak confirming that OpenAI is moving in this direction after other companies had previously announced similar steps, Alberto Romero examines the motivations behind the decision — notably that LLMs are not economically sustainable — and the far-reaching consequences for users.

In a blog post titled [“Why ads on ChatGPT are more terrifying than you think,”](https://www.thealgorithmicbridge.com/p/why-ads-on-chatgpt-are-more-terrifying) Romero argues that this shift means that OpenAI’s primary clients will no longer be users, but advertisers, effectively turning the company into “a full-blown media company selling access to attention.”

While similar dynamics have already transformed search engines and social media platforms, applying this model to generative AI introduces unique risks and complexities that we do not yet fully understand. Because chatbots are built around information synthesis, an LLM will be able to embed ads directly into its answers, likely prioritising responses that benefit advertisers. In “[Advertising is coming to AI. It’s going to be a disaster](https://centerforhumanetechnology.substack.com/p/advertising-is-coming-to-ai-its-going?triedRedirect=true),” Daniel Barcay also warns that “ads can be woven invisibly into the fabric of conversation itself, making it virtually impossible to detect.” He further highlights the legal implications, arguing that this model will push the boundaries of existing fair-advertising regulations.

It also tracks how Italy’s policy response is evolving, including developments linked to the Digital Services Act (DSA). From political leaders and social activists to tech innovators and philanthropists, women are leaving an indelible mark on their communities and the world. These are the women who’ve defined the year with courage, vision and impact.

There’s a peculiar kind of pressure that seems to squeeze women from all sides, no matter what they choose. This tension is at the heart of Margaret Mead’s striking observation about the impossible standards women face - a truth that resonates as deeply today as when she first articulated it in ‘Male and Female’, her 1949 exploration of gender roles across cultures.

Margaret Mead wasn’t just an anthropologist poking around distant societies; she was a trailblazer who challenged the very foundations of how we think about gender. Growing up in a time when rigid binaries ruled both science and society, she dared to ask uncomfortable questions. What if the roles assigned to men and women aren’t carved into our biology but sculpted by culture? What if the expectations placed on women are less about nature and more about the stories societies tell themselves? Her work, often controversial, nudged open these doors, revealing the contradictions that trap women in a no-win scenario: praised or scolded for motherhood, for ambition, for wanting it all or for wanting something else entirely.

This quote captures that paradox with piercing clarity. It’s not just about motherhood; it’s about the broader cultural narrative that refuses to let women off the hook. Wanting to “have your cake and eat it too” is a phrase often tossed around, sometimes dismissively, to criticize women’s desires for both personal fulfillment and traditional roles. But Mead’s insight flips the phrase on its head, showing how society uses it as a weapon to shame women regardless of their choices.

Psychologically, this relentless ambivalence can be exhausting. It fosters a kind of double bind where women internalize conflicting messages, be nurturing but not too much, be independent but not selfish, be ambitious but not neglectful. The toll is subtle but profound: a persistent sense of inadequacy, a feeling that no matter what you do, you’ll be judged. In contemporary culture, this dynamic plays out in endless debates about “having it all,” viral social media moments where women confess their struggles with guilt and expectation, and the ongoing discourse about work-life balance.

Culturally, Mead’s work reminds us that these pressures are not universal truths but social constructs that vary widely across time and place. In some societies she studied, gender roles were far more fluid, and the rigid binaries we take for granted were absent or inverted. This perspective offers a hopeful counterpoint: if these roles are made, they can be unmade or remade. It’s a call to rethink the stories we tell about identity and worth.

Margaret Mead’s own life was marked by challenges to convention. As a woman in a male-dominated field, she faced skepticism and sometimes outright hostility. Yet she persisted, producing work that was both groundbreaking and accessible, influencing generations of thinkers and activists. Her willingness to embrace complexity and contradiction, rather than shy away from them, is what gives her words such enduring power.

In a world still wrestling with gender norms, her observation rings like an invitation to recognize the impossible standards placed on women, to question their origins, and to imagine a culture where desires and identities can coexist without judgment. It’s a reminder that the cake, whatever it represents, should never be a trap but a choice. And that perhaps the real work lies not in women trying to navigate contradictory expectations but in society learning to hold space for their full humanity.

*DAY 355: JAKOBU 1, 2, 3, 4, 5*

*Jakobu 1*
1 Jakọbu, ìránṣẹ́ Ọlọ́run àti ti Jesu Kristi Olúwa,

Sí àwọn ẹ̀yà méjìlá tí ó fọ́n káàkiri, orílẹ̀-èdè.

Àlàáfíà.

Àwọn ìṣòro àti àwọn ìdánwò
2 Ẹ̀yin ará mi, nígbà tí ẹ̀yin bá bọ́ sínú onírúurú ìdánwò, ẹ ka gbogbo rẹ̀ sí ayọ̀; 3 nítorí tí ẹ̀yin mọ̀ pé, ìdánwò ìgbàgbọ́ yín ń ṣiṣẹ́ sùúrù. 4 Ṣùgbọ́n ẹ jẹ́ kí sùúrù kí ó ṣiṣẹ́ àṣepé, kí ẹ̀yin kí ó lè jẹ́ pípé àti aláìlábùkù tí kò ṣe aláìní ohunkóhun. 5 Bí ó bá ku ọgbọ́n fún ẹnikẹ́ni, kí ó béèrè lọ́wọ́ Ọlọ́run ẹni tí fi fún gbogbo ènìyàn ní ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀, tí kì í sì ka àlébù sí; a ó sì fi fún un. 6 Ṣùgbọ́n nígbà tí òun bá béèrè ní ìgbàgbọ́, ní àìṣiyèméjì rárá. Nítorí ẹni tí ó ń sé iyèméjì dàbí ìgbì omi Òkun, tí à ń ti ọwọ́ afẹ́fẹ́ bì síwá bì sẹ́yìn, tí a sì ń rú u sókè. 7 Kí irú ènìyàn bẹ́ẹ̀ má ṣe rò pé, òun yóò rí ohunkóhun gbà lọ́wọ́ Olúwa; 8 Ó jẹ ènìyàn oníyèméjì aláìlèdúró ní ọ̀nà rẹ̀ gbogbo.

9 Ṣùgbọ́n jẹ́ kí arákùnrin tí ó ń ṣe onírẹ̀lẹ̀ máa ṣògo ní ipò gíga. 10 Àti ọlọ́rọ̀, ní ìrẹ̀sílẹ̀, nítorí bí ìtànná koríko ni yóò kọjá lọ. 11 Nítorí oòrùn là ti òun ti ooru gbígbóná yóò gbẹ́ koríko, ìtànná rẹ̀ sì rẹ̀ dànù, ẹwà ojú rẹ̀ sì parun: bẹ́ẹ̀ pẹ̀lú ni ọlọ́rọ̀ yóò ṣègbé ní ọ̀nà rẹ̀.

12 Ìbùkún ni fún ọkùnrin tí ó fi ọkàn rán ìdánwò; nítorí nígbà tí ó bá yege, yóò gba adé ìyè, tí Olúwa ti ṣèlérí fún àwọn tí ó fẹ́ ẹ.

13 Kí ẹnikẹ́ni tí a dánwò kí ó má ṣe wí pé, “Láti ọwọ́ Ọlọ́run ni a ti dán mi wò.” Nítorí a kò lè fi búburú dán Ọlọ́run wò, òun náà kì í sì í dán ẹnikẹ́ni wò; 14 Ṣùgbọ́n olúkúlùkù ni a ń dánwò nígbà tí a bá fi ọwọ́ ìfẹ́kúfẹ̀ẹ́ ara rẹ̀ fà á lọ tí a sì tàn án jẹ. 15 Ǹjẹ́, ìfẹ́kúfẹ̀ẹ́ nígbà tí ó bá lóyún a bí ẹ̀ṣẹ̀, àti ẹ̀ṣẹ̀ náà nígbà tí ó bá dàgbà tán, a bí ikú.

16 Kí a má ṣe tàn yín jẹ, ẹ̀yin ará mi olùfẹ́. 17 Gbogbo ẹ̀bùn rere àti gbogbo ẹ̀bùn pípé láti òkè ni ó ti wá, ó sì sọ̀kalẹ̀ láti ọ̀dọ̀ baba ìmọ́lẹ̀ wá, lọ́dọ̀ ẹni tí kò lè yípadà gẹ́gẹ́ bí òjìji àyídà. 18 Ó pinnu láti fi ọ̀rọ̀ òtítọ́ bí wa kí àwa kí ó le jẹ́ àkọ́so nínú ohun gbogbo tí ó dá.

Gbígbọ́ àti ṣíṣe ọrọ̀ náà
19 Kí ẹ mọ èyí, ẹ̀yin ará mi olùfẹ́; jẹ́ kí olúkúlùkù ènìyàn kí ó máa yára láti gbọ́, kí ó lọ́ra láti fọhùn, kí ó si lọ́ra láti bínú; 20 Nítorí ìbínú ènìyàn kì í ṣiṣẹ́ òdodo irú èyí tí Ọlọ́run ń fẹ́. 21 Nítorí náà, ẹ lépa láti borí gbogbo èérí àti ìwà búburú tí ó gbilẹ̀ yíká, kí ẹ sì fi ọkàn tútù gba ọ̀rọ̀ náà tí a gbìn, tí ó lè gba ọkàn yín là.

22 Ẹ má kan jẹ́ olùgbọ́ ọ̀rọ̀ náà lásán, kí ẹ má ba à ti ipa èyí tan ara yín jẹ́. Ẹ ṣe ohun tí ó sọ. 23 Nítorí bí ẹnikẹ́ni bá jẹ́ olùgbọ́ ọ̀rọ̀ náà tí kò sì jẹ́ olùṣe, òun dàbí ọkùnrin tí ó ń ṣàkíyèsí ojú ara rẹ̀ nínú dígí 24 Nítorí, lẹ́yìn tí ó bá ti ṣàkíyèsí ara rẹ̀, tí ó sì bá tirẹ̀ lọ, lójúkan náà òun sì gbàgbé bí òun ti rí. 25 Ṣùgbọ́n ẹni tí ó bá ń wo inú òfin pípé, òfin òmìnira ni, tí ó sì dúró nínú rẹ̀, tí òun kò sì jẹ́ olùgbọ́ tí ń gbàgbé bí kò ṣe olùṣe rẹ̀, òun yóò jẹ́ alábùkún nínú iṣẹ́ rẹ̀.

26 Bí ẹnikẹ́ni bá rò pé òun ń sin Ọlọ́run nígbà tí kò kó ahọ́n rẹ̀ ní ìjánu, ó ń tan ọkàn ara rẹ̀ jẹ, ìsìn rẹ̀ sì jẹ́ asán. 27 Ìsìn mímọ́ àti aláìléèérí níwájú Ọlọ́run àti baba ni èyí, láti máa bojútó àwọn aláìní baba àti àwọn opó nínú ìpọ́njú wọn, àti láti pa ara rẹ̀ mọ́ láìlábàwọ́n kúrò nínú ayé.

*Jakobu 2*
1 Ẹ̀yin ará mi, gẹ́gẹ́ bí onígbàgbọ́ nínú ògo Olúwa wá Jesu Kristi, ẹ máa ṣe ojúsàájú ẹnikẹ́ni. 2 Nítorí bí ọkùnrin kan bá wá sí ìpéjọpọ̀ yín, pẹ̀lú òrùka wúrà àti aṣọ dáradára, tí tálákà kan sì wá pẹ̀lú nínú aṣọ èérí; 3 tí ẹ̀yin sì bu ọlá fún ẹni tí ó wọ aṣọ dáradára tí ẹ sì wí pé, “Ìwọ jókòó níhìn-ín yìí ní ibi dáradára” tí ẹ sì wí fún tálákà náà pé, “Ìwọ dúró níbẹ̀” tàbí “jókòó níhìn-ín lábẹ́ àpótí ìtìsẹ̀ mi,” 4 ẹyin kò ha ń dá ara yín sí méjì nínú ara yín, ẹ̀yin kò sì di onídàájọ́ tí ó ní èrò búburú bí?

5 Ẹ fi etí sílẹ̀, ẹ̀yin ará mi olùfẹ́: Ọlọ́run kò ha ti yan àwọn tálákà ayé yìí láti jẹ́ ọlọ́rọ̀ nínú ìgbàgbọ́, àti ajogún ìjọba náà, tí ó ti ṣe ìlérí fún àwọn tí ó fẹ́ ẹ? 6 Ṣùgbọ́n ẹ̀yin ti bu tálákà kù. Àwọn ọlọ́rọ̀ kò ha ń pọ́n yin lójú bí; wọn kò ha sì ń wọ́ yín lọ sílé ẹjọ́? 7 Wọn kò ha ń sọ ọ̀rọ̀-òdì sí orúkọ rere nì tí a fi ń pè yín bí?

8 Ṣùgbọ́n bí ẹ̀yin bá ń mú olú òfin nì ṣẹ gẹ́gẹ́ bí Ìwé mímọ́, èyí tí ó wí pé, “Ìwọ fẹ́ ẹni kejì rẹ gẹ́gẹ́ bí ara rẹ,” ẹ̀yin ń ṣe dáradára. 9 Ṣùgbọ́n bí ẹ̀yin bá ń ṣe ojúsàájú ènìyàn, ẹ̀yin ń dẹ́ṣẹ̀, a sì ń dá yín lẹ́bi nípa òfin bí arúfin. 10 Nítorí ẹnikẹ́ni tí ó bá pa gbogbo òfin mọ́, tí ó sì rú ọ̀kan, ó jẹ̀bi rírú gbogbo rẹ̀. 11 Nítorí ẹni tí ó wí pé, “Ìwọ kò gbọdọ̀ ṣe panṣágà,” òun ni ó sì wí pé, “Ìwọ kò gbọdọ̀ pànìyàn.” Ǹjẹ́ bí ìwọ kò ṣe panṣágà, ṣùgbọ́n tí ìwọ pànìyàn, ìwọ jásí arúfin.

12 Ẹ máa sọ̀rọ̀, ẹ sì máa hùwà, bí àwọn tí a ó fi òfin òmìnira dá lẹ́jọ́. 13 Nítorí ẹni tí kò ṣàánú, ni a ó ṣe ìdájọ́ fún láìsí àánú; àánú ń ṣògo lórí ìdájọ́.

Ìgbàgbọ́ àti àwọn iṣẹ́
14 Èrè kí ni ó jẹ́, ará mi, bí ẹni kan wí pé òun ní ìgbàgbọ́, ṣùgbọ́n tí kò ní àwọn iṣẹ́ láti fihan? Ìgbàgbọ́ náà lè gbà á là bí? 15 Bí arákùnrin tàbí arábìnrin kan bá wà ní àìní aṣọ, tí ó sì ṣe àìní oúnjẹ òòjọ́, 16 Tí ẹni kan nínú yín sì wí fún pé, “Máa lọ ní àlàáfíà, kí ara rẹ kí ó má ṣe tutù, kí ó sì yó,” ṣùgbọ́n ẹ kò fi nǹkan wọ̀n-ọn-nì ti ara ń fẹ́ fún wọn; èrè kí ni ó jẹ́? 17 Bẹ́ẹ̀ sì ni ìgbàgbọ́, bí kò bá ní iṣẹ́ rere, ó kú nínú ara rẹ̀.

18 Ṣùgbọ́n ẹnìkan lè wí pé, “Ìwọ ní ìgbàgbọ́, èmi sì ní iṣẹ́:”

Fi ìgbàgbọ́ rẹ hàn mí ní àìsí iṣẹ́, èmi ó sì fi ìgbàgbọ́ mi hàn ọ́ nípa iṣẹ́ rere mi. 19 Ìwọ gbàgbọ́ pé Ọlọ́run kan ní ó ń bẹ; ó dára! Àwọn ẹ̀mí èṣù pẹ̀lú gbàgbọ́ bẹ́ẹ̀, wọ́n sì wárìrì.

20 Ṣùgbọ́n, ìwọ aláìmòye ènìyàn, ìwọ ha fẹ́ ní ìdánilójú pé, ìgbàgbọ́ ní àìsí iṣẹ́ rere asán ni? 21 Kí ha í ṣe nípa iṣẹ́ ni a dá Abrahamu baba wa láre, nígbà tí ó fi Isaaki ọmọ rẹ̀ rú ẹbọ lórí pẹpẹ? 22 Ìwọ rí i pé ìgbàgbọ́ rẹ bá iṣẹ́ rìn, àti pé nípa iṣẹ́ rere ni a sọ ìgbàgbọ́ di pípé. 23 Ìwé Mímọ́ sì ṣẹ́ tí ó wí pé, “Abrahamu gba Ọlọ́run gbọ́, a sì kà á sí òdodo fún un,” a sì pè é ní ọ̀rẹ́ Ọlọ́run. 24 Ǹjẹ́ ẹ̀yin rí i pé nípa iṣẹ́ rere ni à ń dá ènìyàn láre, kì í ṣe nípa ìgbàgbọ́ nìkan.

25 Gẹ́gẹ́ bẹ́ẹ̀ pẹ̀lú kí a dá Rahabu panṣágà láre nípa iṣẹ́ bí, nígbà tí ó gba àwọn ayọ́lẹ̀wò, tí ó sì rán wọn jáde gba ọ̀nà mìíràn? 26 Nítorí bí ara ní àìsí ẹ̀mí ti jẹ́ òkú, bẹ́ẹ̀ gẹ́gẹ́ pẹ̀lú ni ìgbàgbọ́ ní àìsí iṣẹ́ jẹ́ òkú.

*Jakobu 3*
1 Ẹ̀yin ará mi, ẹ má ṣe jẹ́ kí púpọ̀ nínú yín jẹ́ olùkọ́, kí ẹ̀yin kí ó mọ̀ pé àwa ni yóò jẹ̀bi jù. 2 Nítorí nínú ohun púpọ̀ ni gbogbo wa ń ṣe àṣìṣe. Bí ẹnìkan kò bá ṣì ṣe nínú ọ̀rọ̀, òun náà ni ẹni pípé, òun ni ó sì le kó gbogbo ara ní ìjánu.

3 Bí a bá sì fi ìjánu bọ ẹṣin lẹ́nu, kí wọn kí ó le gbọ́ tiwa, gbogbo ara wọn ni àwa sì ń tì kiri pẹ̀lú. 4 Kíyèsi i, àwọn ọkọ̀ ojú omi pẹ̀lú, bí wọ́n ti tóbi tó nì, tí a sì ń ti ọwọ́ ẹ̀fúùfù líle gbá kiri, ìtọ́kọ̀ kékeré ni a fi ń darí wọn kiri, síbikíbi tí ó bá wu ẹni tí ó ń tọ́ ọkọ̀. 5 Bẹ́ẹ̀ pẹ̀lú ni ahọ́n jẹ́ ẹ̀yà kékeré, ó sì ń fọhùn ohùn ńlá. Wo igi ńlá tí iná kékeré ń sun jóná! 6 Iná sì ni ahọ́n, ayé ẹ̀ṣẹ̀ sì ni: ní àárín àwọn ẹ̀yà ara wa, ní ahọ́n ti ń bá gbogbo ara jẹ́, tí yóò sì ti iná bọ ipa ayé wa; ọ̀run àpáàdì a sì tiná bọ òun náà.

7 Nítorí olúkúlùkù ẹ̀dá ẹranko, àti ti ẹyẹ, àti ti ejò, àti ti ohun tí ó ń bẹ ní Òkun, ni à ń tù lójú, tí a sì ti tù lójú láti ọwọ́ ẹ̀dá ènìyàn wá. 8 Ṣùgbọ́n ahọ́n ni ẹnikẹ́ni kò le tù lójú; ohun búburú aláìgbọ́ràn ni, ó kún fún oró ikú tí í pa ni.

9 Òun ni àwa fi ń yin Olúwa àti Baba, òun ni a sì fi ń bú ènìyàn tí a dá ní àwòrán Ọlọ́run. 10 Láti ẹnu kan náà ni ìyìn àti èébú ti ń jáde. Ẹ̀yin ará mi, nǹkan wọ̀nyí kò yẹ kí ó rí bẹ́ẹ̀. 11 Orísun odò kan a ha máa sun omi dídára àti omi iyọ̀ jáde láti orísun kan náà bí? 12 Ẹ̀yin ará mi, igi ọ̀pọ̀tọ́ ha le so èso olifi bí? Tàbí àjàrà ha lè so èso ọ̀pọ̀tọ́? Bẹ́ẹ̀ ni orísun kan kò le sun omíró àti omi tútù.

Oríṣìí ọgbọ́n méjì
13 Ta ni ó gbọ́n tí ó sì ní ìmọ̀ nínú yín? Ẹ jẹ́ kí ó fi iṣẹ́ rẹ̀ hàn nípa ìwà rere, nípa ìwà tútù ti ọgbọ́n. 14 Ṣùgbọ́n bí ẹ̀yin bá ní owú kíkorò àti ìjà ní ọkàn yín, ẹ má ṣe ṣe féfé, ẹ má sì ṣèké sí òtítọ́. 15 Ọgbọ́n yìí kì í ṣe èyí tí ó ti ọ̀dọ̀ Ọlọ́run wá, ṣùgbọ́n ti ayé ni, ti ara ni, ti ẹ̀mí èṣù ni. 16 Nítorí níbi tí owú òun ìjà bá gbé wà, níbẹ̀ ni rúdurùdu àti iṣẹ́ búburú gbogbo wà.

17 Ṣùgbọ́n ọgbọ́n tí ó ti òkè wá jẹ́ mímọ́ ní àkọ́kọ́, ti àlàáfíà, àti ti ìrẹ̀lẹ̀, kì í sì í ṣòro láti bẹ̀, ó kún fún àánú àti fún èso rere, kì í ṣe ojúsàájú, a sì máa sọ òtítọ́. 18 Àwọn tí ó ń ṣiṣẹ́ àlàáfíà a sì máa gbin èso àlàáfíà ní àlàáfíà.

*Jakobu 4*
1 Níbo ni ogun ti wá, níbo ni ìjà sì ti wá láàrín yín? Ìfẹ́kúfẹ̀ẹ́ ara yín ha kọ́ ni tí ó ń jagun nínú àwọn ẹ̀yà ara yín bí? 2 Ẹ̀yin ń fẹ́ ìfẹ́kúfẹ̀ẹ́, ẹ kò sì ní: ẹ̀yin ń pànìyàn, ẹ sì ń ṣe ìlara, ẹ kò sì le ní: ẹ̀yin ń jà, ẹ̀yin sì ń jagun; ẹ kò ní, nítorí tí ẹ̀yin kò béèrè. 3 Ẹ̀yin béèrè, ẹ kò sì rí gbà, nítorí tí ẹ̀yin ṣì béèrè, kí ẹ̀yin kí ó lè lò ó fún ìfẹ́kúfẹ̀ẹ́ ara yín.

4 Ẹ̀yin panṣágà ọkùnrin, àti panṣágà obìnrin, ẹ kò mọ̀ pé ìbárẹ́ ayé ìṣọ̀tá Ọlọ́run ni? Nítorí náà ẹni tí ó bá fẹ́ láti jẹ́ ọ̀rẹ́ ayé di ọ̀tá Ọlọ́run. 5 Ẹ̀yin ṣe bí Ìwé mímọ́ sọ lásán pé, Ẹ̀mí tí ó fi sínú wa ń jowú gidigidi lórí wa? 6 Ṣùgbọ́n ó fún ni ní oore-ọ̀fẹ́ sí i. Nítorí náà ni ìwé mímọ́ ṣe wí pé,

“Ọlọ́run kọ ojú ìjà sí àwọn agbéraga,
    ṣùgbọ́n ó fi oore-ọ̀fẹ́ fún àwọn onírẹ̀lẹ̀ ọkàn.”

7 Nítorí náà, ẹ tẹríba fún Ọlọ́run. Ẹ kọ ojú ìjà sí èṣù, òun ó sì sá kúrò lọ́dọ̀ yín. 8 Ẹ súnmọ́ Ọlọ́run, òun ó sì súnmọ́ yín. Ẹ wẹ ọwọ́ yín mọ́, ẹ̀yin ẹlẹ́ṣẹ̀; ẹ sì ṣe ọkàn yín ní mímọ́, ẹ̀yin oníyèméjì. 9 Ẹ banújẹ́, ẹ ṣọ̀fọ̀, kí ẹ sì hu fún ẹkún. Ẹ jẹ́ kí ẹ̀rín yín kí ó di ọ̀fọ̀, àti ayọ̀ yín kí ó di ìbànújẹ́. 10 Ẹ rẹ ara yín sílẹ̀ níwájú Olúwa, òun ó sì gbé yín ga.

11 Ará, ẹ má ṣe sọ̀rọ̀ ibi sí ara yín. Ẹni tí ó bá ń sọ̀rọ̀ ibi sí arákùnrin rẹ̀, tí ó ń dá arákùnrin rẹ̀ lẹ́jọ́, ó ń sọ̀rọ̀ ibi sí òfin, ó sì ń dá òfin lẹ́jọ́; ṣùgbọ́n bí ìwọ bá ń dá òfin lẹ́jọ́, ìwọ kì í ṣe olùfẹ́ òfin, bí kò ṣe onídàájọ́. 12 Aṣòfin àti onídàájọ́ kan ṣoṣo ní ó ń bẹ, àní ẹni tí ó lè gbàlà tí ó sì le parun, ṣùgbọ́n ta ni ìwọ tí ó ń dá ẹnìkejì rẹ lẹ́jọ́?

Má ṣe ìlérí nípa ọjọ́ ọ̀la

One thing I notice repeatedly while listening to Omar Suleiman’s The Firsts series, which traces the lives of Muslims during the Prophet’s lifetime and shortly after his death, is how ordinary divorce was in the early Muslim community, and how no  shame was attached to it. Marriage existed. Divorce existed. They were treated as normal life processes. People married, separated, remarried and moved on. There were provisions for women, systems that protected the vulnerable, and social structures that made starting over possible. Remarriage was not treated as a moral downgrade. Divorce did not erase a woman’s dignity or value; it simply meant a marriage had ended. And these were people better than us in every way.

Early Islam clearly treated marriage and divorce as life processes, not moral failures. The Qur’an speaks about divorce calmly and procedurally, not emotionally or punitively. There is no language of disgrace, no spiritual branding, no social suspicion attached to women who leave marriages. Instead, the emphasis is on fairness, waiting periods, maintenance, and dignity. The Prophet himself married widows and divorcees. Women initiated divorce. Men divorced and remarried. Life continued. The system anticipated marital breakdown and built ethical structures around it, rather than pretending it would never happen.

So where did the shame come from? Because it is clearly not Qur’anic. It is not rooted in early Islamic practice. The moral panic around divorce, the suspicion of divorced women, the idea that a woman must endure at all costs to remain “honourable”—all of this feels like a later import.

I cannot ignore the role Western conservatism, heavily shaped by Christian permanence theology and Victorian morality, played in this shift, especially in societies that experienced colonial rule, like Nigeria. Christian conservatism carries a different moral framework around marriage. Marriage is treated as near-sacramental, divorce as failure, and women as custodians of marital morality. When colonialism arrived, it did not only bring political domination, it brought moral hierarchies. Indigenous and Islamic approaches to marriage which are more flexible, more process-oriented were framed as backward or unstable, while Christian marital permanence was packaged as civilization and progress. Over time, these values seeped into education systems, legal structures and social respectability politics, including within Muslim communities themselves.

While the same time, disrupting and  dismantling the very systems that once made divorce survivable for women. Early Islamic societies functioned with zakat structures, communal responsibility and enforceable rights. Divorce did not mean economic or social death. But when those systems collapsed and were not rebuilt, provision was replaced with moral control. Instead of safety nets, shame became the deterrent. Divorce was no longer just a legal process, it became a moral stain and leaving  became socially dangerous.

This is why divorce is perceived so differently in Northern Nigeria compared to the South-West. In much of the North, there is little stigma attached to divorce and remarriage. Islamic law and norms retained more structural influence there, with less penetration of Christian moralization. Divorce exists. Remarriage is expected. Women are not automatically treated as socially ruined.

The contrast becomes even clearer when I think about Yoruba culture. My great-grandmother once told me about co-wives who left their husbands simply because they all went broke and they feared they  would not be able to support them during their fathers’ burials. Historically, Yoruba women divorced. They returned to their fathers’ houses, leaned on trade networks, remarried, and continued life without carrying permanent social shame. 

Egyptian women used to divorce their husbands when they can’t provide for them anymore or very well. Mauritanian divorcees are hot cakes.
Some women had one or two ex-husbands. Marriage was social, not sacramental. A woman’s worth was not tethered to staying married at all costs. It was Western conservatism, fused with Christian moral frameworks, not indigenous culture, that introduced the idea of marital permanence as moral superiority and divorce as spiritual or social failure.

That shame is not native.

What we are left with now is a confused moral inheritance. Islamic legal frameworks stripped of their emotional neutrality, fused with Christian shame ethics, and enforced in societies where the original systems of care no longer exist. So we end up with Muslims shaming divorced women, and women staying in abusive marriages out of fear, stigma and poverty. 
And endurance, as taught in the Qur’an and across cultures, as part of the recipe of a healthy marriage became even more moralized into something toxic, especially for women. They are told to endure the worst because endurance itself has become a badge of honour. Divorce is treated as dirty, strange or evil, yet no alternative structures are offered to support those who leave.

This is not early Islam. It is not indigenous African culture either.

It is colonial moral residue and it continues to shape how we judge women’s lives, marriages and choices.

Empirical experience demonstrates that even wealthy powerful empowered and highly vocal women are not immune to TFGBV.

TFGBV operates as a tool of silencing control and intimidation that undermines women’s autonomy participation and access to justice across all strata of society. 

Privilege may shape the form of response available but it does not guarantee protection from harm. 

The digital environment therefore exposes systemic gaps in legal safeguards and institutional preparedness that affect all women albeit in differentiated ways.

Addressing this challenge necessitates the development of robust prevention mechanisms effective and enforceable legal frameworks and sustained inter institutional coordination.

She married eight men, ran businesses across four cities, was arrested multiple times—and built an empire in the only economy that would let a woman control her own money in the 1880s.
Her name was Lizzie Lape. And in Victorian America, where women couldn't vote, couldn't own property in many states, and couldn't even control their own wages if they were married, Lizzie found the one industry where women could own, operate, and profit: sex work.
Born Elizabeth Rogers in Kentucky in 1853, Lizzie grew up during a time when a woman's options were brutally limited. You married well, or you worked in domestic service, or you starved. That was basically it.
Lizzie left Kentucky for Chicago as a teenager. We don't know exactly why—family trouble, poverty, opportunity, escape—history doesn't record those details. But we know what she did when she got there: she set up shop in Chicago's red light district.
She wasn't working the streets. She was running the operation.
At a time when most women couldn't even open a bank account without a husband's permission, Lizzie was managing money, employees, security, and clients. She was, in modern terms, a businesswoman—just in the only business where Victorian society would tolerate female ownership.
In Chicago, she met Jeremiah Lape. They married and moved to Ohio, settling in Plain City, where they had a son, Henry Arville Lape. For a moment, it might have looked like Lizzie was going to live a conventional life—marriage, motherhood, respectability.
It didn't last.
They divorced. And Lizzie went back to what she knew: running establishments.
Her second husband was the manager of a Junction House in Lima, Ohio. He was also a thief. While Lizzie wore stolen silk dresses and jewelry—enjoying the spoils of his crimes—she also paid the price when he got caught. She was arrested and incarcerated as an accomplice.
Think about that. Victorian society would jail a woman for wearing stolen dresses but wouldn't give her the legal right to refuse her husband or control her own earnings. The hypocrisy was built into the system.
After her release, Lizzie left Lima and her second husband. She headed to Marion, Ohio, where she did something remarkable: she bought property.
She purchased a saloon called the White Pigeon and a building known as "The Red House." Both establishments offered liquor, food, gambling, and sex work—full-service entertainment venues that catered to men's desires while putting money directly into Lizzie's pocket.
This wasn't desperation. This was strategy.
Prostitution was illegal, morally condemned, and socially reviled. But it was also wildly profitable—one of the few ways a woman could accumulate significant wealth in the 19th century. Lizzie wasn't just surviving. She was building an empire.
In 1889, the law caught up with her. Lizzie was arrested for "keeping houses of ill repute" and sentenced to sixty days in a workhouse. Newspapers covered the scandal extensively, using language designed to titillate their readers—painting Lizzie as a scandalous, lascivious woman corrupting decent society.
What the newspapers didn't mention: the men who frequented her establishments—the politicians, businessmen, respectable married men—faced no consequences whatsoever.
After her release, there was more trouble. Her first husband, Jeremiah Lape, sued her for child support. Even though she'd been divorced, incarcerated, publicly shamed, and repeatedly arrested, she was still legally responsible for supporting the child from her first marriage.
She paid. And then she moved to Akron.
There, Lizzie opened The Halfway House—a prosperous establishment that was, once again, part saloon, part gambling den, part brothel. By now, she'd perfected the model. She knew how to manage staff, handle law enforcement, navigate legal gray areas, and keep the money flowing.
And somewhere in all of this, she married six more times.
The full list of surnames she collected reads like a historical telephone book: Rogers-Lape-Huffman-Larzelere-DeWitt-Veon-Shetler-France.
Eight husbands. At least six brothels. Multiple arrests. Decades of building businesses, losing them, rebuilding them. A son she supported despite imprisonment and social ostracism. A life lived entirely outside the boundaries Victorian society set for women—and yet, paradoxically, within the only economic system that allowed her independence.
Here's what makes Lizzie's story so complex:
She wasn't a victim. She wasn't a villain. She was a businesswoman operating in an economy that exploited women while simultaneously giving certain women—those willing to work in the sex trade—unusual economic power.
Victorian prostitution was brutal. Women faced violence, disease, legal persecution, and social stigma. Many were coerced, trafficked, or driven by desperate poverty. Lizzie's story doesn't erase that reality.
But Lizzie wasn't just surviving. She was an entrepreneur. She owned property. She hired employees. She managed multiple establishments across different cities. She supported her child. She married repeatedly—possibly for love, possibly for business advantage, possibly because marriage offered legal protections or social cover she needed.
She was doing what women in legitimate businesses couldn't do: controlling her own money, making her own decisions, and building wealth without male permission.
The newspapers that covered her life painted her as scandalous, immoral, lascivious. They sold papers by condemning her. But those same newspapers never questioned why respectable society offered women like Lizzie so few legitimate options. Never asked why a woman with obvious business acumen, management skills, and entrepreneurial drive had to operate brothels because no bank would give her a loan, no business would hire her, and no legitimate industry would let her own property.
Lizzie didn't choose sex work because she was immoral. She chose it because it was one of the only ways a woman in the 1880s could be her own boss.
She lived into the 20th century—witnessing women finally win the right to vote in 1920, though she'd been running businesses and controlling money for forty years by then. She saw the world slowly, grudgingly, start giving women the legal rights she'd had to seize through illegal means.
After her death, her story was largely forgotten—except by her descendants.
In 2010, Lizzie's great-great-granddaughter, author Kris Radish, published "Looking for Lizzie: Searching for the True Story of Elizabeth Jane Rogers Lape and Her Sporting Life Legacy." Radish spent years researching newspaper archives, court records, and family stories, trying to piece together who Lizzie really was beneath the scandalous headlines.
What she found was a woman far more complex than history remembered. Not a saint. Not a simple victim. Not a one-dimensional "madam." But a business owner, a mother, a survivor, and an entrepreneur who built multiple successful enterprises in an era when women were legally and socially powerless.
Lizzie's story doesn't fit neatly into our modern narratives about empowerment or exploitation. It's messy, morally complex, and deeply tied to the brutal realities of 19th-century gender economics.
But here's what's undeniable:
Lizzie Lape owned property when most women couldn't. She ran businesses when most women couldn't. She controlled her own money when most women couldn't. She supported her child when she was supposed to be powerless.
She did all of this by operating outside the law, outside respectability, outside the boundaries Victorian society set for women. And she paid the price—arrests, imprisonment, public condemnation, moral judgment that followed her through eight marriages and six cities.
But she kept going. She kept building. She kept opening new establishments, hiring new staff, serving new clients, making new money.
Because the alternative—obedience, dependence, powerlessness—was worse than scandal.
Victorian society offered women two choices: be controlled by men or be condemned by everyone. Lizzie chose condemnation and freedom over respectability and powerlessness.
That doesn't make her a hero. It doesn't make her a villain. It makes her someone who survived and thrived in a system designed to prevent her from doing either.
In honor of Lizzie Rogers-Lape-Huffman-Larzelere-DeWitt-Veon-Shetler-France (1853-?), who collected eight surnames, ran at least six businesses, was arrested multiple times, and built an economic empire in the only industry that would let a 19th-century woman be her own boss.
History called her immoral. She called herself a businesswoman.
Both were probably right.

Sejak hari itu, rumah Ustadz Maulana tak pernah benar-benar sama.
Bukan karena sepi suara—
melainkan karena satu suara yang paling ia rindukan, tak akan pernah kembali.
Istrinya tercinta, Nur Aliah, telah lebih dulu pulang.
Meninggalkan cinta yang tak sempat menua.
Meninggalkan luka yang tak pernah benar-benar sembuh.
Banyak yang menyangka, waktu akan mengobati segalanya.
Tapi bagi Ustadz Maulana, waktu justru memperdalam rindu.
Sebagai seorang laki-laki, ia paham betul fitrah dan ujian.
Ia tahu nasihat Nabi ﷺ:
“Wahai para pemuda, barang siapa belum mampu menikah, maka berpuasalah.”
Maka ia memilih puasa.
Bukan puasa biasa.
Ia menjalani puasa sunnah setiap hari—
menahan lapar, dahaga, dan gejolak jiwa,
kecuali di hari-hari yang memang dilarang.
Bukan untuk pamer kesalehan.
Bukan untuk mencari simpati.
Puasa itu adalah pelukan sunyi untuk hatinya sendiri.
Setiap fajar, saat ia menahan makan dan minum,
ia juga menahan rindu.
Setiap magrib, saat ia berbuka,
ia menelan air mata yang jatuh diam-diam.
Puasa itu menjadi caranya menjaga diri.
Menjaga kesetiaan.
Menjaga cinta—
meski orang yang dicintai telah tiada.
Anak-anaknya pernah berkata pelan,
“Abi menikah lagi saja…”
Ia tersenyum.
Bukan karena tak ingin,
melainkan karena hatinya masih penuh.
Dan perlahan, anak-anak itu mengerti.
Bahwa ayah mereka bukan menolak bahagia—
ia hanya belum selesai mencintai.
Puasa itu bukan sekadar menahan lapar.
Ia menahan kenangan.
Ia menahan keinginan.
Ia menahan diri agar cintanya tetap bersih,
tetap utuh,
tetap setia—
bahkan setelah maut memisahkan.
Karena bagi sebagian orang,
cinta tidak berhenti saat pasangan pergi.
Ia justru berubah menjadi ibadah.
Menjadi doa panjang.
Menjadi puasa yang tak pernah lelah.
Dan di setiap sujudnya,
Ustadz Maulana hanya berbisik lirih:
“Ya Allah…
jika Engkau pisahkan kami di dunia,
maka jangan pisahkan kami di akhirat.”

She was divorced, a single mother, and running for president. The world had never elected a woman as head of state. Then Iceland changed everything.

When Vigdís Finnbogadóttir announced her candidacy for President of Iceland, political observers were skeptical. Not just because she was a woman—though that was revolutionary enough—but because she represented everything that was supposed to disqualify someone from leadership.
She was divorced in an era when divorce still carried stigma. She was a single mother in a world that questioned whether women could balance family and leadership. She had no traditional political background—she was a theater director and French teacher, not a career politician.
According to conventional wisdom, she had no chance.
Iceland thought differently.
On June 29, 1980, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir became the first woman in world history to be democratically elected as a head of state.
Not appointed. Not inheriting the position. Elected.
By the people. Through democratic vote.
Yes, other women had held presidential titles before—Argentina's Isabel Perón, for instance. But Perón had assumed office after her husband's death, through succession rather than election.
Vigdís was different. The Icelandic people looked at all the candidates and chose her.
It was a statement heard around the world: women could lead nations. Voters would choose them. Democracy could elect them.
Her election alone would have been historic. What she did with the presidency became legendary.
Vigdís understood that as Iceland's head of state, she represented not just a government but a culture. A language. An identity.
Iceland is a small nation—fewer than 250,000 people in 1980. Its language, Icelandic, was spoken almost nowhere else on Earth. Its cultural traditions were unique, ancient, and vulnerable to being overwhelmed by larger global cultures.
Vigdís became Iceland's cultural champion.
She traveled the world as an ambassador for Icelandic language, literature, and arts. She emphasized education, cultural preservation, and Iceland's unique heritage. She made Icelanders proud of their identity while making the world aware of Iceland's contributions.
Her presidency transformed how Iceland saw itself and how the world saw Iceland.
But here's what really proved her effectiveness: the Icelandic people kept choosing her.
In 1984, Vigdís ran for re-election. She won with over 94% of the vote.
In 1988, she ran again. No one bothered to oppose her. She was re-elected unopposed.
In 1992, same story. Unopposed. Re-elected.
Think about that: in a functioning democracy, politicians from across the political spectrum looked at her presidency and collectively decided "Yeah, she's doing great. No point running against her."
Vigdís served 16 years as president—from 1980 to 1996—the longest tenure of any elected female head of state in world history. That record still stands.
Sixteen years of Icelandic voters saying: "We made the right choice. She represents us well. We trust her."
Her presidency wasn't just symbolically important. It was substantively successful.
Under her leadership, Iceland became a global model for gender equality. The nation that had elected the world's first female president continued pushing boundaries:

Iceland developed some of the world's strongest gender equality policies
Women's participation in government and business increased dramatically
The country consistently ranks at or near the top of global gender equality indices

Vigdís didn't just break the glass ceiling. She proved that once broken, women could govern effectively, earn public trust, and leave nations better than they found them.
When she stepped down in 1996 by choice—not due to electoral defeat, but because she decided 16 years was enough—Iceland had been transformed.
The divorced single mother who "couldn't possibly win" had become one of the most beloved leaders in Icelandic history.
Here's what Vigdís Finnbogadóttir's story teaches us:
The barriers we think are insurmountable often exist more in assumptions than reality.
Political establishment wisdom said a divorced single mother with no political background couldn't win the presidency. Iceland's voters disagreed.
Conventional thinking said being "first" was the achievement. Vigdís showed that the real achievement was governing so well that voters kept choosing her for 16 years.
Critics claimed her election was symbolic. She proved it was substantive—using her platform to preserve culture, promote equality, and represent her nation with distinction.
When Vigdís was asked about being the first woman democratically elected president, she didn't focus on her personal achievement. She focused on what it meant for everyone else:
"I didn't just win for myself. I won to show that it could be done."
And once it was done, it couldn't be undone.
After Vigdís, the idea that women couldn't be elected to lead nations became absurd. She'd proven otherwise—not through theoretical arguments but through 16 years of successful governance.
Today, dozens of countries have elected female leaders. That path started in 1980 on a small island nation in the North Atlantic.
With a divorced single mother who loved theater and French literature.
Who believed in her nation's culture.
Who ran for office when everyone said she couldn't win.
And who won. And won again. And again. And again.
Because the Icelandic people recognized something that the rest of the world was about to learn:
Leadership isn't about checking traditional boxes.
It's about vision, dedication, and earning your people's trust.
Vigdís Finnbogadóttir did that. For 16 years. And changed what the world thought was possible.
1980: The world had never democratically elected a woman president.
1996: Iceland had re-elected hers four times.
That's not just breaking barriers. That's proving they should never have existed in the first place.

The Wahhabi movement was established in the mid-eighteenth century by the Hanbali-trained religious figure Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703-1792). 

Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhab was impressed by the writings of Ibn Taymiyya (1263-1328). During his life, Ibn Taymiyya رحمه الله criticized many widespread beliefs and practices accepted by the religious scholars of his day. He claimed that these were repugnant later innovations which had developed after the time of the Salaf (or earliest Muslim generations).

He further argued that some of these beliefs and practices were shirk, or at least encouraged shirk. For instance, he criticized pilgrimage to the Prophet’s ﷺ grave, touching relics for baraka, and tawassul. For him, these were haram because they encouraged shirk, even if they were not shirk themselves. He also argued that istighatha was shirk. Views of this kind conflicted with the developed doctrine of the four legal schools (Hanafi, Shafii, Maliki, Hanbali). For the schools either endorsed these practices or tolerated them.

Shirk is, of course, the greatest sin in Islam. Under standard circumstances, the Muslim who commits shirk is subject to takfir, and declared a disbeliever. He then must be killed, either by court order or by being fought through jihad. The overwhelming majority of scholars in Ibn Taymiyya’s time rejected his unique fiqh opinions regarding shirk, which they saw as an attack on the four legal schools.

Nevertheless, Ibn Taymiyya took a conciliatory stance towards the religious scholars around him. He argued that knowledge had declined since the time of the Salaf, such that the scholars and laypersons of his age deserved to be excused for their ignorance (العذر بالجهل,  al-‘udhr bi-l-jahl). Thus, even if they committed shirk (e.g., istighatha), they were not to be takfired and fought. 

Ibn Taymiyya also respected scholarly ijtihad, even in matters of aqida. So when other scholars came to different opinions about what counts as shirk, Ibn Taymiyya did not oppose them with harshness. Rather he simply sought to convince them with proofs from the Quran and Sunna.

This all changed with Ibn Abd al-Wahhab, who enthusiastically adopted Ibn Taymiyya’s previously marginalized views on shirk. The Muslims of Ibn Abd al-Wahhab’s day followed the standard doctrine of the four legal schools. They engaged in practices that Ibn Taymiyya considered problematic for either being shirk or for encouraging shirk.

Yet Ibn Abd al-Wahhab would deviate from Ibn Taymiyya in two fundamental ways:

First, Ibn Taymiyya excused his contemporaries for their ignorance, even in matters of shirk. But Ibn Abd al-Wahhab did not do this. On the contrary, he takfired all those around him as polytheists or mushriks. He even argued that they had a lower religious status than the mushriks (مشركين, polytheists) who fought the Prophet ﷺ like Abu Jahl.

Second, unlike Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Abd al-Wahhab also rejected tolerance for scholarly differences in opinion. He harshly attacked all the scholars of his era for endorsing (what he deemed to be) shirk or for tolerating shirk. He further claimed that whoever disagreed with his views on shirk was a disbeliever. This followed from his principle, in his book نواقض الإسلام  Nawaqid al-Islam, that whoever does not takfir the person guilty of shirk becomes himself a kafir /disbeliever. 

In other words, all scholars are obliged to adopt Ibn Abd al-Wahhab’s views on shirk, and they are required to takfir those who engage in such shirk (e.g., istighatha). The scholars of Ibn Abd al-Wahhab’s day did not do this, so they became disbelievers (كفار, kuffar) to him.

Today many Muslims call themselves Salafi. The Salafi movement has been influenced by various figures like Ibn Hanbal, Ibn Taymiyya, and Ibn Abd al-Wahhab. However, Salafis are a diverse group. Those who stick closely to the views on Ibn Hanbal and Ibn Taymiyya cannot be called Wahhabis. However, those who stick closely to the views of Ibn Abd al-Wahhab can be called Wahhabis. A Wahhabi can be thought of a Salafi who is focused on mass takfir or blanket takfir.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb initiated a long-term partnership between his movement and the Saud dynasty (السعود, Āl Suʿūd). This became a marriage of politics and religion. 

Together they established an expanding state in the central Arabian region of Najd. The emerging Saudi state entered into a long-term conflict with the Ottoman empire (1299-1922). The Ottomans claimed to be a Caliphate responsible for protecting Sunnī Islam as codified in the four schools. They ruled Anatolia and much of the Arab world. Thus, they ruled most of the Arabian peninsula including the Hijaz, with the holy cities of Makka and Madina. Ibn Abd al-Wahhab claimed that the type of Islam embraced by the Ottomans was actually shirk. He takfired Ottoman government officials and laypersons. He also takfired scholars from all four legal schools, teaching at Ottoman centers of learning such as Makka, Madina, Cairo’s al-Azhar, and Istanbul’s Suleymaniye.

In response, virtually all scholars of Ibn Abd al-Wahhab’s day branded him a heretic. 

Many also accused him of being a Kharijite, for like the Kharijites he takfired all the Muslims around him and fought them in jihad.

Wahhabism was considered a heretical doctrine by Muslims across the world until the mid-twentieth century. 

At this point the Ottoman empire had collapsed after being defeated in World War I. Its holdings in the Hijaz had been absorbed by the Saudi state. The Saudi state had also just discovered oil, giving it unprecedented wealth. With these new resources the Saudi state began to propagate Wahhabism across the world. This process led to the gradual erasure of the older Islam associated with the four schools and the Ottoman empire.

The most important feature of Wahhabism is its focus on takfiring other Muslims.

The Saudi state has always used this feature of Wahhabism to advance its political ends. Thus, at the time of Ibn Abd al-Wahhab, they takfired the whole Ottoman empire. This justified jihad against the Ottomans, along with the taking of their lands and properties. 

During World War I, the Saudi state and the Wahhabi religious establishment allied with the British to help destroy the Ottoman empire. Wahhabis claimed that the Ottoman empire consisted in mushrik disbelievers with a lower status than British Christians. The same pattern itself has repeated itself throughout history.

During the first Gulf War (1990-1991), the Saudi state allied with the US to destroy Iraq. At the time various Wahhabi scholars like Ibn Baz issued fatwas justifying this alliance, takfiring Saddam and his government, and permitting US troops on Saudi soil.

Wahhabi scholars regularly mass takfir Shia Muslims. It is argued that just as traditional Sunnis are mushrik disbelievers, Shia are even worse mushrik disbelievers. This is used to justify the Saudi state’s alliance with Israel and the US against various Shia states and organizations like Iran and Hezbollah. For example, in 2006, there was a major conflict between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon. The leading Wahhabi scholar Ibn Jibrin issued a fatwa in favor of Israel, ordering all Muslims to refrain from supporting Hezbollah against Israel. The fatwa also stated that any Muslim who helps Hezbollah against Israel becomes a kafir. Wahhabi preferences for Jews over Shia are now being used to justify normalization with Israel and the Abraham Accords.

🌐 Unlocking the Future of Ethical Hacking with AI 🚀

In today’s complex digital landscape, security professionals constantly face unseen vulnerabilities and ever-evolving threats. The integration of machine learning and automation is transforming penetration testing, threat detection, and vulnerability management, offering unprecedented speed and precision. Here’s an analytical overview of how AI enhances ethical hacking and what it means for cybersecurity teams:

🧠 Adaptive Models Accelerate Testing  
Machine learning compresses hours of manual reconnaissance into minutes, enabling continuous monitoring and faster detection. These models identify anomalies, zero-day patterns, and misconfigurations that traditional tools often miss, reducing false positives and streamlining analyst workflows.  

🔍 Enhanced Reconnaissance and OSINT Capabilities  
Automated open-source intelligence gathers signals from social media, dark web forums, and web leaks, prioritizing high-risk targets with risk scoring. Entity resolution reduces noise and consolidates data points, enabling more targeted and efficient testing strategies.  

🛡️ Smarter System Mapping and Vulnerability Detection  
Parallel scanning across cloud, on-premises, and IoT environments accelerates asset discovery. Anomaly detection flags suspicious responses, uncovering hidden vulnerabilities and zero-day-like behaviors. Credential and authentication flow enumeration further sharpens focus on high-impact attack vectors.  

⚙️ AI-Driven Exploit Development and Workflow Optimization  
Automated fuzzing and natural language processing facilitate rapid vulnerability discovery and exploit mapping. Expert review remains critical, but AI proposes attack chains, speeds up payload generation, and refines attack paths with minimal human intervention, increasing overall efficiency.   

🤖 Ethical Social Engineering with AI  
Deepfake technology and synthesized voice simulations heighten social engineering risks. Advanced behavioral analytics and microexpression analysis help detect AI-generated phishing attempts and manipulated media, safeguarding human agents from sophisticated scams.  

📝 Continuous Testing, Reporting, and Risk Management  
Automated reporting tools convert findings into actionable insights, linking vulnerabilities to owners and mitigation steps. Feedback loops and model validation reduce false positives, improve detection accuracy, and support compliance with governance frameworks.  

⚠️ Governance, Risks, and Ethical Constraints  
Responsible AI deployment mandates strict scope, privacy considerations, and legal compliance. Regular model validation, bias audits, and adversarial testing are essential to prevent drift and misuse. Transparency and detailed documentation underpin trustworthy AI integration.  

🔧 Building Skills and Platforms for AI-Enabled Penetration Testing  
The right tools should offer explainable detection, integrability with existing workflows, and actionable evidence exports. Training should blend hands-on labs, red-team exercises, and continuous upskilling to develop robust, future-ready security professionals.  

✅ Summary Checklist  
- Machine learning speeds up and scales testing ✅  
- Automated OSINT and vulnerability scanning improve coverage 🔍  
- Anomaly detection surfaces zero-day and misconfigurations 🚩  
- AI-driven exploit tools accelerate discovery ⚡  
- Behavioral analytics detect AI-generated phishing and deepfakes 🕵️‍♂️  
- Continuous feedback reduces false positives 🧑‍💻  
- Strict governance and compliance safeguard responsible use ⚖️  
- Skilled teams integrate tools with strategic oversight 🧠  

Embracing AI responsibly empowers security teams to stay ahead in an ever-changing threat landscape. Focus on marrying technological advancement with ethical standards, governance, and human expertise for resilient cybersecurity defenses.

Sheekada Somaliland (Dhulka Soomaalida)

Sheekada Somaliland (Dhulka Soomaalida) waxay bilaabatay dabayaaqadii qarnigii 19-aad, xilligii gumaysiga Yurub uu kala qaybsaday Soomaalida weyn, isaga oo aan tixgelin taariikh, midnimo bulsho iyo juqraafi toona.

Waqooyiga, oo markii dambe loo bixiyay Somaliland, wuxuu galay gacanta Ingiriiska; koonfurta iyo bartamaha waxaa gumaystay Talyaaniga; halka woqooyiga ugu fog ee Soomaalida uu galay gacan Faransiis, kana noqday waxa maanta loo yaqaan Jabuuti. Sidoo kale, qaybo ka mid ah dhulka Soomaalida waxaa gumaystaha Ingiriisku ku daray Itoobiya iyo Kenya. Sidaas ayaa hal shacab loogu kala qaybiyay maamullo kala duwan, waxaana la beeray abuurkii kala-qaybsanaanta ka hor intii aysan dawladdu dhalan.

Soomaalidu kama aamusin arrintaas; waddanku wuxuu arkay halgan joogto ah oo lagaga soo horjeeday gumaysiga, oo ay hoggaaminayeen hoggaamiyeyaal, culimo iyo dhaqdhaqaaqyo waddani ah. Ugu dambayn, sanadkii 1960-kii, waqooyigu wuxuu qaatay xornimo, maalmo kadibna koonfurta, waxaana lagu dhawaaqay Jamhuuriyadda Soomaaliya.

Sanadihii hore, Soomaaliya waxay lahayd nidaam rayid ah, xisbiyo badan, iyo hay’ado dawli ah oo soo koraya. Balse 1969-kii, kadib afgambi militari, waddanku wuxuu galay marxalad xukun ciidan ah. Muddo kadib, dawladdu way daciiftay, khilaafaadkii gudaha way bateen, hay’adihii way burbureen, ilaa ay Soomaaliya si buuxda u burburtay 1991-kii, waddankuna galay firaaq siyaasadeed iyo dagaal sokeeye oo ba’an.

Burburkaas dhexdiisa, waqooyigu wuxuu ku dhawaaqay Somaliland, isaga oo dib u xusuustay xuduudihii gumaysigii Ingiriiska. Ku dhawaaqistaasi ma ahayn rabitaan kala-go’ fudud, balse waxay ahayd isku day badbaado iyo dhisid nidaam keena amni iyo xasillooni, xilli uu deegaanka ku hareeraysnaa fowdo.

In ka badan 30 sano, Somaliland waxay raadinaysay aqoonsi caalami ah, iyada oo ku doodaysa xasillooni, dhisidda hay’ado, iyo qabashada doorashooyin. Si kastaba ha ahaatee, beesha caalamku waxay ku adkaysatay midnimada Soomaaliya, waxayna diiday aqoonsi hal-dhinac ah.

Kadib 30 sano, waxaa soo baxay hadal ku saabsan aqoonsi ka imanaya hal dhinac oo keliya, kana yimid dowlad madaxweynaheeda laga raadinayo Maxkamadda Dambiyada Caalamiga ah. Aqoonsigaas, haddii uu dhaco, looma arko taageero masiiri ah, balse waxaa loo fasiranayaa tallaabo siyaasadeed oo lagu carqaladaynayo xasilloonida Geeska Afrika, laguna adeegsanayo nuglaanta gobolka si loo fuliyo dano shisheeye.

Sheekada Somaliland ma aha sheeko gooni-u-goosad fudud, balse waa muraayad ka tarjumaysa taariikh gumaysi, midnimo, iyo burbur. Xalka mustaqbalkeedu ma aha mid ka dhasha aqoonsiyo siyaasadeysan, balse waa inuu ka yimaadaa hannaan sharci ah oo caddaalad ku dhisan, kana ilaaliya karaamada shucuubta iyo xasilloonida gobolka.

Maanta, Somaliland guduheeda ayaa mushkilado ka jiraan; maamulka SSC ayaa ka goostay, Awdalna xaalad kacsan ayay wajahayso. Sidaas darteed, aqoonsi ka yimaada dal aan sharciyad buuxda haysan muxuu tarayaa?

Qof ka soo jeeda Somaliland si cad kuuma sheegi karo sabab macquul ah oo uu u rabo in uu Soomaaliya kaga go’o, taasina waa cilladda ugu weyn ee haysata mashruucaasi.

Gender-Based Violence (TFGBV)

TFGBV aka online violence, cyberviolence and digital violence, is “any act of gender-based violence against women that is committed, assisted or aggravated in part or fully by the use of information, communication technologies (ICT), such as mobile phones and smartphones, the Internet, social media platforms or email, against a woman because she is a woman, or affects women disproportionately

As more women and girls around the world have access to mobile phones and the Internet, more are exposed to violence perpetrated using this technology by a wide range of people - current and former partners, acquaintances and strangers

All forms of online gender-based violence are used to control and attack women and to maintain and reinforce patriarchal norms, roles and structures and an unequal power relationship. This is particularly evident when violence, threats and harassment follow speeches or expression related to gender equality and feminism, or where defenders of women’s rights are targeted for their work

The motivations behind perpetration of acts of TFGBV  include seeking to humiliate, intimidate or cause fear, retribution, embarrass, coerce, control and/or exploit. Online violence is also used to silence and undermine women’s and girl’s voices and rights, and their participation in public forums, debates and discussions 

All women with access to mobile phones and the Internet are at risk of TFGBV in the same way that all women are at risk of offline GBV.

This is due to patriarchal social relations which create and maintain structural gender inequality and discrimination and that subordinate women in relation to men.   However, some women are more likely to experience it because of who they are or what they do.
Reports show that women with multiple intersectional identities based on race, ethnicity, ability, caste, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression face higher rates of online harassment and attacks

According to GBV specialists, perpetrators of IPV are using technology to monitor, stalk, abuse and control their partners. This includes restricting and controlling survivors’ access to and use of technology, effectively exerting control over every aspect of a woman’s life.

The following five priority actions are suggested as practical first steps GBV practitioners and specialists can do to help
 

1.     Build your own and others’ knowledge and awareness about TFGBV. See below for resources to help with this.

 

2.     Safely include TFGBV in GBV assessments to learn from and with women and girls and their organizations in your context about:

·        How technology-facilitated abuse and violence is manifesting and impacting women and girls;

·        The specific TFGBV experiences, risks and impacts on different groups of women and girls. This includes displaced, refugee and migrant women, young women, racial, ethnic and religious minority women and girls, women and girls with disability, those with diverse sexual and gender identities, and women’s rights activists;

·        Women and girls’ solutions to TFGBV and how to support them to implement solutions.

 

3.     Safely share information generated about TFVGBV with national and local GBV and women’s rights organizations, humanitarian and national decision-makers, donors and other relevant stakeholders.

 

4.     Advocate with humanitarian and national decision-makers and donors to direct attention and resources to research and other knowledge-building activities on TFGBV.

 

5.    
Include research, evaluation and other knowledge-generation activities on TFGBV
in GBV prevention, risk mitigation and prevention programming. Document and share knowledge and evidence generated.

“Behind the Screen: The Silent Harm of Online Bullying on Women and Girls”

Online bullying, also called cyberbullying, is a form of abuse that occurs through digital platforms such as social media, messaging apps, forums, or emails. Women and girls are particularly vulnerable to online bullying because it often targets their gender, appearance, behavior, or personal choices. While it may not leave physical marks, its emotional and psychological impact can be profound.

Online bullying can take many forms: harassment, threats, spreading false information, sharing private images without consent, trolling, or relentless criticism. For women and girls, this can create fear, anxiety, shame, and feelings of powerlessness. Constant exposure to online attacks may affect mental health, leading to depression, low self-esteem, and social withdrawal. In some cases, online bullying can escalate to offline harassment or even physical danger.

One of the most harmful aspects of online bullying is that it can follow women and girls everywhere. Unlike traditional bullying, which may happen in a school or workplace, cyberbullying can invade private spaces, including their homes, making it difficult to find safety or peace. The public and permanent nature of online content adds to the stress, as abusive messages, images, or posts can be shared widely and remain online indefinitely.

Online bullying also discourages women and girls from fully participating in digital spaces. It can silence their voices, reduce their confidence, and limit opportunities for self-expression, learning, networking, and leadership. This perpetuates inequality and reinforces harmful stereotypes about gender roles.

Addressing online bullying requires awareness, support, and action. Women and girls must know that they are not to blame, and that reporting abuse, using privacy settings, and seeking help from trusted adults or organizations are valid ways to protect themselves. Communities, schools, and social media platforms have a responsibility to enforce rules against harassment and provide safe online spaces.

Empowering women and girls to navigate digital spaces safely, speak out against abuse, and support one another is key to preventing the harmful effects of online bullying. Every girl and woman deserves respect, dignity, and safety both online and offline.

-MUSLIM SHOULD NOT ATTACH ANY IMPORTANCE TO JANUARY 1ST

 Bismillahi Rahman Raheem

 Any act or word that gives or attempts to give unnecessary recognition to this day must be discouraged. This is one of the aspects which shows that ignorance of Muslims is parts the biggest problems facing Islam today. Celebration of January 1st is one of the most common innovation in Nigeria and the world over. As Muslims, we must caution ourselves not to fall into the pit of ignorance of celebrating or wishing anyone on it. A Muslim is expected to appreciate his existence on daily basis. When a Muslim wakes up, he says "AlhamduliLahi lladhi ahyaana ba'da maa amaatanaa wa ilaihi nnushur" This is enough for us, we must not immitate the Kuffaar. It is exaperating when some Muslims give the excuse that in Nigeria, our lives is being regulated with the gregorian calendar, we are being paid salaries based on it etc? It is true that the Nigerian government uses this date for it activities. Almighty Allah would not punish us for what we have no power or authority to change without offending the Maqoosidu Shari'ah (Objectives of the Shari'ah). However, we must reject all forms of bid'ah and injustice being perpetrated against us to the best of our ability. We may not have the power to change the Nigerian calendar from Gregorian to Hijriy. But we do not only have the power not to celebrate any festival attached to it, we also have the constitutional right to discourage ourselves from giving undue recognition to any of its dates. Afterall, no security agency can arrest or detain you for not celebrating or preaching against the celebration of Januray 1st. That would never happen. It is our duties and responsilities as Muslims to desist from celebrating it. It is our duties and responsilities to admonish our household and the entire Muslim community against its celebration. It therefore means that any Muslim who did not sleep overnight today because of January 1st (irrespective of his status) is Jaahil. Some of us deceive themselves with one tahajjud or the other. If the intention is to commemorate January 1st, they have committed sins of perpetrating and promoting bid'ah. Some Muslims would even say "Gbogbo odun toba bani la'ye ni agbudo se" (we must celebrate every festival that meet us on earth). When you ask them for their proofs for this in the shari'ah, they have no answer. They will start saying "Sheu Kini, Shehu Kini". Please, let us stop all these nonsense and face the realities. The worst thing in life is for a Muslim to be thrown into hell-fire on the day of judgement just because he perpetrated bid'ah. May Allah forgive us and grant us the ability to reject all forms of bid'ah in our society.

In his commentary of this verse, the great Muffasir Hadrat Isma’eel Haqqi رحمه الله states in his Tafseer, Roohul Bayaan that it has been agreed by Muhadditheen that kissing the nails of the thumbs and the Shahadah finger should be acted upon as it inclines people towards good deeds and instils fear within them.

EVIDENCE FROM AHADITH...

1) Whenever he (Abu Bakr رضي الله عنه) heard the Muathin say, 
“‘I bear witness that Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah’, he would repeat this phrase (as this is the Sunnah) and would kiss the tip of the index fingers (or thumbs) and wipe his eyes.

RasulAllah ﷺ said, 
‘Whoever does what my friend (I.e Abu Bakr) did, my intercession will be essential for him.’”

[REFERENCE: Maqasid-e-Hasana 1,021]

2) Once, RasulAllah ﷺ entered the Masjid and sat down near a pillar. 
Hadrat Abu Bakr Siddiq رضي الله عنه was seated beside him. 
Hadrat Bilal رضي الله عنه then stood up and commenced with the Athaan. 
When he said ‘Ash hadu Anna Muhammadur RasulAllah’, Hadrat Abu Bakr Siddiq رضي الله عنه placed both the thumb nails on to his eyes and said “Qurratu Aini Bika Ya RasulAllah ﷺ”, 
(You are the coolness of my eyes Ya RasulAllah ﷺ). 
When Hadrat Bilal رضي الله عنه completed the Athaan, 
RasulAllah ﷺ said, 
“O Abu Bakr, whosoever does like you have done, Almighty Allah will forgive all his sins.”

[REFERENCE: Tafseer Roohul Bayaan for Qur’an Al-Karim, Verse 5:58 and Al-Daylami] 

3) “That person, who when hearing my name in Athaan, kisses his thumb nails and turns it over to his eyes, he shall never go blind.”

[REFERENCE: Tafseer Roohul Bayaan for Qur’an Al-Karim, Verse 5:58]

4) RasulAllah ﷺ said, 
“Whosoever has touched the name Muhammad ﷺ with his hands, then kissed his hands with his lips and rubbed his eyes, then he will see Allah Azawajal just as the righteous ones see and my intercession will be close to him even though he is a sinner.”

[REFERENCE: An Nawafi Ul Atriyaa, Page 51]

5) RasulAllah ﷺ is reported to have said, 
“On the day of resurrection, I shall search for the person who used to place his thumbs on his eyes when hearing my name during the Athaan. 
I shall lead him into Jannah.”

[REFERENCE: Salaat-e-Masoodi 23.1, Volume 2, Chapter 20 and Bahrur-Raaiq Ramili, Volume 1]

None of these ahadith are fabricated or made up (Maudu) but some can be argued to be ‘Weak’ with regards to hadith classification. 
In terms of Shari’ah, a weak hadith does not mean it is made up or should be rejected, only that such actions mentioned are considered as Fadaail a’maal (extra actions of devotion). 
We don’t use such ahadith to make actions Fard (compulsory) or Waajib (compulsory via presumption) unless supported by a stronger ahadith. 
At the very least Scholars have indicated that such an act is permissable and even Mustahab (rewarding if done).

For decades, we were taught a simple idea: hundreds of millions of sperm race toward the egg, and the fastest one wins. But science has now discovered something even more remarkable—the egg plays a powerful role in choosing the sperm.

New research reveals that the egg doesn’t passively wait to be fertilized. Instead, it releases chemical signals called chemoattractants. These signals guide sperm toward it, but not all sperm respond equally. In fact, the egg seems to attract certain sperm more than others—suggesting a preference at the cellular level.

Published in journals like eLife and Nature Communications, studies show that this “molecular communication” varies depending on genetic compatibility. Eggs appear to favor sperm with the best match for producing a healthy embryo, rather than just the fastest swimmer. This biological selection process could even explain why some couples face unexplained infertility—if the egg and sperm aren’t a good match, fertilization might not happen despite both being healthy.

This changes everything. You weren’t simply the fastest sperm. You were chosen by the egg in a highly selective and intelligent biological interaction that prioritized compatibility and strength.

It’s a powerful reminder that life doesn’t begin with a race. It begins with selection. With intelligence. With connection. You were not just lucky—you were preferred by nature for a reason.

This discovery reshapes how we understand fertility, genetics, and even human identity.
