Two years ago, the warning signs were already there.
Today, the evidence is undeniable.

In 2022, studies by SLAWIJ and Internews showed that 64% of women journalists, human rights defenders, and women politicians in Sierra Leone had experienced online and offline harassment. At the time, Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence (TFGBV) was already emerging as a serious threat—but it remained largely invisible in policy, funding, and national data systems.

My current research shows that TFGBV has not only persisted but intensified. Despite increased global attention on digital violence against women and girls, Sierra Leone’s GBV response frameworks, donor classifications, and reporting mechanisms do not explicitly recognise online abuse. Millions are invested in ending GBV, yet TFGBV remains structurally uncaptured, underfunded, and underreported.

Survivors continue to navigate harassment, image-based abuse, cyberstalking, and digital threats with little institutional support—while the data meant to protect them simply does not see them.

This is not just a technology issue.
It is a gender, governance, and accountability issue.

Recognising TFGBV explicitly in policy, funding, and data systems is no longer optional—it is urgent.

2026 Ahead of 2027: Tension in APC as 5 Defected Governors and Loyal Lawmakers Risk Political Fallout"

BARELY 13 months to the 2027 general elections, a wave of high-profile defections into the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, has dramatically altered the political landscape across several states.

While the movement of sitting Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, governors into the party has strengthened APC’s numerical advantage, it has also exposed deep fault lines, setting the stage for fierce internal battles over leadership, structure and, ultimately, party tickets.

From Akwa Ibom to Delta, Bayelsa, Rivers, Plateau and Enugu, the central question confronting the APC is whether it can convert elite consensus into grassroots cohesion or whether unresolved rivalries will implode at the primaries.

Sharing of APC tickets to test Akpabio-Eno alliance in A/Ibom

Ahead of the polls, the APC in Akwa Ibom State faces the real prospect of internal crisis following the June 2025 defection of Governor Umo Eno from the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP.

At the heart of the looming tension is how the party’s two dominant power centres -Governor Eno, who controls state resources, and Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who commands federal influence -will share party tickets for state and National Assembly offices without triggering implosion.

In his defection speech, Governor Eno spoke glowingly of mutual trust between himself, Akpabio and President Bola Tinubu, stressing that the understanding guaranteed automatic tickets for his second-term bid and Akpabio’s political future, while committing all three to deliver Akwa Ibom to the APC.

Conspicuously absent, however, was any assurance for the 26 PDP lawmakers and political appointees who defected alongside him. Apart from Akpabio, even serving APC lawmakers at the National Assembly are uncertain about their chances of securing return tickets.

Fearing backlash from displaced incumbents with strong voter bases, Governor Eno has unveiled the slogan “Akwa Ibom United,” a political doctrine first popularised by the recently displaced PDP chairman, Aniekan Akpan.

Critics describe it as a euphemism for total political control across party lines, blending inducement with coercion. In the weeks before his defection, Eno reportedly gifted SUVs to PDP chairmen and the Inter-Party Advisory Council, IPA, ostensibly to promote harmony.

Yet, that posture contrasts sharply with his hardline warning: “We will not leave PDP for thieves to hijack and use against us.”

A party chieftain alleged that dissenters were declared “sacked,” noting that two aides were dismissed for attending the PDP convention in Ibadan.

The strategy, insiders say, is to keep a firm grip on the opposition and deny displaced aspirants viable platforms. But analysts warn that an unresolved Akpabio–Eno ticket-sharing battle could weaken APC’s chances or, if managed ruthlessly, hand it total victory.

Delta: Old warhorses, new alliances

Governor Sheriff Oborevwori’s April 28, 2025 defection to the APC, alongside his predecessor, Senator Ifeanyi Okowa, has reshaped Delta State politics. Since then, Oborevwori has consolidated control of the party, enjoying the backing of the Omeni-Sobotie-led State Working Committee and key stakeholders, including Chief Festus Keyamo, O’tega Emerhor, Senators Ned Nwoko and Ede Dafinone.

The governor has been widely endorsed as APC’s sole governorship candidate for 2027. The governor is also getting support and series of endorsement from APC faithful and stakeholders across the three senatorial districts, federal constituencies and local government areas in the state as consensus governorship candidate of the party in the 2027 general elections.

However, uncertainty lingers over the ambition of former Deputy Senate President, Senator Ovie Omo-Agege, the party’s 2023 governorship candidate, who has remained silent.

Omo-Agege, who is the immediate past Deputy President of the Senate, has been a longstanding governorship aspirant in the state and had vied for the position severally under the platforms of various political parties.

Though he welcomed the governor into the APC and attended the defection ceremony, Omo-Agege has since then been silent, giving nothing away as to whether he is ready to give up his ambition or not.

With former PDP and old APC members now cohabiting, analysts foresee friction, particularly where incumbents and aspirants collide.

Ethiope Federal Constituency, home of former governor James Ibori, is one flashpoint, with tensions between supporters of his daughter, the incumbent lawmaker, and a rival camp led by Chief Ighoyota Amori.

In fact, an Ibori and Amori feud, if not resolved, could cause big issues.

Delta North Senatorial district is susceptible to rancour in the build up to 2027 as relations between former Governor Ifeanyi Okowa and incumbent Senator Ned Nwoko remain strained. Whether Okowa backs a rival aspirant or Nwoko resists pressure to step aside could determine APC’s internal stability.

Before the defection, there were rumours that Okowa was touting someone that will run under the PDP, though it was misrepresented that he was the one that wanted to go back to the Senate.

Ned Nwoko defected from the PDP to the APC and now both of them are back in the same party.

Will Okowa bring someone to run against Nwoko in the APC? Will Nwoko give up and allow someone else to take the ticket from him? This is an issue that could cause chaos in the party, if not properly managed.

Will Diri’s inclusive style count in Bayelsa APC?

Bayelsa State is experiencing a major shift in its political landscape following Governor Douye Diri’s defection from the PDP to the APC. This move is seen as a key boost to the APC, strengthening its hold on the state and paving the way for increased federal support and investment.

With the defection, the APC now controls the state executive and legislative arms of government, giving it an advantage in the upcoming general elections. This shift in power dynamics will no doubt affect opposition parties’ chances in subsequent polls in the state.

However, this has sparked mixed reactions, with some welcoming the decision and others predicting potential instability. Analysts warn that defections don’t guarantee automatic success, emphasizing the importance of internal party structures and agreements, a pointer that the governor’s new role will require navigating the party’s internal factions and managing tensions with his former PDP colleagues.

Interestingly, the party’s internal dynamics are complex, with factions loyal to the Minister of State for Petroleum (Oil), Senator Heineken Lokpobiri and former Governor Timipre Sylva.

Recall that the then ruling party, the PDP exploited the wrangling within the APC in the last governorship polls to cement its place as the dominant party in Bayelsa until the surprised November 2025 switch by Governor Diri to the APC alongside the Speaker, Abraham Ingobere and members of the state House of Assembly. His commissioners and local government council chairmen under the banner of the PDP also joined the defection train.

One major obstacle is the internal party dynamics, as some APC members have expressed concerns about the governor’s defection from PDP, questioning his loyalty and electoral value as he’s already serving his second term.

Though the Lokpobiri faction has since accepted Diri as the leader of the party in the state by virtue of his position as a governor, he still faces the challenge of winning the trust of some old party members, especially those in the Sylva camp who have been loyal to the party since it berthed in the state and see their principal as its leader.

However, Diri’s leadership style, known for its inclusiveness irrespective of party affiliations and peaceful disposition, will be put to test in his new role as the leader of the party as both old and new members slug it out for positions in the days ahead in the predominantly civil service state where politics has turned out to be a lucrative business for many.

The governor is also expected to bring to bear his wealth of experience and leadership acumen to reconcile the factions within the APC and avoid past mistakes that cost the party dearly at the polls as witnessed in the last governorship election in the state when the party went into battle with the PDP as a divided house.

The outcome of these political maneuvers will no doubt have significant implications for 2027 which focus is to return the President at the centre and help secure Bayelsa State for the APC, reminiscence of the PDP era of dominance in the South South geopolitical zone.

How Fubara’s defection sparked fresh political crisis In River

Governor Siminalayi Fubara’s December 9, 2025 defection to the APC reignited political tensions in Rivers State, especially within the camp of FCT Minister Nyesom Wike.

Wike’s anger reportedly stems from Fubara’s failure to consult him before meeting President Tinubu and defecting, a move allegedly facilitated by APC Governors’ Forum chairman, Hope Uzodimma.

Wike has openly declared that Fubara cannot be the political leader of Rivers, even as governor, a stance echoed by APC National Vice Chairman Victor Giadom.

However, Senator John Azuta-Mbata countered that Fubara remains the recognised governor, underscoring the fragile and unresolved nature of the crisis as 2027 approaches.

Fubara’s decision to join the APC came barely a few days after about 16 lawmakers loyal to Wike defected to the APC citing “irreconcilable” differences in the PDP.

The governor who had a closed-door meeting with President Tinubu in the Villa on Monday night before his defection, boasted that his joining the APC was a mark of respect and, perhaps, the best way of saying “thank you Mr. President” for standing with Rivers State.

Since a few months into his government after swearing in on May 29, 2023, Fubara has never known peace. Political crisis that erupted between him and Wike, his godfather that almost consumed the state lasted for close to two years until President Tinubu wielded the big stick on March 18, 2025 by declaring a state of emergency in Rivers followed by the suspension of Fubara, his deputy and the House of Assembly for six months.

Vice Admiral Ibok Etteh Ibas, retd, was appointed to administer the state for six months when the suspension lasted. He handed over reins of power to Fubara on September 18, 2025.

However, the latest political development did not go down well with the camp of the FCT Minister, Wike who angrily reacted that singing Tinubu’s political slogan “on your mandate we shall stand” would not guarantee an automatic ticket for Fubara’s second term in 2027.

Investigation showed that Wike’s anger stemmed from the fact that Fubara never sought his consent before meeting President Tinubu on December 8 to finalize plans to defect to the APC. The tactical plan was said to have been mooted by the Imo State Governor and chairman of APC Governors’ Forum, Senator Uzodimma, to spite Wike.

Wike believes that Fubara has blatantly failed to implement some of the agreements made by President Tinubu to resolve the lingering political crisis in the state. According to Wike, Fubara had not been working with the state House of Assembly as it ought to be. But the governor insisted that it is the Minister that ought to arrange for such a meeting where all of them including the elders would sit and settle scores.

Wike has also insisted that despite being in a different party, Fubara can never be the political leader of Rivers State despite being a governor. This position has further sparked wide division among political elites in the state with the National Vice Chairman of the APC, Victor Giadom, saying that Fubara can never get anything without passing through Wike.

Giadom, who described Wike as a “dependable leader” in Rivers State politics, assured the minister that there would be no political force in Gokana (his local government area) other than him (Wike).

“I guarantee, on behalf of my brothers, that the Gokana people are for Wike and Tinubu and nobody will challenge Wike’s influence in Gokana.

“Gokana is a ‘no-go area’ for anybody, even Governor Fubara. For him to win anything in Gokana, he must pass through Wike,” he said.

Nevertheless, the political leader of Eneka Clan in Obio/Akpor local government area of the state and President General of Ohanaeze Ndigbo Worldwide, Senator John Azuta-Mbata, declared that the people of Eneka recognized Siminalayi Fubara as the only Governor of Rivers State.

He assured the Governor of the clan’s “continued friendship and support”, describing the relationship as “firm and unbroken”.

The latest political development, however, is an indication that the peace accord brokered by President Tinubu between Governor Fubara and Wike, was just a fluke.

Plateau: Mutfwang’s defection shakes PDP stronghold

Governor Caleb Mutfwang’s defection has rattled Plateau State, long regarded as a PDP bastion. While APC leaders welcomed the move cautiously, PDP loyalists see it as a betrayal.

Analysts warn that without reconciliation and transparent leadership, APC risks factionalisation that could blunt its electoral edge and reopen space for opposition resurgence.

Plateau State has long prided itself as the traditional stronghold of the PDP, a reputation built on the state’s pivotal role in the formation, growth and sustenance of the Party over the years.

From the advent of the Fourth Republic, the PDP enjoyed overwhelming acceptance across the state, embedding itself deeply in the political consciousness of the people.

For many politically aware citizens, loyalty to the PDP went beyond mere party affiliation and was often likened to a belief system. Adherence to the party line was regarded as a civic duty, while any form of deviation in the recent past was viewed by supporters as political apostasy.

This entrenched loyalty largely explains why opposition parties struggled for relevance and electoral success in Plateau State for many years.

This political pattern, however, witnessed a significant shift with the emergence of the All Progressives Congress, APC, which broke the PDP’s dominance and governed the state between 2015 and 2023.

The period marked a notable departure from Plateau’s long-standing political tradition and demonstrated that voter loyalty, though deeply rooted, was not immutable.

Following the 2023 general elections, the PDP returned to power in Plateau State, rekindling hopes among its supporters that the Party’s supremacy had been restored.

However, internal crises and protracted leadership disputes at the national level of the PDP soon cast a shadow over this resurgence. These unresolved tensions reportedly culminated in the defection of Governor Mutfwang to the APC, a move that sent shockwaves through the state’s political landscape.

The defection was met with mixed reactions. While some leaders within the APC initially expressed reservations, questioning the political implications of the move, grassroots supporters of the PDP were equally unsettled, perceiving it as a profound betrayal of the Party’s long-standing ideals and support base.

As events unfold, the Plateau State chapter of the APC appears poised to grapple with significant internal challenges.

Analysts foresee the emergence of factional alignments and leadership disputes driven by competing loyalties to existing party structures and newly formed power blocs. Such divisions, if not carefully managed, could weaken internal cohesion and disrupt the Party’s organisational effectiveness.

These tensions may also adversely affect grassroots mobilisation, undermine confidence among Party faithful and potentially trigger defections of some members. The risk of deepening discord remains high, particularly if the Party fails to articulate a unified vision or adopt transparent mechanisms for conflict resolution.

Ultimately, without timely reconciliation, inclusive leadership and credible internal democratic processes, the APC risks diminishing its effectiveness and electoral competitiveness in Plateau State.

Such a scenario could create political openings for other contending parties to gain traction and reshape the state’s political dynamics in 2027.

Enugu: Why APC may avoid implosion

Unlike elsewhere, Enugu APC appears poised for relative stability following Governor Peter Mbah’s defection. Strategic realignments, the exit of former power brokers and the emergence of Dr. Ben Nwoye as caretaker chairman have effectively handed party control to the governor’s camp.

With funding, structure and national backing aligned, insiders say harmonisation is inevitable, though zoning adjustments may be required to balance senatorial interests.

When Governor Mbah, in October, defected to the ruling APC he literally collapsed the hitherto entire PDP structure into the APC. He moved with all PDP structures from ward to state level. Before then, APC structure in the state was under the control of Chief Uche Nnaji, then the minister of Science and Innovation, with Barr.

Ugochukwu Agballa as the chairman of the party. But the party was not very peaceful. There were incessant disagreements between the former minister and the leadership of the party on one side and other senior party members and stakeholders on the other side. Major stakeholders of the party, including former Senate President, Chief Ken Nnamani, former Governor Sullivan Chime, former DG of Voice of Nigeria, Osita Okechukwu, among others, were suspended and alienated from the party by the then party leadership of Agballa.

Meanwhile, the relationship between the former minister and the governor was not cordial, they were not working together as minister and governor aimed at one good purpose- development of the state; even when both of them are of Nkanu clan.

With the leadership crisis in PDP, Mbah’s former party not abating, the former APC chairman, Dr. Ben Nwoye, also an Nkanu man, and who was not happy with the Agballa leadership of the party, worked behind the scenes with estranged stakeholders and tactic support of the governor, and schemed back his way as the chairman of the party, further dividing the party, and contesting the leadership of the party with Ugochukwu Agballa.

With support from Abuja and stakeholders, he openly started wooing Gov. Mbah to join APC.

The minister’s resignation automatically changed a lot in the party. It cleared the way for Nwoye with the backing of the governor and hitherto estranged stakeholders of the party, to take complete control of the party in the state. And he got the nod of the party at the national level to take over as caretaker chairman.

With the party under the control of the governor’s man, the way became express for him to join which he did.

With the circumstances surrounding his movement into the party and the intrigues that removed those that could have constituted a stumbling block for him, it is unlikely that there may be leadership crisis in the party under him, more so in Nigeria political clime, the governor provides the funds and therefore he dictates the tune too.

So it is expected that before long there will be a seamless harmonization and selection of new leaders of the party in the state to reflect the required political balance. This is necessary because the governor and the party chairman should not come from the same senatorial district as presently constituted. Both of them are from Enugu East districts.

Standar Ganda Wahabi dalam Isu Ketaatan dan Demonstrasi

Dalam banyak kajian Wahabi, satu kaidah terus diulang: ketaatan kepada pemerintah yang sah adalah kewajiban mutlak. Segala bentuk perlawanan (termasuk demonstrasi) dianggap haram, bid‘ah, bahkan disebut sebagai jalan menuju neraka. Rakyat dituntut diam atas nama stabilitas, sementara kritik terhadap penguasa diposisikan sebagai fitnah yang dianggap lebih berbahaya daripada kezaliman itu sendiri. Kaidah ini diklaim sebagai manhaj salaf, seolah bersifat universal dan tak mengenal pengecualian.

Namun kaidah tersebut terbukti mandul, tumpul, dan runtuh ketika berhadapan dengan realitas politik tertentu. Saat rakyat Iran turun ke jalan memprotes pemerintahnya, banyak Wahabiyun justru mengalihkan narasi. Demonstrasi tidak lagi dipermasalahkan sebagai keharaman, melainkan fokus diarahkan pada kecaman terhadap ketidakadilan rezim Iran. Pola yang sama terlihat pada gejolak Mesir di masa Presiden Mursi. Pihak-pihak yang menentang pemerintahan yang sah tidak dicap sebagai bughat, bahkan diberi justifikasi dan dukungan, karena Mursi diasosiasikan dengan Ikhwan yang dianggap menyimpang secara akidah.

Di titik ini, menjadi jelas bahwa masalahnya bukan demonstrasi, bukan ketaatan, dan bukan pula manhaj salaf. Masalahnya adalah siapa penguasanya dan siapa yang didemo. Jika penguasa sejalan dengan ideologi Wahabi, ketaatan diwajibkan secara mutlak. Jika berbeda mazhab atau afiliasi gerakan, kaidah dilonggarkan, dibalik, atau ditinggalkan sama sekali. Bahkan penilaian sering bergeser pada siapa pendemonya: bila berbeda ideologi, hukum kembali ke pakem lama, demo haram dan pelakunya dicela.

Ini bukan prinsip, melainkan inkonsistensi. Bukan manhaj salaf, melainkan standar ganda yang membungkus kepentingan politik dengan bahasa sunnah. Manhaj seperti ini bukan menjaga agama, tetapi melakukan seleksi kebenaran berdasarkan loyalitas ideologis. Bukan fiqh ketaatan, melainkan fiqh keberpihakan.

Mike Bloomfield did not arrive quietly in American music; he arrived informed, disciplined by listening, and fiercely committed to the language of the blues. Born in Chicago, he stepped away from comfort and privilege to learn directly from the city’s South Side masters, absorbing phrasing, tone, and structure at a time when blues was still a living, local tradition rather than a museum piece.

His ascent came through the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, where Bloomfield helped redefine what electric blues could sound like in the 1960s. His guitar work was sharp but conversational, rooted in tradition while pushing toward longer forms and expanded improvisation. On landmark recordings such as East-West, he demonstrated that blues-based music could stretch into modal exploration without losing its emotional center.

Bloomfield’s career continued to defy easy categorization. With the Electric Flag, he explored soul, jazz, and rock as parts of a single musical vocabulary, resisting commercial formulas in favor of artistic restlessness. Even in later years, away from the spotlight, his playing retained a directness that spoke more to musicians than to trends.

Mike Bloomfield remains a central figure in the evolution of American guitar music, not for spectacle or image, but for his seriousness of purpose. He treated the blues as a language to be respected, expanded, and carried forward, leaving behind a body of work that still instructs as much as it inspires.

She spent Election Day 1872 in jail. Her crime? Running for President of the United States as a woman—50 years before women could even vote.
Victoria Woodhull's story reads like fiction. But every astonishing detail is real.
Born into poverty in rural Ohio in 1838, married off at fifteen to an alcoholic morphine addict, divorced at twenty-six when divorce meant social death, she somehow clawed her way from traveling medicine shows to Wall Street's most notorious brokerage firm to a presidential campaign that terrified America's most powerful men.
And they made her pay for every audacious step.
January 11, 1871. House Judiciary Committee hearing room, Washington D.C.
Victoria Woodhull stood before rows of congressmen, flanked by Susan B. Anthony and Isabella Beecher Hooker. She was about to become the first woman in American history to testify before a congressional committee.
Chairman John Bingham looked at her with unconcealed contempt. His message was clear: You don't belong here.
"Madam," he reportedly sneered, "you are no citizen—you are a woman!"
Victoria's hands trembled. Then she began to speak.
Women already possessed the right to vote under the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, she argued. The Constitution guaranteed citizenship rights to all persons born in the United States. Women were citizens. Therefore, women had the right to vote. Congress simply needed to clarify what the Constitution already granted.
It was brilliant constitutional reasoning. It was also revolutionary—and the congressmen listening knew it threatened everything.
But Victoria Woodhull had spent her entire life refusing to accept the world's limitations.
Her childhood was a nightmare. Her father Buck was a con artist, swindler, and arsonist who'd been run out of their hometown after burning down his own mill for insurance money. Her mother communed with spirits and believed her daughters had supernatural powers.
The family traveled from town to town in a medicine show. Young Victoria and her sister Tennessee performed as "amazing child clairvoyants," telling fortunes, peddling homemade remedies that were mostly alcohol in bottles. Victoria attended school for exactly three years before her father pulled her out at age eleven.
At fourteen, desperate to escape her father's exploitation, she married Dr. Canning Woodhull.
He was a hopeless drunk who spent his time in taverns and brothels. While pregnant with her first child, Victoria discovered his morphine addiction. Their son was born mentally disabled, likely due to his father's substance abuse.
Victoria worked multiple jobs—cigar store clerk, seamstress, stage actress—to feed her children while her husband drank away whatever money he earned.
After eleven years, she did something that marked her as a woman without respectability: she divorced him.
In 1860s America, divorced women were social outcasts. Damaged goods. Morally compromised. But Victoria refused to accept that shame. She became an outspoken advocate for "free love"—not promiscuity, but the radical idea that women shouldn't be trapped in marriages with abusive or unfaithful husbands. That divorce should carry no stigma. That love should be freely chosen, not legally enforced.
It was a philosophy born from brutal experience.
Then came the transformation that would change everything.
In 1868, Victoria and Tennessee moved to New York City and somehow connected with Cornelius Vanderbilt—the railroad magnate and one of the wealthiest men in America. He'd recently lost his wife and son, had developed an interest in spiritualism, and hired the sisters as clairvoyants.
Whether through genuine spiritual gifts or shrewd observation of the shipping industry, the sisters obtained financial advice that proved extraordinarily profitable. Acting on tips from Vanderbilt, they built a fund of nearly $700,000 within six weeks—equivalent to over $15 million today.
In February 1870, they opened Woodhull, Claflin & Company on Wall Street.
The first women to operate a brokerage firm in American financial history. The press treated them as a novelty—"the Bewitching Brokers," "the Queens of Finance"—expecting them to fail spectacularly.
But Victoria viewed the brokerage as something more strategic: a platform for building political power.
On May 14, 1870, using Wall Street profits, the sisters founded Woodhull & Claflin's Weekly—a newspaper championing women's suffrage, labor reforms, and a single moral standard applying equally to men and women.
Revolutionary at a time when society tolerated married men keeping mistresses while condemning women for any sexual freedom.
The Weekly became notorious. It advocated for licensed prostitution, dress reform, vegetarianism. And on December 30, 1871, it made history by publishing the first English-language version of Karl Marx's Communist Manifesto in America.
But Victoria's ambitions extended far beyond publishing.
In April 1870, she'd announced something unprecedented: she was running for President of the United States.
On May 10, 1872, the Equal Rights Party officially nominated her. She was thirty-four years old—one year below the constitutional age requirement. She selected Frederick Douglass as her running mate, though he never acknowledged or accepted the nomination.
Her platform was remarkably progressive: women's suffrage, regulation of monopolies, nationalization of railroads, eight-hour workday, direct taxation, abolition of the death penalty, welfare for the poor.
The press savaged her.
Political cartoonist Thomas Nast depicted her as "Mrs. Satan" in Harper's Weekly—complete with demonic horns and wings, holding a sign proclaiming "Be Saved By Free Love."
But Victoria had learned something from her childhood in medicine shows: survival sometimes required exposing hypocrisy.
One of her harshest critics was Reverend Henry Ward Beecher—brother of Uncle Tom's Cabin author Harriet Beecher Stowe, one of America's most famous religious leaders. Beecher condemned Victoria's free love philosophy from his Brooklyn pulpit.
He was also secretly conducting an affair with Elizabeth Tilton, a married parishioner.
Victoria learned of the hypocrisy and decided to act.
On November 2, 1872—just days before the election—Woodhull & Claflin's Weekly published a detailed account of Beecher's adultery.
U.S. Marshals immediately arrested Victoria, her sister Tennessee, and Colonel Blood on charges of publishing obscene material through federal mail. They confiscated 3,000 copies of the newspaper.
The sisters were thrown into New York's notorious Ludlow Street Jail, normally reserved for civil offenses but housing hardened criminals.
Victoria Woodhull—the first female presidential candidate in American history—spent Election Day 1872 in jail.
The irony was crushing. Arrested under obscenity laws for exposing a man's adultery, while that same moral standard never applied to men who openly discussed women's bodies or sold materials objectifying women.
After seven months of legal proceedings, Victoria and Tennessee were acquitted on a technicality. But the battle had cost them nearly $500,000 in legal fees.
They were bankrupt.
The election itself? President Ulysses S. Grant won decisively. Victoria wasn't on the ballot in any state. No official count of votes cast for her exists. She may have received zero votes.
But the vote count was never the point.
"Even if my bid for the presidency is not successful," Victoria had said, "it will be an education for women."
She was right. For the first time, Americans had to imagine a woman in the highest office. Had to confront the question: Why not?
But Victoria paid dearly for forcing that question.
Susan B. Anthony withdrew her support, finding Victoria too radical even for the suffrage movement. Harriet Beecher Stowe called her an "impudent witch" and "vile jailbird." Former allies abandoned her.
When Cornelius Vanderbilt died in 1877, his heirs likely paid the sisters to move to England—removing them as potential challengers to his will.
In England, Victoria reinvented herself one final time. She lectured, wrote, charmed a wealthy banker named John Biddulph Martin, and married him in 1883. She became known for philanthropy and was accepted in British high society—a stunning transformation from the scandalous American activist who'd spent Election Day in jail.
She lived comfortably until her death in 1927 at age eighty-eight.
Victoria Woodhull was nobody's idea of a perfect feminist icon.
She was calculating. Ambitious. Sometimes ruthless. She used spiritualist con-artistry to gain wealth. She exposed private affairs for public gain. She exploited Frederick Douglass's name without his consent.
But she was also a survivor who transformed childhood exploitation into adult agency. A woman who refused to be defined by poverty, limited education, or society's brutal expectations.
She opened Wall Street to women decades before it seemed possible.
She published radical ideas that challenged conventional morality.
She stood before Congress and demanded recognition as a citizen when the chairman sneered that she was merely a woman.
She ran for president fifty years before women could vote—not because she expected to win, but because the campaign itself would force Americans to imagine what had seemed unimaginable.
She spent Election Day in jail for daring to challenge powerful men.
And she paid for that audacity with bankruptcy, exile, and historical obscurity.
Most Americans have never heard her name. History books skip over her. When we celebrate the first woman to run for president, we usually mean Hillary Clinton in 2016.
But 144 years earlier, a divorced, bankrupt, scandal-plagued woman from rural Ohio stood on a presidential debate stage in her mind—even if the actual stage was denied her—and demanded to be taken seriously.
They laughed at her. Arrested her. Exiled her. Erased her.
But they couldn't undo what she'd proven: that a woman could run for president. That a woman could open a Wall Street firm. That a woman could testify before Congress. That a woman could demand equality and refuse to be silenced.
On November 5, 1872, Victoria Woodhull sat in a jail cell while men voted for president.
On November 8, 2016, millions of women voted for a female presidential candidate.
That 144-year journey started with a woman brave—or reckless—enough to run when running seemed impossible.
Victoria Woodhull was born into poverty, married off as a child, divorced and shamed, jailed for her ambitions, exiled for her audacity.
And she changed American politics forever—whether history remembers her name or not.
Every woman who runs for office stands on her shoulders.
Every woman who refuses to accept limitations honors her legacy.
Every woman who demands to be taken seriously echoes her defiant voice before that congressional committee: I am a citizen. I belong here. You cannot erase me.
They tried to erase Victoria Woodhull.
But 186 years after her birth, her story refuses to stay buried.
Because women who dare to break barriers never truly disappear—they just wait for history to finally catch up and remember.

When women’s professional confidence is judged against their private life, a standard never applied to men, it amounts to psychological violence.

I’m not here to shame anyone for how they voted. Voting is an American right;  that’s the point. You were free to choose.

But we also have to be honest about what’s happening after that choice.

If you voted for Trump, I’m asking you to look at the results, not the rhetoric. He has repeatedly lied to the people who trusted him, and those lies don’t just affect “the other side.” They affect your neighbors. They affect your family. They affect you.

Being born here does not automatically make you safe. Power without accountability never does.

The Constitution is at risk. American democracy is at risk. And the hardest part is this: the very freedom that allowed you to vote for the man you believed in is now being undermined by him. That isn’t fair to you. It isn’t fair to any of us.

You don’t have to say it out loud. You don’t have to post about it. But at least acknowledge, internally, what’s happening. Our futures; our children’s futures, our grandchildren’s futures, are genuinely at risk.

This isn’t an attack. It’s a plea: listen to your neighbors. Read the Constitution. And if you’re Christian, read the Bible too ;because protecting the vulnerable and holding power accountable is not radical. It’s foundational.

Marka taariikh ahaan laga hadlayo ereyga “Somaliland”, waxaa loola jeedaa magac juqraafi iyo mid gumeysi oo Ingiriisku u adeegsaday waqooyiga dhulka Soomaaliyeed intii u dhaxaysay dabayaaqadii qarnigii 19-aad iyo bartamihii qarnigii 20-aad. Magacani ma ahayn astaan qaran oo ka tarjumaysa dal madax-bannaan ama ummad gaar ah, balse wuxuu ahaa hab ay quwad gumeysi u kala saartay dhulka uu maamulayo, si ay ugu fududaato maamul, ciidan iyo dano istaraatiiji ah.

Ingiriisku wuxuu dhulkan u bixiyay British Somaliland kaddib heshiisyo uu la galay qaar ka mid ah suldaanadii iyo cuqaashii degaanka. Ujeeddada ugu weyn ee Ingiriiska kama ay ahayn dhisidda dawlad Soomaaliyeed, balse waxa ay ahayd ilaalinta marin-badeedka Gacanka Cadmeed iyo sugidda sahayda iyo amniga saldhiggiisa istaraatiijiga ah ee Cadan. Sidaas awgeed, Somaliland waxa ay ahayd protectorate, taas oo micnaheedu yahay in Ingiriisku gacanta ku hayay arrimaha dibadda, difaaca iyo go’aamada waaweyn, halka maamul gudaha ahi uu ahaa mid xaddidan oo ku tiirsan gumeysiga.

Intii uu jiray xukunka gumeysiga, dadka ku noolaa dhulka loo bixiyay Somaliland ma aysan lumin aqoonsigooda Soomaaliyeed. Af, diin, dhaqan iyo taariikhba waxay wadaageen dhammaan ummadda Soomaaliyeed ee ku noolaa dhulalka kale ee uu gumeysiga kala qaybiyay. Kala soocidda magacyada sida Somaliland, Italian Somaliland ama French Somaliland ma ahayn kala sooc bulsho ama qaran, balse waxay ahaayeen magacyo ay quwadihii shisheeye u sameysteen si ay u kala maamulaan dhulka Soomaaliyeed.

  Markii uu dhammaaday xilligii gumeysiga, British Somaliland waxay 26-kii Juun 1960 ay heshay madax-bannaani rasmi ah, madax-bannaanidaasi waxa ay jirtay muddo aad u kooban, taas oo muujinaysa in ujeeddadu aysan ahayn dhisidda dal gaar ah oo gooni u taagan, balse ay ahayd tallaabo ku-meel-gaar ah oo horseed u ah midowga Soomaaliyeed. 1-dii Luulyo 1960, dhulkii British Somaliland iyo kii Talyaanigu gumaysan jiray waxay si ikhtiyaari ah ugu midoobeen Jamhuuriyadda Soomaaliyeed, iyaga oo ku dhisay rajo qaranimo, midnimo iyo dawlad Soomaaliyeed oo mideysan.

Sidaas darteed, taariikh ahaan Somaliland looma fahmi karo dawlad madax-bannaan oo waqti dheer soo jiray. Waa magac ka dhashay gumeysi, kuna ekaa duruufo taariikheed oo gaar ah. Fahamkaas taariikheed ayaa muhiim u ah kala saaridda wixii hore u jiray iyo doodaha siyaasadeed ee dambe. Ka dib burburkii dawladnimada Soomaaliyeed 1991, magaca Somaliland waxaa mar kale loo adeegsaday mashruuc siyaasadeed oo garac ah, kaas oo ujeedkiisu yahay gooni-isu-taag. Si kastaba ha ahaatee, isticmaalka maanta ee magacaasi ma beddelayo xaqiiqada ah in asalkiisu ahaa mid gumeysi, kana mid ahaa qaybo ka mid ah dhulka Soomaaliyeed ee mideysnaa.

For Immediate Release
13TH January 2026

NGOCC CONDEMNS SEXIST RHETORIC AND VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN IN ELECTIONS (VAWE)

The Non-governmental Gender Organisations Coordinating Council (NGOCC) strongly condemns the recent discriminatory remarks published on Simon Mwewa Lane Television on Friday 9th January 2026, suggesting that a single woman is "unworkable" for the office of Mayor and that the position should be reserved for a "family man."

Such statements are not merely "political opinions"; they are a direct assault on the spirit of the Zambian Constitution and the Gender Equity and Equality Act No. 22 of 2015. By using marital status as a litmus test for leadership, these comments perpetuate a dangerous culture of Violence Against Women in Elections (VA WE).

As Zambia moves toward the August 13, 2026, General Elections, the use of sexist remarks serves one purpose: to intimidate women and discourage them from seeking high-level Presidential, Parliamentary, and Local Authority seats.

When women's professional confidence is judged against their private life, a standard never applied to men, it amounts to psychological violence. Such rhetoric undermines democracy by suggesting that leadership for half the population is conditional. It fuels harassment and emboldens online misogynists to attack female candidates on personal grounds rather than their political manifestos.

Genuine gender balance is about fair representation, not reinforcement of patriarchal stereotypes. No candidate should be targeted for their gender or personal life.

With the 2026 election cycle now in motion, NGOCC demands the following:

l. An Unconditional Retraction: We call on the Simon Mwelwa Lane Television that published this harmful statement and commit to a more inclusive political discourse.

Political Party Accountability: We urge all political parties to strictly enforce "Zero Tolerance" policies against VAWE and sexist campaigning within their ranks.

ECZ Oversight: We call upon the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) to monitor and sanction those who use discriminatory language that violates the Electoral Code of Conduct.

Voter Alertness: We encourage the Zambian public to reject leaders who promote division and discrimination. A leader's ability to serve Lusaka or any part of Zambia is measured by their vision, integrity, and competence, not their marriage certificate.

We wish to state categorically:
The leadership of a woman is not a threat to the family or the nation; it is an asset.

As we approach the 2026 National Presidential, Parliamentary, and Local Authority elections, we must reject the use of sexist attacks designed to intimidate women and shrink the civic space. A leader's competence is measured by their integrity, vision, and service to the people not by their marriage certificate.

In our commitment to a peaceful and inclusive electoral process, we would like to urge the public to immediately report perpetrators of all forms of violence, whether verbal, psychological, physical including electoral violence to the toll-free helpline: 116.

All cases received via this line will be documented and reported to the relevant Authorities.

We are calling on all political parties, the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ), and the general public to uphold a "Zero Tolerance" policy toward gender-based harassment.

NGOCC remains fully committed to ensuring that the 2026 elections are free, fair, and safe for all candidates, regardless of gender or marital status.

THE BROTHER WHO MOCKED HIM FOR BEING SINGLE NEVER SAW THIS COMING 😱

“Still single at thirty-five, huh?”

Bryce’s voice cut across the backyard like a knife.

Plastic cups froze halfway to lips.

A few cousins went quiet just to hear him drag me.

My mother had promised this Keller family reunion would be “harmless.”

One afternoon.

Food. Family. Old stories.

“Nothing dramatic,” she’d said.

She forgot to factor in my brother. Or maybe she just hoped he’d behave.

Bad call.

I’d parked my dented gray Honda two houses down on purpose.

At thirty-five, rolling in late was the only power move I had left.

If I couldn’t show up rich, at least I could show up on my own terms.

The Keller backyard looked like a brochure for suburban perfection.

Fresh-cut grass.

Rental tent.

White folding tables loaded with potato salad, grilled chicken, and cheap wine trying its best to be fancy.

Kids tore around barefoot while the adults clumped together in little circles, laughing too loudly, pretending their lives matched their Facebook posts.

I slipped through the side gate, wishing I could be invisible.

No such luck.

“Logan!”

I heard my name like an accusation.

Bryce had spotted me.

Of course he did.

Two years older.

Married right after college.

Big house in a gated community twenty minutes away.

Senior manager at some corporate firm whose logo was all over the gift bags on the table.

He was what the Keller clan pointed to when they said, “See? It’s not that hard.”

Bryce crossed the lawn toward me, beer in hand, wearing a polo that somehow looked more expensive than my entire outfit.

He gave me that slow up-and-down scan, like he was checking inventory at a thrift store.

“Wow,” he said, loud enough for the nearby relatives to hear. “You actually came.”

My mother hurried over, wiping her hands on her apron, eyes shining with a mix of pride and panic.

She hugged me too tightly, like she was afraid I might bolt.

“You look tired,” she whispered into my shoulder.

“I am,” I said, because I didn’t have the energy to lie.

Bryce chuckled.

Not in my face.

Not outright.

That wasn’t his style.

His specialty was death by a thousand “jokes.”

The kind of comments that didn’t sound like a big deal unless you added them up over twenty years.

“So,” he said, lifting his beer, voice casual but amplified, “still alone at thirty-five?”

The words landed harder than they should have.

Heads turned.

A couple of cousins smirked into their cups.

Somebody snorted.

Boom.

There it was.

My role.

The family screw-up.

The one who “never settled down.”

The one who “chased dreams” instead of “being responsible.”

I felt that familiar heat behind my eyes.

The urge to turn it into a joke and laugh with them so it would hurt less.

“Yeah,” I said, forcing a grin. “Guess I missed the deadline.”

A few people laughed.

Bryce smirked like he’d just won something.

“Well,” he added, clinking his beer against my plastic cup of lemonade, “not everyone’s meant for the whole wife-and-kids thing. Some of us grow up. Some of us… don’t.”

🔥 There it was.

Right on schedule.

He never missed a chance.

When my first startup tanked, he’d said, “At least you got it out of your system before forty.”

When I moved into a tiny studio on the sketchy side of town, he’d joked, “Hey, minimalist living is trendy now.”

When our dad died and the will left Bryce the house “because he had a family to support,” Bryce had looked at me and said, “You’re flexible. You’ll figure it out.”

Everyone had nodded like that was reasonable.

Like I hadn’t been the one sitting in the hospital every night.

Like my time didn’t count because I didn’t have a wife and kids.

“Logan, grab a plate,” my aunt called, breaking the tension. “You’re skin and bones. What are you eating out there, ramen?”

Laughter again.

Same old script.

I moved toward the buffet table, aware of every glance, every whispered comment.

He always lands on his feet.

He’s just… drifting.

He’s allergic to responsibility.

They had no idea.

They didn’t know about the 3AM emails.

The ten years of hustle nobody believed in.

The meetings that went nowhere.

The savings I burned to the ground.

They didn’t know what had happened last week.

Or this morning.

They only knew the version of me they wanted to see.

Bryce followed me, still talking.

“Seriously though,” he said, lowering his voice just enough to pretend it was private while still being heard. “You should really think about getting your life together. You’re not twenty-five anymore, man.”

I loaded my plate with food I wasn’t hungry for.

“Working on it,” I muttered.

“Doing what?” he pressed. “That… app thing still? Or are you back to delivering takeout?”

He laughed before I could answer.

“Just messing with you,” he said, clapping me on the shoulder a little too hard. “Hey, someone’s gotta be the free spirit, right? The family mascot.”

The word mascot stung.

I glanced at my phone.

Notifications climbed up the screen.

Unread messages from my attorney.

A missed call from a New York number.

A text from “V” with a screenshot: Wire confirmed. It’s done. Proud of you. 💸

My chest tightened.

I locked the screen before anyone could see.

If Bryce knew the company his firm had been trying to land as a client for six months had just bought my app for eight figures…

If he knew the “mysterious tech founder” his bosses kept whispering about in meetings…

Yeah.

He’d find out soon enough.

“Attention, everyone!” Bryce’s father-in-law suddenly boomed, tapping a plastic cup with a fork. “Let’s raise a glass to our boy Bryce. Just heard he’s on track for another promotion. Team player. Family man. The example we want our kids to follow.”

Applause.

Whistles.

Bryce lifted his beer, basking in it.

“And hey,” he added, nodding toward me with a grin, “maybe one day we’ll be toasting Logan too. For… I don’t know… hitting a thousand followers on his podcast?”

More polite laughter.

My mother’s eyes flashed warning, but she stayed silent.

She always stayed silent when it was me.

I swallowed hard.

My jaw clenched.

I could feel it—the humiliation, the anger, the years of being the punchline bubbling just under my skin.

I was one insult away from walking back to my car and never coming back.

That was when it happened.

A sharp, clear voice cut through the chatter.

“Daddy!”

Everything froze.

The word hit the yard like a grenade.

Every head turned toward the side gate.

A little girl, maybe five years old, sprinted across the grass, dark curls bouncing, tiny sneakers kicking up bits of dirt.

She wasn’t one of Bryce’s kids.

Everyone knew their faces by heart from the Christmas cards.

This little girl was brand new.

My mother blinked.

My aunt frowned.

Bryce’s wife stiffened, eyes narrowing.

The little girl blew past Bryce like he didn’t exist.

Her eyes were locked on one person.

Me.

“Daddy!” she yelled again, launching herself at my chest.

I barely had time to set my plate down before she collided with me, arms wrapping around my neck like she’d done it a thousand times.

I caught her automatically.

Muscle memory.

My heart thudded against my ribs.

Conversations died mid-sentence.

Someone dropped a fork.

Bryce’s jaw actually dropped.

The whole Keller clan watched, stunned, as this tiny stranger buried her face in my shoulder like it was the safest place in the world.

“Hey, peanut,” I said softly, my voice betraying me. “You found me.”

She pulled back just enough to look at me, eyes sparkling.

“You said I could come see Grandma’s house if I finished my pancakes,” she reminded me, very seriously.

A ripple went through the crowd.

Grandma’s house.

Every gaze pivoted to my mother.

Her face had gone white.

“I—Logan?” she stammered. “Who… whose child is this?”

The gate creaked again.

Every adult who still had functioning neck muscles turned.

A woman stepped into the yard like she was walking into a boardroom.

Tall.

Black blazer over a silk top.

Heels that did not belong on grass.

Designer sunglasses pushed up into her hair.

Even the kids went quiet.

She scanned the scene in one smooth, assessing glance and then walked straight toward us, the kind of walk that said she was used to people making room when she moved.

Which they did.

“Sorry we’re late,” she said, voice warm but edged with that unmistakable city confidence. “Traffic from the airport was a nightmare.”

She leaned in, kissed my cheek, and rested a hand on my arm like it belonged there.

“Hey, stranger,” she smiled. “Ready for your big day?”

If the little girl had confused them, this shattered them.

“Logan,” Bryce’s wife managed, “who is… this?”

The woman turned, offering a polite smile.

“Vanessa Cole,” she said. “Nice to meet you all. I’ve heard… a lot.”

The name landed.

Several adults exchanged looks.

Someone whispered, “Wait, Cole? As in Cole Ventures?”

Bryce’s father-in-law choked on his drink.

“You’re… you’re with Cole Ventures?” he stuttered. “The private equity firm? We’ve been trying to get a meeting with—”

She held up a manicured hand, still smiling, but her eyes were sharp.

“We’ve met,” she said. “Multiple times.”

Her hand tightened briefly on my arm.

“With Logan.”

Silence.

My phone buzzed in my pocket.

Vanessa glanced at her watch.

“By the way,” she added, turning to me, “congratulations. The acquisition paperwork just hit my inbox. The board is thrilled. They can’t wait to announce that the founder of Loopline is officially joining as executive partner.”

Bryce’s face drained of color.

“Loopline?” he repeated, voice cracking. “You… you built Loopline?”

He looked at me like he’d never seen me before.

Loopline.

The same company his bosses had been chasing for months.

The same client whose logo was on half the slides in his last quarterly presentation.

“The new owner of your division is on that call in twenty minutes,” Vanessa said casually, nodding at my buzzing phone. “They want you on camera, by the way. They’re very big on ‘family values.’”

She let that hang.

Her gaze flicked to Bryce’s beer, his smirk, his little audience.

Logan’s little girl tugged my sleeve.

“Daddy,” she whispered loudly enough for everyone to hear, “are these the people who said you were a loser?”

Every eye snapped back to me.

Bryce’s hands clenched around his cup.

His smile was gone.

She was 17, and the law said she had to marry her rapist—or be dishonored forever.
She said no.
In 1965, Franca Viola was a teenager living in Alcamo, Sicily, when she made a decision that would change Italian history. But first, she had to survive.
Franca had ended a relationship with Filippo Melodia, a man with mafia connections who didn't accept rejection. On December 26, 1965, Melodia and a group of armed men stormed her family's home. They beat her mother. They abducted Franca and her eight-year-old brother Mariano, who tried desperately to protect his sister.
Mariano was released. Franca was not.
For eight days, she was held captive. Raped. Terrorized. And constantly pressured to agree to marry her attacker.
Because in 1965 Italy, that was the solution. That was the law.
Article 544 of the Italian Penal Code allowed a rapist to escape all punishment if he married his victim. It was called "matrimonio riparatore"—rehabilitating marriage. The idea was that marriage would "restore" the woman's honor, which had been destroyed by the rape.
Her honor. Not his crime.
This wasn't ancient history. This was 1965—the year the Beatles released "Yesterday," the year America sent troops to Vietnam. In modern Italy, rape victims were expected to marry their rapists or live as damaged, unmarriageable outcasts.
When Franca was finally released after eight days, everyone—her community, society, even some in her own family—expected her to do what women always did: accept the marriage and move on with her ruined life.
Franca Viola said no.
With her father's support, she refused to marry Filippo Melodia. Instead, she did something unprecedented: she pressed charges. She took him to court.
The backlash was immediate and brutal. Her family was shunned. Their fields were set on fire. Their name became synonymous with dishonor. In Sicily, where honor codes ran deep and mafia influence was strong, defying this tradition was dangerous.
But Franca didn't back down.
The trial became a national sensation. For the first time, Italians across the country had to confront the horror of a law that protected rapists and punished victims. Newspapers covered every detail. The country divided between those who supported Franca's courage and those who condemned her for "shaming" herself and her family.
In 1966, Filippo Melodia was convicted and sentenced to eleven years in prison.
Franca Viola became the first woman in Italian history to publicly refuse "rehabilitating marriage" and successfully prosecute her rapist.
The cultural shift was seismic. Italy's President Giuseppe Saragat received her. Pope Paul VI—the Pope himself—met with her, a quiet acknowledgment that the Church recognized something fundamental was changing.
In 1968, Franca married Giuseppe Ruisi, her childhood friend who loved her without prejudice, who saw her as a whole person rather than a "dishonored" woman. Their marriage was a statement: victims of violence deserved love, respect, and normal lives.
But the law didn't change immediately. Article 544 remained on the books.
It took fifteen more years. Fifteen years of activism, of cultural shifts, of other women finding courage in Franca's example. Finally, in 1981, the Italian Parliament abolished the "rehabilitating marriage" law.
Rapists could no longer escape justice by marrying their victims.
Franca Viola, a 17-year-old girl from Sicily who simply said "no," had helped change the law of an entire nation.
She never sought fame. She lives quietly with Giuseppe, their children and grandchildren. She rarely gives interviews. She was never interested in being a symbol—she just wanted justice for what happened to her.
But history made her a symbol anyway.
Because sometimes one person's refusal to accept injustice can crack open an entire system. Sometimes a teenage girl's courage can force a modern nation to confront laws built on ancient shame and patriarchal control.
Franca Viola proved that a woman's honor isn't defined by what's done to her—it's defined by how she responds.
She was 17 years old. The law, her community, tradition, and fear all told her to submit.
She said no.
And Italy changedforever

NGOCC chastens Simon Mwewa against making sexist remarks against female politicians.
By Vanguard reporter 

The Non-governmental Gender Organisations Coordinating Council (NGOCC) has strongly condemned what it has described as sexist and discriminatory remarks directed at women aspiring for political leadership, warning that such rhetoric fuels Violence Against Women in Elections (VAWE).

In a press statement released on Tuesday, NGOCC criticised comments aired on Simon Mwewa Lane Television on Friday, January 9, 2026, which suggested that a single woman is “unworkable” for the position of mayor and that the office should instead be reserved for a “family man.”

NGOCC Chairperson Beauty Katebe said the remarks go beyond political debate and constitute a direct violation of the spirit of the Zambian Constitution and the Gender Equity and Equality Act No. 22 of 2015. She noted that using marital status as a criterion for leadership perpetuates discrimination and undermines women’s participation in democratic processes.

“As Zambia moves toward the August 13, 2026 General Elections, such sexist narratives are designed to intimidate women and discourage them from contesting presidential, parliamentary, and local government positions,” Katebe said.

The organisation stated that judging women’s professional competence based on their private lives amounts to psychological violence, particularly as the same standard is not applied to male candidates. NGOCC warned that this rhetoric emboldens online harassment and shifts political discourse away from policy and competence toward personal attacks.

NGOCC emphasised that genuine gender equality is about fair representation and not the reinforcement of patriarchal stereotypes, adding that no candidate should be targeted on the basis of gender or marital status.

As the 2026 election cycle gains momentum, the organisation issued several demands, including an unconditional retraction from Simon Mwewa Lane Television and a commitment to more inclusive political discourse. It also called on political parties to enforce zero-tolerance policies against sexist campaigning and VAWE, and urged the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) to monitor and sanction violations of the Electoral Code of Conduct.

NGOCC further encouraged voters to reject leaders who promote division and discrimination, stressing that leadership should be assessed on vision, integrity, and competence rather than marital status.
“The leadership of a woman is not a threat to the family or the nation; it is an asset,” the statement read.

The organisation also appealed to the public to report all forms of violence — including verbal, psychological, physical, and electoral violence — through the toll-free helpline 116, noting that all reported cases would be documented and referred to relevant authorities.

NGOCC reaffirmed its commitment to advocating for a peaceful, inclusive, free, and fair electoral process ahead of the 2026 presidential, parliamentary, and local authority elections.

The Historical Value of the Cherokee People
The Cherokee people are among the most historically significant Native American nations in North America. For centuries, they have demonstrated resilience, adaptability, and cultural depth that continue to inspire today.

Ancient Roots and Culture

The Cherokee trace their roots back thousands of years in the Appalachian Mountains and surrounding regions. They developed a sophisticated society with farming, trade networks, oral traditions, and a strong spiritual connection to the land. Their communities were organized around clan systems, emphasizing kinship, responsibility, and respect for nature.

Innovation and Adaptability

One of the most remarkable aspects of Cherokee history is their ability to adapt while preserving their identity. They adopted new technologies and practices from Europeans, yet maintained their own governance, art, and traditions. Sequoyah’s invention of the Cherokee syllabary in the early 19th century became a symbol of cultural pride, giving the Cherokee one of the most advanced literacy systems among Native nations.

Struggles and Survival

The 19th century brought enormous challenges. Through forced removals such as the Trail of Tears in the 1830s, thousands of Cherokee were displaced from their homelands. Despite this tragedy, they rebuilt their communities in Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma) and preserved their traditions, language, and spirit of unity. Their survival is a testament to strength in the face of injustice.

Enduring Legacy

Today, the Cherokee Nation stands as the largest federally recognized tribe in the United States. Their contributions in education, governance, art, and cultural preservation highlight the historical value of their people. The Cherokee remind us of the importance of resilience, heritage, and the power of cultural continuity through centuries of change.

 The story of the Cherokee people is not only one of struggle but also of endurance, wisdom, and cultural richness. Their history is a vital part of the American narrative and a lasting legacy for future generations.

She was 17, and the law said she had to marry her rapist—or be dishonored forever.
She said no.
In 1965, Franca Viola was a teenager living in Alcamo, Sicily, when she made a decision that would change Italian history. But first, she had to survive.

Franca had ended a relationship with Filippo Melodia, a man with mafia connections who didn't accept rejection. On December 26, 1965, Melodia and a group of armed men stormed her family's home. They beat her mother. They abducted Franca and her eight-year-old brother Mariano, who tried desperately to protect his sister.

Mariano was released. Franca was not.
For eight days, she was held captive. Raped. Terrorized. And constantly pressured to agree to marry her attacker.

Because in 1965 Italy, that was the solution. That was the law.
Article 544 of the Italian Penal Code allowed a rapist to escape all punishment if he married his victim. It was called "matrimonio riparatore"—rehabilitating marriage. The idea was that marriage would "restore" the woman's honor, which had been destroyed by the rape.

Her honor. Not his crime.
This wasn't ancient history. This was 1965—the year the Beatles released "Yesterday," the year America sent troops to Vietnam. In modern Italy, rape victims were expected to marry their rapists or live as damaged, unmarriageable outcasts.

When Franca was finally released after eight days, everyone—her community, society, even some in her own family—expected her to do what women always did: accept the marriage and move on with her ruined life.
Franca Viola said no.
With her father's support, she refused to marry Filippo Melodia. Instead, she did something unprecedented: she pressed charges. She took him to court.
The backlash was immediate and brutal. Her family was shunned. Their fields were set on fire. Their name became synonymous with dishonor. In Sicily, where honor codes ran deep and mafia influence was strong, defying this tradition was dangerous.

But Franca didn't back down.
The trial became a national sensation. For the first time, Italians across the country had to confront the horror of a law that protected rapists and punished victims. Newspapers covered every detail. The country divided between those who supported Franca's courage and those who condemned her for "shaming" herself and her family.

In 1966, Filippo Melodia was convicted and sentenced to eleven years in prison.
Franca Viola became the first woman in Italian history to publicly refuse "rehabilitating marriage" and successfully prosecute her rapist.

The cultural shift was seismic. Italy's President Giuseppe Saragat received her. Pope Paul VI—the Pope himself—met with her, a quiet acknowledgment that the Church recognized something fundamental was changing.

In 1968, Franca married Giuseppe Ruisi, her childhood friend who loved her without prejudice, who saw her as a whole person rather than a "dishonored" woman. Their marriage was a statement: victims of violence deserved love, respect, and normal lives.
But the law didn't change immediately. Article 544 remained on the books.

It took fifteen more years. Fifteen years of activism, of cultural shifts, of other women finding courage in Franca's example. Finally, in 1981, the Italian Parliament abolished the "rehabilitating marriage" law.

Rapists could no longer escape justice by marrying their victims.
Franca Viola, a 17-year-old girl from Sicily who simply said "no," had helped change the law of an entire nation.

She never sought fame. She lives quietly with Giuseppe, their children and grandchildren. She rarely gives interviews. She was never interested in being a symbol—she just wanted justice for what happened to her.

But history made her a symbol anyway.
Because sometimes one person's refusal to accept injustice can crack open an entire system. Sometimes a teenage girl's courage can force a modern nation to confront laws built on ancient shame and patriarchal control.

Franca Viola proved that a woman's honor isn't defined by what's done to her—it's defined by how she responds.

She was 17 years old. The law, her community, tradition, and fear all told her to submit.
She said no.
And Italy changed forever.

‘Atiku, Obi can’t solve Nigeria’s problems’

Former African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate Dumebi Kachikwu, has criticised leading opposition figures Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, for not offering concrete solutions to Nigeria’s recurring crises beyond social media commentary.
Speaking on national television, Kachikwu said Nigeria’s opposition politics has been reduced to what he described as “performative outrage,” where prominent politicians react to tragedies with statements and tweets but fail to propose actionable alternatives.
According to him, whenever the country is hit by major incidents ranging from insecurity and violent crimes to economic hardship, the same political figures emerge to condemn the situation without outlining how they would address it if entrusted with power.
“In the last two years, every time we’ve had a national tragedy, all you hear from the people you mentioned Atiku, Obi is talk, mostly tweets. ‘It’s a shame,’ ‘It’s a tragedy,’ ‘We are sorry,’” Kachikwu said. “They jab at the government, but they never, ever speak to solutions.”
He argued that such responses fall short of the responsibility expected from politicians who aspire to lead a country of over 200 million people, especially given Nigeria’s persistent security and economic challenges.
Kachikwu stressed that meaningful opposition should go beyond criticism and instead present clear policy options, particularly on issues such as terrorism, kidnappings, violent crime, and governance failures. He questioned why opposition leaders have not articulated detailed plans on tackling insecurity, reforming the economy, or strengthening institutions.
The former presidential candidate warned that Nigerians must become more critical of political messaging and resist being swayed by rhetoric without substance. He maintained that without concrete proposals, repeated condemnations of government failures amount to political grandstanding rather than leadership.
Kachikwu’s remarks add to the growing debate over the quality of opposition politics ahead of the 2027 general elections, as political alignments intensify and public scrutiny of both the ruling party and opposition figures deepens.
