     Topic: Reason of the Battle

We have already spoken about Al-‘Ushairah Invasion when a caravan belonging to Quraish had escaped an imminent military encounter with the Prophet (Peace be upon him) and his men. 

When their return from Syria approached, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) despatched Talhah bin ‘Ubaidullâh and Sa‘id bin Zaid northward to scout around for any movements of this sort. The two scouts stayed at Al-Hawra’ for some days until Abu Sufyan, the leader of the caravan, passed by them. The two men hurried back to Madinah and reported to the Prophet (Peace be upon him) their findings. Great wealth amounting to 50 thousand gold Dinars guarded by 40 men moving relatively close to Madinah constituted a tempting target for the Muslim military, and provided a potentially heavy economic, political and military strike that was bound to shake the entire structure of the Makkan polytheists. 

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) immediately exhorted the Muslims to rush out and waylay the caravan to make up for their property and wealth they were forced to give up in Makkah. He did not give orders binding to everyone, but rather gave them full liberty to go out or stay back, thinking that it would be just an errand on a small scale.  The Muslim army was made up of 300-317 men, 82-86 Emigrants, 61 from Aws and 170 from Khazraj. They were not well-equipped nor adequately prepared. 

They had only two horses belonging to Az-Zubair bin Al-‘Awwam and Al-Miqdad bin Al-Aswad Al-Kindi, 70 camels, one for two or three men to ride alternatively. The Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him) himself, ‘Ali and Murthid bin Abi Murthid Al-Ghanawi had only one camel. Disposition of the affairs of Madinah was entrusted to Ibn Umm Maktum but later to Abu Lubabah bin ‘Abdul Mundhir.

 The general leadership was given to Mus‘ab bin ‘Umair Al-Qurashi Al-‘Abdari, and their standard was white in colour. The little army was divided into two battalions, the Emigrants with a standard raised by ‘Ali bin Abi Talib, and the Helpers whose standard was in the hand of Sa‘d bin Mu‘adh. 

Az-Zubair bin Al-‘Awwam was appointed to the leadership of the right flank, Al-Miqdad bin ‘Amr to lead the left flank, and the rear of the army was at the command of Qais bin Abi Sa‘sa‘ah. 

The General Commander-in-Chief was the Prophet (Peace be upon him), of course. 

The Prophet (Peace be upon him), at the head of his army, marched out along the main road leading to Makkah. He then turned left towards Badr and when he reached As-Safrâ’, he despatched two men to scout about for the camels of Quraish. 

Abu Sufyan, on the other hand, was on the utmost alert. He had already been aware that the route he was following was attended with dangers. He was also anxious to know about the movements of Muhammad (Peace be upon him). His scouting men submitted to him reports to the effect that the Muslims were lying in ambush for his caravan.

 To be on the safe side, he hired Damdam bin ‘Amr Al-Ghifari to communicate a message asking for help from the Quraishites. The messenger rode fast and reached Makkah in frenzy. Felling himself from his camel, he stood dramatically before Al-Ka‘bah, cut off the nose and the ears of the camel, turned its saddle upside down, tore off his own shirt from front and behind, and cried: “O Quraish! Your merchandise! It is with Abu Sufyan. 

The caravan is being intercepted by Muhammad (Peace be upon him) and his companions. I cannot say what would have happened to them. Help! Help!” 

The effect of this hue and cry was instantaneous and the news stunned Quraish and they immediately remembered their pride that was wounded when the Muslims had intercepted Al-Hadrami caravan. They therefore swiftly mustered almost all of their forces and none stayed behind except Abu Lahab, who delegated someone who owed him some money. They also mobilized some Arab tribes to contribute to the war against the Prophet (Peace be upon him). 

All the clans of Quraish gave their consent except Banu ‘Adi. Soon an excited throng of 1300 soldiers including 100 horsemen and 600 mailed soldiers with a large number of camels, was clamouring to proceed to fight the Muslims. For food supplies, they used to slaughter an alternate number of camels of ten and nine every day. 

They were however afraid that Banu Bakr, on account of old long deep-seated animosity, would attack their rear. At that critical moment, Iblis (Satan) appeared to them in the guise of Suraqa bin Malik bin Ju‘sham Al-Mudlaji — chief of Bani Kinana — saying to them: “I guarantee that no harm will happen from behind.” 

They set out burning with indignation, motivated by a horrible desire for revenge and exterminating anyone that might jeopardize the routes of their caravans: “…boastfully and to be seen of men, and hinder (men) from the path of Allah. ” [8:47] Or as the Prophet (Peace be upon him) said: “O Allah these are the haughty and conceited; they have come defying Allah and defying His Messenger.” They moved swiftly northward to Badr.

On the way they received another message from Abu Sufyan asking them to go back home because the caravan had escaped the Muslims. Incidentally, Abu Sufyan, on learning the intention of the Muslims, led his caravan off the main route, and inclined it towards the Red Sea. By this manoeuvre, he was able to slip past the Madinese ambush and was out of their reach. 

On receiving Abu Sufyan’s message, the Makkan army showed a desire to return home. The tyrant Abu Jahl, however haughtily and arrogantly insisted that they proceed to Badr, stay three nights there for making festivities. Now they wanted to punish the Muslims and prevent them from intercepting their caravans, and impress on the Arabs that Quraish still had the upper hand and enjoyed supremacy in that area. 

Abu Jahl’s threats and insistence notwithstanding, Banu Zahrah, acting on the advice of Al-Akhnas bin Shuraiq, broke away and returned to Makkah. Thenceforth Al-Akhnas remained ‘the well-rubbed palm tree’ for Bani Zahrah and was blindly obeyed in all relevant matters. Banu Hashim were also inclined to break away, but Abu Jahl’s threats made them desist from that idea. 

The rest of the army, now 1000 soldiers, approached Badr and encamped themselves beyond a sand dune at Al-‘Udwat Al-Quswa. 

‘The intelligence corps’ of the Madinese army reported to the Prophet (Peace be upon him) that a bloody encounter with the Makkans was inescapable, and that a daring step in this context had to be taken, or else the forces of evil would violate the inviolable and would consequently manage to undermine the noble cause of the Islam and tread upon its faithful adherents. 

The Muslims were afraid that the pagan Makkans would march on and start the war activities within the headquarters of Islam, Madinah. A move of such nature would certainly damage and produce an infamous impact on the dignity and stance of the Muslims. 

On account of the new grave developments, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) held an advisory military emergency meeting to review the ongoing situation and exchange viewpoints with the army leaders. Admittedly, some Muslims feared the horrible encounter and their courage began to waver; in this regard, Allah says: 

“As your Lord caused you (O Muhammad [Peace be upon him) ] to go out from your home with the Truth, and verily, a party among the believers disliked it, disputing with you concerning the Truth after it was made manifest, as if they were being driven to death while they were looking (at it).” [8:5, 6] 

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) apprised his men of the gravity of the situation and asked for their advice. Abu Bakr was the first who spoke on the occasion and assured the Prophet (Peace be upon him) of the unreserved obedience to his command. 

‘Umar was the next to stand up and supported the views expressed by his noble friend. Then Al-Miqdad bin ‘Amr got up and said: “O Messenger of Allah! Proceed where Allah directs you to, for we are with you. We will not say as the Children of Israel said to Moses (Peace be upon him): “Go you and your Lord and fight and we will stay here;” Rather we shall say: “Go you and yourLord and fight and we will fight along with you.” By Allah! If you were to take us to Bark Al-Ghimad, we will still fight resolutely with you against its defenders until you gained it.” 

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) thanked him and blessed him. 

The three leaders who spoke were from the Emigrants, who only constituted a minor section of the army. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) wanted, and for the more reason, to hear the Helpers’ view because they were the majority of the soldiers and were expected to shoulder the brunt of the war activities. Moreover, the clauses of Al-‘Aqabah Pledge did not commit them to fighting beyond their territories. 

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) then said: “Advise me my men!” by which he meant the Helpers, in particular. Upon this Sa‘d bin Mu‘adh stood up and said: “By Allah, I feel you want us (the Helpers) to speak.” The Prophet (Peace be upon him) directly said: “Oh, yes!”

 Sa‘d said: “O Prophet of Allah! We believe in you and we bear witness to what you have vouchsafed to us and we declare in unequivocal terms that what you have brought is the Truth. We give you our firm pledge of obedience and sacrifice. We will obey you most willingly in whatever you command us, and by Allah, Who has sent you with the Truth, if you were to ask us to plunge into the sea, we will do that most readily and not a man of us will stay behind. We do not grudge the idea of encounter with the enemy. We are experienced in war and we are trustworthy in combat. We hope that Allah will show you through our hands those deeds of valour which will please your eyes. Kindly lead us to the battlefield in the Name of Allah.” 

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) was impressed with the fidelity and the spirit of sacrifice which his companions showed at this critical juncture. 

Then he said to them: “Forward and be of cheer, for Allah has promised me one of the two (the lucrative course through capturing the booty or strife in the cause of Allah against the polytheists), and by Allah it is as if I now saw the enemy lying prostrate.” 

In the immediate vicinity of Badr, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) and his cavemate Abu Bakr conducted a scouting operation during which they managed to locate the camp of Quraish. They came across an old bedouin nearby whom they manipulated and managed to extract from him the exact location of the army of the polytheists. 

In the evening of the same day, he despatched three Emigrant leaders, ‘Ali bin Abi Talib, Az-Zubair bin Al-‘Awwam and Sa‘d bin Abi Waqqas to scout about for news about the enemy. They saw two men drawing water for the Makkan army. On interrogation, they admitted that they were water carriers working for Quraish. 

But that answer did not please some Muslims and they beat the two boys severely in order to exact from them an answer, even if it isn’t true, alluding to the caravan laden with wealth. The two boys thus lied, and so they were released. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) was angry with those men and censured them saying: “On telling the truth, you beat them, and on telling a lie, you released them!” He then addressed the two boys and after a little conversation with them he learned a lot about the enemy: number of soldiers, their exact location and names of some of their notables.

He then turned to the Muslims and said: “Hearken, Quraish has sent you their most precious lives.” The same night it rained on both sides. For the polytheists it obstructed further progress, whereas it was a blessing for the Muslims. It cleaned them and removed from them the stain of Satan. Allah sent rain to strengthen their hearts and to plant their feet firmly therewith. They marched a little forward and encamped at the farther bank of the valley. Muhammad (Peace be upon him) stopped at the nearest spring of Badr.

Al-Hubab bin Mundhir asked him, “Has Allah inspired you to choose this very spot or is it stratagem of war and the product of consultation?” The Prophet (Peace be upon him) replied “It is stratagem of war and consultation.” Al-Hubab said: “This place is no good; let us go and encamp on the nearest water well and make a basin or reservoir full of water, then destroy all the other wells so that they will be deprived of the water.” 

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) approved of his plan and agreed to carry it out, which they actually did at midnight. 

Sa‘d bin Mu‘adh suggested that a trellis be built for the Prophet (Peace be upon him) to function as headquarters for the Muslim army and a place providing reasonable protection for the leader. Sa‘d began to justify his proposal and said that if they had been victorious, then everything would be satisfactory.

 In case of defeat, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) would not be harmed and he could go back to Madinah where there were more people who loved him and who would have come for help if they had known that he was in that difficult situation, so that he would resume his job, hold counsel with them and they would strive in the cause of Allah with him again and again. 

A squad of guards was also chosen from amongst the Helpers under the leadership of the same man, Sa‘d bin Mu‘adh, in order to defend the Prophet (Peace be upon him) in his headquarters. 

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) spent the whole night preceding the day of the battle in prayer and supplication. The Muslim army, wearied with their long march, enjoyed sound and refreshing sleep, a mark of the Divine favour and of the state of their undisturbed minds.

 “(Remember) when He covered you with a slumber as a security from Him, and He caused rain to descend on you from the sky, to clean you thereby and to remove from you the Rijz (whispering, evil suggestions, etc.) of Satan, and to strengthen your hearts, and make your feet firm thereby.” [8:11] 

That was Friday night, Ramadan 17th., the year 2 A.H. 

In the morning, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) called his men to offer the prayers and then urged them to fight in the way of Allah. As the sun rose over the desert, the Prophet(Peace be upon him) drew up his little army, and pointing with an arrow which he held in his hand, arranged the ranks. 

Quraish, on the other hand, positioned their forces in Al-‘Udwat Al-Quswa opposite the Muslim lines. A few of them approached, in a provocative deed, to draw water from the wells of Badr, but were all shot dead except one, Hakeem bin Hizam, who later became a devoted Muslim.

 ‘Umair bin Wahab Al-Jumahi, in an attempt to reconnoiter the power of the Muslims, made a scouting errand and submitted a report saying that the Muslim army numbered as many as 300 men keen on fighting to the last man. 

On another reconnaissance mission he came to the conclusion that neither reinforcements were coming nor ambushes laid. He understood that they were too brave to surrender and too intent on carrying out their military duties to withdraw without slaying the largest number possible of the polytheists. 

This report as well as kindred relations binding the two belligerent parties together, slackened the desire to fight among some of the Quraishites. To counteract this reason-based opposition advocated by a rival of his, ‘Utbah bin Rabi‘a and others, Abu Jahl started an anti-campaign seeking vengeance on Muhammad’s followers for the Quraishites killed at Nakhlah.

In this way, he managed to thwart the opposite orientation, and manipulated the people to see his evil views only. 

When the two parties approached closer and were visible to each other, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) began supplicating Allah “O Allah! The conceited and haughty Quraishites are already here defying You and belying Your Messenger. O Allah! I am waiting for Your victory which You have promised me. I beseech You Allah to defeat them (the enemies).” 

He also gave strict orders that his men would not start fighting until he gave them his final word. He recommended that they use their arrows sparingly and never resort to sword unless the enemies came too close. 

Abu Jahl also prayed for victory, saying: “Our Lord, whichever of the two parties was less kind to his relatives, and brought us what we do not know, then destroy him tomorrow.”. 

They were confident ththeir superior number, equipment and experience would be decisive. The Noble Qur’ân, with a play on the word, told them that the decision had come, and the victory — but not in the sense they had hoped for: “(O disbelievers) if you ask for a judgement, now has the judgement come unto you and if you cease (to do wrong), it will be better for you, and if you return (to the attack), so shall we return, and your forces will be of no avail to you, however numerous it be, and verily, Allah is with the believers.” [8:19] 

The first disbeliever to trigger the fire of the battle and be its first victim was Al-Aswad bin ‘Abdul Asad Al-Makhzumi, a fierce bad-tempered idolater. He stepped out swearing he would drink from the water basin of the Muslims, otherwise, destroy it or die for it. 

He engaged with Hamzah bin ‘Abdul Muttalib, who struck his leg with his sword and dealt him another blow that finished him off inside the basin. 

The battle had actually started. Protected by armour and shields, ‘Utbah bin Rabi‘a stepped forth between his brother Shaibah and his son Al-Waleed bin ‘Utbah from the lines of Quraish and hurled maledictions at the Muslims. 

Three young men of the Helpers came out against them: ‘Awf and Mu‘wwadh — the sons of Harith, and ‘Abdullah bin Rawaha. But the Makkans yelled that they had nothing to do with them. They wanted the heads of their cousins. 

Upon this the Prophet (Peace be upon him) asked ‘Ubaidah bin Al-Harith, Hamzah — his uncle, and his cousin ‘Ali (May Allah be pleased with him) to go forward for the combat. The three duels were rapid. Hamzah killed Shaibah, while ‘Ali killed Al-Waleed. ‘Ubaidah was seriously wounded but, before he fell, Hamzah fell upon ‘Utbah and with a sweep of his sword, cut off his head. ‘Ali and Hamzah carried ‘Ubaidah back with his leg cut off. 

He died four or five days later of a disease in the bile duct. 

‘Ali was possessed of a deep conviction that Allah’s Words were revealed: “These two opponents (believers and disbelievers) dispute with each other about their Lord.” [22:19] 

These verses were revealed in connection with men of Faith who confess their Lord and seek to carry out His Will (i.e. Muhammad ’s followers at Badr Battle), and men who deny their Lord and defy Him (the people of Quraish). 

The duel was followed by a few more duels but the Makkans suffered terrible defeats in all the combats and lost some of their most precious lives. They were too much exasperated and enraged and fell upon the Muslims to exterminate them once and for all. The Muslims, however, after supplicating their Lord, calling upon Him for assistance, were made to hold to their position and conduct a defensive war plan that was successful enough to inflict heavy losses on the attackers.

 The Prophet (Peace be upon him) used to pray to his Lord ceaselessly persistently and day and night to come to their succour. When the fierce engagement grew too hot he again began to supplicate his Lord saying:

 “O Allah! Should this group (of Muslims) be defeated today, You will no longer be worshipped.” 

He continued to call out to his Lord, stretching forth his hands and facing Al-Qiblah, until his cloak fell off his shoulders. Then Abu Bakr came, picked up the cloak, and put it back on his shoulders and said: “O Prophet of Allah, you have cried out enough to your Lord. He will surely fulfill what He has promised you.” 

Immediate was the response from Allah, Who sent down angels from the heavens for the help and assistance of the Prophet (Peace be upon him) and his companions. The Noble Qur’ân observes: “Verily, I am with you, so keep firm those who have believed. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who have disbelieved.” [8:12] 

Allah, the All-Mighty, also inspired another message to His Messenger, saying: “I will help you with a thousand of the angels each behind the other (following one another) in succession.” [8:9]

 The Prophet (Peace be upon him), in his trellis, dozed off a little and then raised his head joyfully crying: “O Abu Bakr, glad tidings are there for you: Allah’s victory has approached, by Allah, I can see Gabriel on his mare in the thick of a sandstorm.” He then jumped out crying: “Their multitude will be put to flight, and they will show their backs.” [54:45] 

At the instance of Gabriel, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) took a handful of gravel, cast it at the enemy and said: “Confusion seize their faces!” 

As he flung the dust, a violent sandstorm blew like furnace blast into the eyes of the enemies. With respect to this, Allah says: 

“And you [i.e. Muhammad (Peace be upon him) ] threw not when you did throw but Allah threw.” [8:17] 

Only then did he give clear orders to launch a counter-attack. He was commanding the army, inspiring confidence among his men and exhorting them to fight manfully for the sake of their Lord, reciting the Words of Allah: “And be quick for forgiveness from your Lord, and for Paradise as wide as are the heavens and the earth.” [3:133] 

The spirit he infused into his men was clearly witnessed by the valour of ‘Umair, a lad of sixteen, who flung away some dates he was eating crying out: 

“These (the dates) are holding me back from Paradise.” 

So saying he plunged into the thick of the battle and died fighting bravely. Unique deeds of valour, deep devotion and full obedience to the Prophet (Peace be upon him) were exhibited in the process of the battle. The army of the faithfuls was borne forward by the power of enthusiasm which the half-hearted warriors of Makkah miserably lacked. 

A large number of the polytheists were killed and the others began to waver. No wonder! The standard-bearers of Truth were given immediate help, and supernatural agencies (the angels), were sent to their assistance by their Lord to help them defeat the forces of evil. 

The records of Hadith speak eloquently of the fact that the angels did appear on that day and fought on the side of the Muslims. 

Ibn ‘Abbas said: “While on that day a Muslim was chasing a disbeliever and he heard over him the swashing of a whip and the voice of the rider saying: ‘Go ahead Haizum’. 

He glanced at the polytheist who had (now) fallen down on his back. The Helper came to the Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him) and related that event to him. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) replied: ‘You have told the truth. This was the help from the third heaven.” 

One of the Helpers captured ‘Abbas bin ‘Abdul Muttalib, who said: “O Messenger of Allah, by Allah this man did not capture me. I was captured by a man who was bald and had the most handsome face, and who was riding a piebald horse, I cannot see him here among the people.”

 The Helper interrupted: “I captured him, O Messenger of Allah.” The Prophet (Peace be upon him) replied: “Be quiet, Allah the All-Mighty strengthened you with the help of a noble angel.” Iblîs, the archsatan, in the guise of Suraqah bin Malik bin Ju‘sham Al-Mudlaji, on seeing angels working in favour of the Muslims, and Quraish rapidly losing ground on the battlefield, made a quick retreat despite the polytheists’ pleas to stay on. He ran off and plunged into the sea. 

The ranks of Quraish began to give way and their numbers added nothing but confusion. The Muslims followed eagerly their retreating steps, slaying or taking captive all that fell within their reach. Retreat soon turned into ignominious rout; and they flied in haste, casting away their armour, abandoned beasts of burden, camp and equipage. 

The great tyrant Abu Jahl, however, on seeing the adverse course of the battle, tried to stop the tidal wave of the Islamic victory by nerving the polytheists and encouraging them by all means available and adjuring them by Al-Lat and ‘Uzza and all symbols of paganism to stand firm in place and retaliate against the Muslims, but to no avail. Their morale had already been drastically reduced to zero, and their lines broken down. He then began to realize the reality of his arrogance and haughtiness. None remained around him except a gang of doomed polytheists whose resistance was also quelled by an Islamic irresistible storm of true devotion-based valour and Islam-orientated pursuit of martyrdom. Jahl was deserted and left by himself on his horse waiting for death at the hand of two courageous lads of the Helpers.

‘Abdur-Rahman bin ‘Awf related the following interesting story in this regard: I was in the thick of the battle when two youths, still seemingly inexperienced in the art of fighting, one on the right and the second on the left. One of them spoke in a secret voice asking me to show him Abu Jahl. I asked about his intention, to which he replied, that he had a strong desire to engage with him in a combat until either of them was killed. It was something incredible to me. I turned left and the other said something to the same effect and showed a similar desire. I acceded to their earnest pleas and pointed directly at their target. 

They both rushed swiftly towards the spot, and without a moment’s hesitation struck him simultaneously with their swords and finished him off. 

They went back to the Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him), each claiming that he had killed Abu Jahl to the exclusion of the other. 

The Prophet (Peace be upon him)asked if they had wiped the blood off their swords and they answered that they had not. He then examined both swords and assured them that they both had killed him.

 When the battle concluded, Abu Jahl’s spoils were given to Mu‘adh bin ‘Amr bin Al-Jumuh, because the other Mu‘awwadh bin Al-‘Afrâ’ was later killed in the course of the same battle. At the termination of the battle, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) wanted to look for this archenemy of Islam, Abu Jahl. ‘Abdullah bin Mas‘ud found him on the verge of death breathing his last.

 He stepped on his neck addressing him: “Have you seen how Allah has disgraced you?” The enemy of Islam still defiantly answered: “I am not disgraced. I am no more than a man killed by his own people on the battlefield.” And then inquired “Who has won the battle?” Ibn Mas‘ud replied “Allah and His Messenger.”

 Abu Jahl then said with a heart full of grudge “You have followed difficult ways, you shepherd!” Ibn Mas‘ud used to be a shepherd working for the Makkan aristocrats. 

Ibn Mas‘ud then cut off his head and took it to the Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him) who, on seeing it, began to entertain Allah’s praise: “Allah is Great, praise is to Allah, Who has fulfilled His Promise, assisted His servant and defeated the confederates alone.” 

He then set out to have a look at the corpse. 

There he said: “This is the Pharaoh of this nation.”

WHAT’S UP NEW BRUNSWICK 

By Cory Dewitt — The News Guy 

Digital Creator | Business Owner | Community News & Awareness 

Human trafficking isn’t what movies make it out to be. It rarely looks like dramatic kidnappings or people chained in dark rooms. Most of the time, it’s quiet, gradual, and hidden in plain sight — happening in homes, workplaces, hotels, online spaces, farms, and small communities, including right here in New Brunswick.
Trafficking is built on force, fraud, or coercion — often by someone the victim knows and trusts. It exploits vulnerability, not weakness. Poverty, housing insecurity, past trauma, addiction, isolation, and discrimination are commonly targeted — and victims are slowly groomed into dependence before they even realize what’s happening.
Leaving isn’t simple. Many victims don’t identify as victims. Others fear violence, retaliation, homelessness, or harm to loved ones. For some, the trafficker is the only source of food, shelter, or emotional connection they have left.
Labor trafficking is just as real — and just as overlooked. It often begins as a job offer and turns into withheld wages, threats, stolen documents, debt bondage, or exploitation tied to immigration status. Agriculture, construction, hospitality, caregiving, and seasonal work are common risk areas across Canada.
In New Brunswick, trafficking is often invisible because it blends into everyday life. Small communities don’t protect people — they can actually make exploitation easier to hide. Many victims appear “fine” to the outside world. That invisibility is what allows abuse to continue.
---
WHAT THE PUBLIC SHOULD KNOW
Trafficking is about patterns, not single signs:
Someone can’t speak freely or seems coached
No access to ID, money, or a phone
Fear, anxiety, or extreme control by another person
Living and working in the same place
Owing unexplained “debts”
Sudden changes in behavior or appearance
Myths hurt victims.
Most people know their trafficker. Men, women, and gender-diverse people are trafficked. Rescue alone doesn’t fix everything — long-term, voluntary support does.
---
HOW YOU CAN HELP
Learn how trafficking actually works — not just the stereotypes
Share accurate information and support resources
Support local shelters, outreach programs, and survivor-led organizations
Ask practical, non-judgmental questions when something feels off
Remember: awareness and compassion save lives
Based in Moncton, New Brunswick, What’s Up New Brunswick delivers real stories that matter to real people — from breaking local news and community alerts to in-depth awareness pieces that don’t shy away from hard truths.
Founded and run by Cory Dewitt, the page focuses on:
Local news & community issues
Public safety & awareness
Human-interest stories
Advocacy, accountability, and education
This isn’t clickbait. It’s information people need — shared clearly, responsibly, and with compassion.
FINAL WORD
Human trafficking isn’t “somewhere else’s problem.” It’s local, hidden, and sustained by silence and misinformation. When communities understand what trafficking really looks like, people get seen — and lives can change.
One informed person can make the difference.
— What's Up New Brunswick

Samuel Jackson, “Stop Blaming the Dead”: Liberian Economist Challenges Post-War Leadership on Poverty and Accountability

By: Julius Konton 

A Century of Promises, Decades of Excuses
More than one hundred years after Firestone Rubber Company established operations in Liberia, and twenty-three years after the guns of civil war fell silent, the country remains trapped in what critics describe as structural poverty, weak governance, and chronic leadership failure.

That stark verdict has been delivered once again , this time by Liberian economist Samuel Jackson, whose latest commentary has ignited intense national debate and exposed uncomfortable comparisons between Liberia and global success stories.

“Liberia should not be celebrating a US$1.2 billion national budget,” Jackson argues, “when Singapore with nearly the same population operates a US$143 billion budget and a GDP that dwarfs ours by hundreds of billions.”

The Numbers That Shame a Nation

Liberia, with a population of approximately 5.3 million, currently records a GDP of about US$4.7 billion, according to World Bank estimates.

 By contrast, Singapore, home to roughly 5.9 million people, boasts a GDP of approximately US$647 billion more than 137 times larger.

For Jackson, the comparison is not meant to flatter Singapore, but to expose Liberia’s governance deficit.

“Population is not our problem,” he insists.

 “Leadership is. Vision is. Accountability is.”

He further highlights Singapore’s direct social support system, where:
Every household receives about US$800 in government vouchers, and

Every citizen turning 21 receives between US$600 and US$800 in state support.

“In Liberia,” Jackson notes, “citizens receive speeches, slogans, and excuses but little economic dignity.”

“Stop Blaming the Dead”

Perhaps the most controversial aspect of Jackson’s argument is his outright rejection of Liberia’s long-standing habit of blaming historical figures for present failures.

Former President Samuel K. Doe died nearly 36 years ago.

Former President Charles Taylor was removed from power nearly 23 years ago.

“Why are we still blaming them?” Jackson asks.

“How long does a nation mourn before it takes responsibility?”

According to him, Liberia has experienced 23 uninterrupted years of post-war governance, with no armed conflict, no rebel factions, and billions of dollars in aid, loans, and concessions.

“There has been no gunfire only logos, slogans, and branding,” he writes, mocking what he calls the politics of public relations over policy substance.

Concessions, Corruption, and a Bloated State

Jackson points to structural corruption, opaque concession agreements, and an overextended civil service estimated at over 70,000 government employees as key drivers of Liberia’s economic paralysis.

“These concessions enrich companies and political elites,” he argues, “but they leave communities poor, roads broken, and hospitals empty.”

He describes it as a post-war political economy designed for survival, not development, one that prioritizes loyalty networks over productivity.

A Direct Attack on the ‘Rescue Mission’ Narrative

Jackson reserves his harshest criticism for members of the current political leadership, particularly those now governing under slogans such as “Rescue Mission” and “Love Liberia.”

“I am surprised,” he writes, “to now see leaders claiming to love Liberia after years of rhetoric that damaged the country’s image.”

He recalls past political campaigns that accused former President George Weah of:
Being an alleged drug dealer,

Orchestrating a fake US$16 billion ‘missing money’ scandal,

Even spreading claims that young people were killed for ritual purposes.

“Was that loving Liberia?” Jackson asks pointedly.

“Or was it political desperation disguised as activism?”

He further criticizes past calls for U.S. sanctions against Liberia, arguing that such actions undermined investor confidence and national credibility.

A Generational Reckoning

At the core of Jackson’s argument is a demand for generational accountability.

“It is ignorant,” he writes, “to keep blaming old men and women who were caught up in the chaos of 1980, instead of demanding results from those who have governed peacefully for more than two decades.”

For him, Liberia’s tragedy is no longer war, it is wasted peace.

Poverty Is a Choice, Not a Curse

Jackson’s critique has divided public opinion, with supporters praising his brutal honesty, while critics accuse him of oversimplifying Liberia’s historical challenges.

Yet one reality remains difficult to dismiss: Liberia has had peace, time, and resources but little transformation.

As Jackson bluntly concludes:
“Poverty in Liberia is no longer inherited. It is maintained.”

German soldiers called them "Night Witches"—and learned to fear the sound of silence in the dark.Summer of 1942. German forces occupying Soviet territory. A soldier on night watch hears something—a faint whooshing sound, like fabric tearing through air. He looks up but sees nothing in the darkness. Then silence.Then explosions.By the time he realizes what's happening, the bombs have already fallen. His anti-aircraft guns fire uselessly into empty sky. Whatever attacked them is already gone, vanishing into the night like ghosts.The Germans had a name for these phantom attackers: Nachthexen. Night Witches.They were right to be afraid.What they didn't know—what would have shocked them even more—was that these pilots terrorizing the Wehrmacht's finest soldiers were women. Young Soviet women, many still teenagers, flying wood-and-canvas biplanes that had been obsolete before the war even started.And one of the deadliest among them was 19-year-old Nadezhda Popova. Nadezhda—"Nadya" to her friends—had wanted to fly since she was 15, when she first saw a biplane soaring over her village. By 16, she'd joined a flying club. By 19, when Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, she was already a trained pilot watching her country burn.The Soviet Air Force initially refused women pilots. But as casualties mounted and the Nazi advance seemed unstoppable, desperation opened doors that had been previously locked. Aviation hero Marina Raskova lobbied Stalin personally to create all-female aviation units.In October 1941, Stalin approved three regiments of women pilots, navigators, and ground crew. Nadezhda Popova enlisted immediately in the 588th Night Bomber Regiment—later renamed the 46th Taman Guards Night Bomber Aviation Regiment after earning "Guards" status for their valor.They were given the worst planes in the Soviet arsenal: Polikarpov Po-2 biplanes. These were crop-dusting aircraft, training planes—flimsy open-cockpit contraptions made of plywood and canvas that could barely fly over 90 mph. They had no radios, no guns, no armor, no parachutes, no enclosed cockpits. In winter, the pilots flew in temperatures that could reach -40°C (-40°F), the wind tearing at their faces.The male pilots laughed at them. Mechanics refused to work on "toy planes for little girls." Even other Soviet airwomen flying more modern fighters looked down on the Po-2 pilots.But Nadezhda and her sisters turned limitations into weapons.Because the Po-2 was made of wood and canvas, it didn't show up well on radar. Because it flew low and slow—sometimes just 500 feet off the ground—it was nearly impossible to track. And because it had a small engine, they could do something no modern plane could do: shut off the engine mid-flight and glide.This is what created the "Night Witch" terror.A typical mission worked like this: Nadya and her navigator (who sat in a separate open cockpit behind her) would take off at dusk carrying bombs—often 4-6 bombs weighing 50-100kg each, strapped under the wings and fuselage. They'd fly to the front lines, locate their target, then climb to about 3,000 feet.Then Nadezhda would cut the engine.The plane would go nearly silent—just the whisper of wind through canvas and wires, like a ghost ship sailing through darkness. She'd glide over German positions, her navigator dropping bombs by hand over the side of the cockpit, and they'd be gone before the Germans even knew what hit them.The Germans tried everything to stop them. Searchlights, anti-aircraft guns, fighter planes. But the Po-2 flew too low and too slow for fighters—German Messerschmitts kept stalling out trying to fly slowly enough to target them. The Po-2's maximum speed was slower than a Messerschmitt's stall speed, which meant the Night Witches could dodge by simply flying normally while the German fighters had to break off or crash.So the Germans offered bounties. Any pilot who shot down a Night Witch received an automatic Iron Cross—the same decoration they gave for shooting down a large bomber or 10 regular fighters. That's how much the Germans feared these women in their plywood planes.But terror had a cost.On the night of July 24-25, 1942, Nadezhda Popova and her navigator Yekaterina Ryabova flew 18 bombing sorties. Eighteen. In a single night. That meant 18 takeoffs, 18 times cutting the engine and gliding into enemy fire, 18 times finding their way back in darkness to reload and refuel.Each sortie took about 40 minutes round trip. They flew continuously from dusk until dawn with barely enough time between missions to refuel, reload bombs, and grab water. No food. No rest. Just mission after mission after mission while German guns filled the sky with tracers trying to kill them.By the 18th sortie, both women were beyond exhaustion. Their hands were cramping from the cold and gripping the controls. Their eyes burned from searching through darkness for landmarks. But they kept flying because their ground forces needed them, because German positions needed to be destroyed, because stopping meant someone else would die.This wasn't unusual for Nadya. This was her job. And she was exceptional at it.Over the course of the war, Nadezhda Popova flew 852 combat missions—more missions than most pilots flew in a lifetime. She was shot down multiple times, making emergency landings behind enemy lines. She had to dodge searchlights, tracers, and German fighters nearly every single night. She lost friends—so many friends—shot down or killed in crashes or dying from wounds sustained in the freezing open cockpits.The mortality rate for Night Witches was staggering. Of the roughly 400 women who served in the regiment throughout the war, 30 were killed in action—a 7.5% death rate. But the psychological toll was even higher. These women flew night after night after night with death constantly inches away, in planes that could catch fire instantly if hit, with no parachutes to escape if things went wrong.And Nadya kept flying.By the end of the war, she'd been awarded the Hero of the Soviet Union—the USSR's highest military honor—along with numerous other decorations. Her navigator Yekaterina Ryabova (who'd flown that legendary 18-sortie night with her) also received the Hero of the Soviet Union.The 46th Guards Regiment had dropped over 23,000 tons of bombs on German forces and flown more than 23,000 sorties—more than 30,000 if you count training and transport missions. These women in their "toy planes" had terrorized the Wehrmacht across the Eastern Front, from Stalingrad to Berlin.But when the war ended, Soviet society had complicated feelings about its women warriors. Stalin wanted everyone to return to traditional gender roles. The Night Witches were heroines, yes—but they were also reminders of desperate times, of moments when the motherland had needed even its daughters to fight.Many Night Witches struggled with civilian life. How do you go back to being "normal" after you've been a warrior? How do you adjust to peace after years of nightly combat? Nadezhda married a fellow pilot, Semyon Kharlamov, who she'd met during the war. They understood each other in ways civilians couldn't. They'd both seen the same darkness, lived in the same constant presence of death.For decades, the Night Witches' story was known mainly in the Soviet Union and later Russia. The West barely knew they existed. When they were mentioned, it was often with skepticism—propaganda, exaggeration, surely women couldn't have actually done that.But the German war diaries confirm it. The accounts from Soviet ground forces confirm it. The 23 Night Witches who received Hero of the Soviet Union confirm it. The German soldiers who heard that whisper of canvas in the dark and knew what was coming—they confirm it most of all.Nadezhda Popova lived until July 8, 2013, dying at age 91. Near the end of her life, as the Night Witches' story finally reached international audiences, she gave interviews about her service. She was asked if she'd ever been afraid."Of course I was afraid," she said. "Every night. But fear didn't matter. The mission mattered. Our soldiers on the ground mattered. Stopping the fascists mattered."She was asked what she wanted people to remember about the Night Witches."Remember that we were soldiers," she said. "Not curiosities, not propaganda—soldiers who did our duty. We didn't ask for special treatment. We asked for the chance to fight. And when they finally gave us that chance, we proved we belonged in the sky."In 1995, British historian Anne Noggle published a book about the Night Witches that brought their story to English-speaking audiences. Modern historians now recognize the 588th/46th Guards as one of the most effective light bomber units of World War II, regardless of gender.Video games and movies have started featuring them—their story is simply too extraordinary to ignore any longer. "Night Witches" has become a symbol of courage, skill, and defying expectations.But perhaps the truest measure of the Night Witches' effectiveness is this: the Germans were so terrified of them that any German pilot who shot one down received an automatic Iron Cross, their highest military honor. Think about that. The Wehrmacht, one of the most powerful militaries in history, feared women flying wood-and-canvas biplanes so much that they made killing them equivalent to destroying 10 regular aircraft.That's not propaganda. That's respect born from terror.The next time you hear silence in the darkness, remember Nadezhda Popova, 19 years old, cutting her engine and gliding through enemy fire to drop bombs on German positions, then somehow making it back to do it again and again and again, 852 times, until the war was won.The Night Witches didn't just fight in World War II. They proved that courage has no gender, that outdated equipment wielded by brilliant tacticians beats superior technology wielded by arrogance, and that sometimes the most terrifying thing in warfare isn't the roar of a massive bomber—it's the whisper of canvas wings in the dark

First, the assertion that Samoans are blindly supporting Israel or seeking validation from foreign nations oversimplifies the motivations and perspectives within our community. Many Samoans engage thoughtfully with international relationships, weighing the potential benefits and risks for our nation. Suggesting that our people are “championing the death of innocent indigenous people” is an unfair generalization. Samoans, like others, hold diverse views and often advocate for peace, justice, and dignity for all. To reduce our community’s position to mere desperation or ignorance does not do justice to the complexity of our values and decisions.
Second, regarding the influence of ancestry—whether German, Samoan, or otherwise—identity is deeply personal and multifaceted. While historical ties can shape our sense of belonging, they do not define our worth or the legitimacy of our voice in global or local matters. Dismissing someone’s contributions or character based solely on their last name or heritage undermines the very inclusivity and respect that we strive for as a community.
Finally, dialogue about international affairs and heritage should be rooted in constructive engagement rather than divisive rhetoric. As highlighted in the surrounding context, addressing challenges—whether related to youth, family, or national identity—requires collective responsibility and thoughtful action. Let us focus on fostering unity, understanding, and authentic representation, rather than perpetuating blame or shame. Fonoia

Oscar Mbo is back in the spotlight and not for his music. The deep house DJ and podcaster is facing serious allegations after his ex-girlfriend Ursula Dlamini shared disturbing claims on her Instagram close friends stories. Her emotional post, which later leaked online, includes photos showing her face bruised and swollen, with captions describing years of alleged abuse at the hands of Oscar.

Fans are divided, some are calling for accountability, others are asking for more evidence. THE ADO KINGSHIP 👑

With profound gratitude to God, we celebrate the Proclamation, Coronation, and Enthronement of His Royal Majesty, King Dr. Godknows Okubienembofori Tam-George Dokube (Ado X) as Amanyanabo of Okrika Kingdom and Clan Head of Wakirike, duly installed by the revered Egweme King Makers of Okrika Kingdom.

The Ado Throne, founded in 1605 by King Ado, is one of the most ancient and respected traditional institutions in the Niger Delta, standing strong for 421 years. 

The throne is seated in Kirike Town, one of the Nine Clans of Okrika Kingdom (Wakirike), and reigns supreme over the entire kingdom.

Historically known as the “Treaty Kingship,” the Ado Throne led Okrika into significant treaties with European powers in the 19th century and was instrumental in the acceptance of Christianity in Wakirike. 

The throne fostered a historic relationship with Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther, the first African Bishop, and Venerable Dandeson Coates Crowther, leading to the establishment of the mission station and the building of the iconic St. Peter’s Cathedral Church, Okrika—the pride of Christianity in Wakirike Nation.

CHRONOLOGY OF THE ADO THRONE
King Ado — Ado I (1605–1650)
King Dokube — Ado II (1655–1690)
King Boka — Ado III (1690–1750)
King Nemiduko — Ado IV (1760–1815)
King Fibika — Ado V (1832–1874)
King Ibanichuka — Ado VI (1876–1896)
King Zed T. Fibika — Ado VII (1959–1960)
King S. P. U. Ogan — Ado VIII (1964–1997)
King A. S. Abam — Ado IX (1999–2024)
King G. T-G. Dokube — Ado X (2026– )

The peaceful and historic coronation of HRM King Dr. Godknows O. Tam-George Dokube (Ado X) commenced on Monday, 5th January 2026, as the entire Wakirike Nation rolled out drums and colours in joyful celebration. 

The week-long festivities culminated on Sunday, 11th January 2026, with a solemn Thanksgiving Service at the Altar of Grace, St. Peter’s Cathedral Church, Okrika.

To God be the Glory.

"Lusaka mayor office is for everyone regardless of gender"

The Non-Governmental Gender Organisations Coordinating Council (NGOCC) has strongly condemned sexist and discriminatory remarks aired on Simon Mwewa Lane Television, warning against rhetoric fuels Violence Against Women in Elections (VAWE) ahead of the 2026 polls.

Recently, 55-year-old vlogger Simon Mwewa has been advocating for a male Lusaka mayor in the upcoming general election to oust the current female mayor Chilando Chitangala.

But NGOCC Chairperson Beauty Katebe said such comments suggesting that a single woman is “unworkable” for mayoral office and that leadership should be reserved for a “family man” are a direct attack on Zambia’s Constitution and the Gender Equity and Equality Act of 2015.

In a statement unleashed through Lusaka Reporters, Ms Katebe warned that judging women’s leadership ability based on marital status amounts to psychological violence, designed to intimidate women and push them out of political contestation as the country heads toward the August 13, 2026 General Elections.

She said the remarks reinforce patriarchal stereotypes, embolden online harassment, and undermine democracy by shifting focus from policies and competence to personal life - a standard never applied to male candidates.

“This is not free speech; it is sexist political violence,” she stated, stressing that leadership is measured by vision, integrity and service—not a marriage certificate.

Ms Katebe, therefore, wants an unconditional retraction from Mr Mwewa.

She also wants zero tolerance enforcement by political parties against sexist campaigning

She demanded for strict monitoring and sanctions by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ).

Lusaka Reporters, 13 January 2026.

Gender-Based Violence and Femicide (GBVF) is a serious human rights violation and a national crisis in South Africa. It affects women, children, persons with disabilities, the LGBTQIA+ community, and families as a whole.

‼️WHAT IS GBVF?
GBVF is violence directed at a person because of their gender or power imbalance. It can happen at home, in public spaces, online, at school, or in the workplace.

‼️COMMON ACTS OF GBVF
Domestic Violence: Physical, emotional, verbal, sexual, or financial abuse by a partner or family member
Sexual Violence: Rape, sexual assault, harassment, exploitation.

‼️Femicide: Killing of women and girls because of their gender.

‼️Child Abuse: Sexual abuse, neglect, physical and emotional harm.

‼️Harmful Practices: Forced marriage, ukuthwala without consent.

‼️Violence Against LGBTQIA+ Persons: Hate crimes, corrective rape.

‼️Online GBV: Cyberbullying, sextortion, sharing private images without consent.

‼️SIGNS OF ABUSE
Fear of a partner or family member
Unexplained injuries
Isolation from friends and family
Control over money, movement, or communication

‼️Threats, insults, or constant humiliation

In response, a unique and enormous she-camel, which was ten months pregnant, miraculously emerged from the mountains as a sign from Allah.

Saleh warned the people to respect the camel and allow it to drink freely from their water supply. However, some disbelievers among the Thamud people, defying Saleh’s warnings, hamstrung and killed the camel.

This act of defiance led to their downfall, as Allah’s punishment came upon them in the form of a devastating earthquake, destroying the disbelievers and leaving only the faithful followers of Saleh.

This story serves as a lesson on the consequences of disobedience and the importance of heeding the messages of prophets.

When Family Becomes Foe: Nigeria’s Inheritance Wars and the Struggle Over Wills, Power and Legacy

By Kio Amachree

When my father died — Chief Godfrey Kio JaJa Amachree, Queen’s Counsel, statesman, and Prince of the Kalabari Kingdom — I became, as the eldest child and son, the sole executor of his will. In Nigeria, that role does not simply confer responsibility. It confers authority. And authority, in matters of inheritance, can be explosive.

In the days before his death, I spent three uninterrupted days with him in Port Harcourt. No lawyers. No relatives. Just father and son. He spoke openly about his life, his struggles, his achievements, and, with striking honesty, about his children. At one moment, overwhelmed by anger and disappointment, he told me there was one child he wanted me to give my gun to “deal with.” I did not comply. I understood his pain, but I also understood that inheritance is not a place for revenge.

My father was trained in the British legal tradition. A Queen’s Counsel to the core. His will reflected that discipline and restraint. He asked for no lavish funeral. He requested Psalm 25, the hymn Abide With Me, and a quiet burial without ceremony. But my father was not only a lawyer. He was a Kalabari chief, a pioneer, the first lawyer his people had ever produced. When the will was read, his people — my people — told me plainly that this Oyinbo simplicity was not going to happen.

And it did not.

What followed was a magnificent, deeply traditional Kalabari send-off. Days of ceremony, celebration, chiefs, elders, and history on full display. It was a farewell befitting a trailblazer, a man who had carried his people into modern Nigeria. In death, as in life, he belonged to more than one world.

Then came the real test.

I knew with absolute clarity that if I followed the will strictly, there would be trouble. I had seen it before in Nigeria’s great families — estates frozen in courtrooms, siblings turned enemies, eldest sons asserting dominance, outside children erased, and lawyers growing rich while families collapsed. Across Nigeria, the death of a loved one is too often not an end, but the beginning of a new kind of conflict: a bitter struggle over who gets what, who controls the narrative, and who is pushed aside.

In Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, and far beyond, Nigeria’s courts are clogged with inheritance and land disputes that drag on for years, sometimes decades. What should be an orderly transfer of assets becomes an identity war, where land, homes, and property transform into symbols of power and legacy. The courtroom becomes the final battlefield of family feuds.

One of the most public examples is the estate of Herbert Wigwe, the Access Bank co-founder who died in a helicopter crash in early 2024 alongside his wife and son. Despite a clear will that provided for his surviving children and elderly parents, tensions erupted among extended family members, trustees, and business interests. The dispute spilled into court, accompanied by online rumors and competing narratives, illustrating how modern inheritance wars are now fought simultaneously in legal filings and on social media timelines.

But these conflicts are not confined to billionaires. In Kaduna, the family of former Secretary to the Government of the Federation Alhaji Saidu Gidado Idris has been locked in years-long disputes over access to property and wills, with siblings accusing a stepmother of withholding documents and defying court orders. Appeals have been made not only to judges but to traditional rulers and public opinion, revealing how fragile enforcement can be even when the law is clear.

Some disputes spiral beyond courts entirely. Across Nigeria, inheritance battles have ignited violence, including cases where siblings have attacked — and even killed — one another over land and assets. These flashpoints often follow the absence of a clear will or bitter disagreements over ancestral land, a deeply emotive issue in a country where property is inseparable from heritage, livelihood, and identity.

The legal landscape only deepens the tension. In many communities, customary practices historically favored male primogeniture, excluding daughters from inheritance. Although landmark court rulings have challenged these norms, the clash between tradition and statutory law remains unresolved in practice. When no will exists, Nigeria’s Administration of Estates laws attempt to impose order, prioritizing spouses and children, yet ambiguity invites extended relatives into the fray, turning grief into litigation.

Standing at that crossroads, I made a decision.

I chose not to rule as executor. I chose not to punish, reward, or dominate. I shared my father’s estate equally among all nine of his children. No hierarchy. No exclusions. No favorites. I put my sister in charge of the process, boarded a plane, and returned to Sweden.

There were no fights.
No court cases.
No police.
No judges.

Just nine heirs to a big man.

This outcome is rare in Nigeria.

Behind every inheritance dispute lies an emotional cost that cannot be measured in property or money. Families fracture. Spouses are alienated. Children feel erased. Siblings sever ties. Ancestral homes, meant to anchor memory and identity, become symbols of betrayal rather than legacy.

In Nigeria’s inheritance wars, wealth is only one prize. The other is dignity. And in the struggle to claim both, families often lose far more than they will ever inherit.

I was given power.

I chose peace.

Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo Maa-Baap ki na-farmaani karte hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Aur Aap ke Rabb ne hukm farma diya hai ke ALLĀH ki siwa kisi ki ibaadat mat karo aur waalidain ke saath husne sulook kiya karo, Agar tumhare saamne dono me se koi ek ya dono budhaape ko pahunch jaayen to unhe ‘uf’ bhi na kehna aur unhe jhidakna bhi nahi aur un dono ke saath badi adab se baat kiya karo.’

(4) Aap ne kuchh Aurte dekhi jin ke Munh siyah  hai aur Aankhe neeli hain, Aur unhe Aag ka libaas pehnaaya gaya hai. Farishte un ko Aag ke gurz se maar rahe hain aur wo aurten takleef ki shiddat ki wajah se gadhe aur kutto ki tarah cheekh rahi hain.
Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye apne shohar ki na-farmaani karne waali aurten hain.”

Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Mard haakim hai aurto par.’

(5) Aap ne kuchh aise log dekhen jo jaanwaro ki tarah char rahe hain aur Zaqqum [zehrile paudhe] aur Dozakh ke patthar khaa rahe hain.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo apne Maal ki zakaat ada nahi karte aur Faqeero Miskeeno par raham nahi karte.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Jo log sona-chaandi jama karte hain aur use ALLĀH ki raah me kharch nahi karte unhe dardnaak azaab ki khush-khabri suna do.’
(Qur'ān : 9 Soorah Tauba, Aayat 112)

(6) Aap ne kuchh aise log dekhen jin ke jabde khole jaa rahe hain, un ka gosht kaatkar khoon ke saath unhi ke munh me dhakela jaa raha hai. Aur kuchh aise log bhi dekhen jin ke Naakhoon taambe ke the wo apne chehro aur seeno ko chheel rahe the.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo logo ke aib talaash karte hain aur Gheebat kiya karte hain.”

Isi tarah Aap ne aise log dekhen jin ko Murdaar jaanwar ke gosht ke tukde khilaaye jaa rahe hain.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo Chugli kiya karte hain aur ek bhai se dusre bhai ka gila shikwa karte hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Aye  eimaan waalo ziyadatar gumaan se bacha karo beshak ba’az gumaan gunaah hote hain aur (kisi ke aib ya raaz ki) justajoo na kiya karo aur na peeth peeche ek dusre ki buraai kiya karo, Kya tum me se koi shakhs ye pasand karega ke wo apne murda bhaai ka gosht khaaye, So tum us se nafrat karte ho, Aur ALLĀH se daro beshak ALLĀH tauba ko bahot qubool farmaane waala bahot raham farmaane waala hai.’

(7) Aap ne aise log dekhen jin ke Chehre kaale aur aankhe kaali thi. Un ke neeche ka honth sar ke upar tha. Aag ke piyaalo me Dozakh ka zard paani unhe pilaaya jaa raha tha. Jis ke sabab munh se Khoon aur Peep tapakta tha aur takleef ki wajah se Gadhe ki tarah cheekhte chillaate the.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo apni zindagi me Sharaab peete hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Aye eimaan waalo Beshak sharaab aur juva aur nasab kiye hue but aur faal ke teer sab napaak shaitaani kaam hain, So un se parhez karo taake tum falaah paao.’
(Qur'ān : 5 Soorah al-Maa'idah, Aayat 90)

(8 ) Aap ne aise log dekhen jin ke paas 2 handiya hain, Ek me paka hua gosht hai aur dusri me Kharaab kacha gosht hai. Magar wo pake hue gosht ko chhodkar sada hua kacha gosht khaa rahe hain.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo apni halaal aur paakiza biwi ke hote hue Ghair aurat ke paas jaate hain aur wo Aurten hain jo halaal aur paak khaawind hote hue dusre mard ke paas jaati hain.”

Isi tarah Aap ne dekha ke kuchh aurto ko chhati aur paanv se latkaaya gaya hai.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo aurten hain jo badkaari karne ke ba’ad aulaad paida hone par un ko qatl kar deti hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Aur Badkaari ke paas na jaao beshak woh behayaai aur bahot hi bura raasta hai.’

(9) Aap ne kuchh aise log dekhen jin ke pet sujhkar Kothe jaise ho gaye hain, aur un me saanp nazar aa rahe the, un ke Chehre pile ho gaye hain, Gardano me tok, Haatho aur paanvo me janzeeren aur bediya padi hain. Jab wo chaahte hain ke uthkar khade ho jaayen to wo pet ke wazan ke sabab gir jaate hain aur upar aur neeche dono taraf se azaab me mubtila hai.
Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye Sood khor hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
 ‘Wo sood khaate hain (qayaamat ke din sahi tarah se) khade na ho sakenge magar jaise woh shakhs khada hota hai jise shaitaan [aaseb] ne chhookar bad-hawaas kar diya hai.’
(Qur'ān : Soorah al-Baqarah, Aayat 175)

(10) Aap ne aise log dekhen jin ke honth oonto ki tarah hai aur chingaariya khaa rahe hain aur aag ki wo chingaariya un ke pait ko jalaati hui neeche aa jaati hai aur yeh silsila isi tarah jaari hai.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo Yateemo ka maal Na-haq khaaya karte hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Beshak jo log yateemo ke maal na-haq tareeqe se khaate hain wo apne pait me nari aag bharte hain aur wo jald hi dehakti hui aag me jaa girenge.’
(Qur'ān : 4 Soorah an-Nisa, Aayat 10)

(11) Aap ne kuchh aise log dekhen jin ko aag ki chhuri se farishte zibah kar rahe hain aur un ki gardan se kaala khoon beh raha hai. Woh log baar baar zinda ho jaate hain aur farishte har baar unhe foran zibah kar dete hain.
Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jinho ne logo ko Na-haq Qatl kiya hai.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Aur jo koi musalman ko jaan-bujh kar qatl kare to us ka badla jahannam hai ke muddato muddat ibr me rahe aur ALLĀH ne us par ghazab kiya aur ALLĀH ne us par la'anat ki aur us ke liye bada azaab tayyaar rakha hai.’

(12) Aap ne kuchh aise log dekhen jin ki Soorte badalkar Suwwar jaisi ho gai hai aur sar se pair tak azaab me mubtila hain.
Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo Jhooti Gawaahi diya karte hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘To tum door raho jhooto ki baato ki gandagi se aur jhooti baat se.’

(13) Aap ne kuchh aise log dekhen jinho ne apni peeth par bahot wazandaar bojh utha rakha hai aur us ki wajah se wo hil bhi nahi sakte magar is ke baa-wajood bhi wo kehte jaa rahe hai ke “Haan, Aur bojh rakh do.” Is liye un ki peeth par aur bojh laada jaa raha hai.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo Amaanat me khayaanat karte hain aur bahot se logo ke Huqooq in ki gardan par hain lekin in huqooq ko ada karne ke bajaay aur zyada haq ko apne upar lete rehte hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
 ‘Aye eimaan waalo ALLĀH aur Rasool se dhoka na karo aur apni amaanato me jaante hue khayaanat na karo.’

(14) Aap ne kuchh aise log dekhen jin ke hontho ko aag ki qainchiyo se kaate jaa rahe hain.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye Khateeb aur Waa'iz hain jo logo ko neki aur bhalaai ki hidaayat karte hain aur apne aap ko bhool jaate hain [ya’ani khud nek kaam nahi karte hain] aur ALLĀH ki Kitaab padhte hain magar us par Amal nahi karte.”
(Mishkaat)

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Kya tum dusre logo ko neki ka hukm dete ho aur khud ko bhool jaate ho haalaanke tum kitaab [Qur’an majeed] padhte ho to kya tum (is ke anjaam ke baare me) nahi sochte?’

(15) Aap ne aise log dekhen jin ke Hontho aur zabaan ko Aag ki qainchi se kaata jaa raha hai. Phir jab apni asli haalat par aate hain Farishten phir kaat dete hain. Un ko ek pal ki bhi mohlat nahi dete.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo Baadshaaho ke paas jaakar un ki jhooti Khushaamaden karte hain aur un ki jhooti baato par Haan me Haan milaate hain. Ye log Baadshaaho ko Zulm aur Fisq o Fujoor [buri baato] se nahi rokte aur na un ko Insaaf aur ehsaan ke ehkaam bataate hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Aur Zaalimo ki taraf na jhuko ke tumhe aag chhuegi.’

(16) Aap ne aise giroh ko dekha jin ke seeno par aag ke tabaak rakhe hue hain. Un ke chehre siyah aur aankhe neeli hain, Katran ke kapde pehne hue hain aur farishte un ko Aag ke gurz se maar rahe hain.
Is ke baare me Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo Behuda gaane gaaya karte hain.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Aur kuchh log khel ki baaten khareedte hain ALLĀH ki raah se behuda ke be-samjhe aur ise hansi khel bana len, In ke liye zillat ka azaab hai.’

(17) Aap ne kuchh aise log dekhen jinhe aam raasto par sooli par latkaaya jaa raha hai aur un sooliyo me khatarnaak qism ke kaante hain jo un ke jism aur libaas dono ko noch lete hain.
Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Ye wo log hain jo raasto me baithkar Raah me chalne waalo ko takleef diya karte the.”

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Aur har raaste par yun na baitho ke raahgeero ko daraawo aur ALLĀH ki raah se unhe roko.’

(18) Aap ne ek shakhs ko dekha jo noor se dhanka hua hai.
Hazrat Jibr'eel alaihis salaam ne bataaya ki “Yeh woh khush-naseeb shakhs hai jis ki zabaan ALLĀH ke zikr se tar rehti thi aur jis ka dil masjid me laga rehta tha aur yeh kabhi apne waalidain ko bura kahe jaane ka ya un ki be-izzati ka sabab na bana.”

(19) Aap ne chand buland o baala mahelaat dekhe jo Ghussa pee jaane waale aur dar guzar karne waale aur muaf karne waalo ke liye hain.

Is ke baare me Irshaade Rabbul aalameen hai :
‘Ye wo log hain jo faraakhi aur tangi (dono haalaat me khairaat me) kharch karte hain aur ghussa pee jaane waale hain aur logo se dar guzar karne waale hain, Aur ALLĀH ehsaan karne waalo se mohabbat farmaata hai.’
(Qur'ān : 3 Soorah Aale Imraan, Aayat 134)

Huzoor sallallāhu alaihi wa sallam ne khush hokar aap ko ‘Siddeeq e akbar’ ka laqab ata farmaaya ya’ani Tamaam Siddeeq me sab se bada. (Siddeeq ka ma’ana hai Sach ka saath dene waala.)

The Plantation Mistress Who Defied Society: Choosing Her Strongest Slave Over Her Husband

In the sultry heat of 1851, beneath the sprawling shadows of Magnolia Ridge, a plantation in the heart of Virginia, a secret would emerge that would bring an empire to its knees. A plantation that had long been a symbol of wealth, power, and tradition, was now poised to unravel—not from the outside, but from within the very walls that held it all together. And at the center of this unraveling was a woman who had spent years suppressing her desires, her fears, and her understanding of the world that bound her. This is the story of Charlotte Harrow, the plantation mistress who would choose her strongest slave over her husband—and in doing so, defy every expectation placed upon her.

Magnolia Ridge was an estate built on Southern pride, where grand columns rose high above the fields of cotton and sugarcane. The Harrow family, old and powerful, had built their legacy on the backs of those they enslaved, holding both wealth and influence in a world where such power was rarely questioned. At the heart of this world stood Thomas Harrow, the head of the estate. Respected in public, feared in private, Thomas had always embodied the epitome of patriarchal control. His presence commanded respect, and his word was law, especially within the family.

But behind the stern exterior and public perfection lay a deeply hidden flaw—one that would unravel the entire family. Thomas could not produce an heir. A scandalous truth in a world where inheritance and legacy were everything. It wasn’t just a personal failure; it was a death sentence for the Harrow name. A lineage without children was a lineage doomed to fade into obscurity, and Thomas knew it.

Charlotte Harrow, his young wife, was a woman who had once dreamed of a life of ease and luxury. She had been raised in society’s most privileged circles, where beauty and manners could elevate a woman to greatness. At first, her life with Thomas had been one of opulence, but soon, the gilded cage she lived in began to feel suffocating. She was expected to smile, to maintain her composure, to host dinners, and to show her husband’s wealth to the outside world. But she could never escape the isolation, the quiet desperation of being nothing more than an ornament in Thomas’s collection.

Charlotte’s world, already small and confined, grew even narrower when she discovered the truth about Thomas’s infertility. It was a cruel revelation, and one that shattered the last vestiges of hope she had for a family, for a future that was not solely dependent on the expectations of others. For years, she had silently endured the blame—her own, and the whispered judgments of others in the town who looked at her as the barren wife. But when she uncovered the truth about Thomas’s condition, something inside her snapped.

Charlotte was no longer willing to carry the weight of the family’s shame alone. The realization that Thomas had known the truth all along, and that he had left her to bear the blame, pushed her to the edge. His need to maintain the Harrow name and legacy was all-consuming, but he cared not a bit for her suffering. He expected her to smile and pretend, to continue the facade that they could one day have the children that would save their family’s name. But the time for pretending was over.

It was in the darkness of a stormy night, when the winds howled outside and the shutters rattled in their frames, that Charlotte made her choice. Her heart raced as she thought of the only man on the estate who could give her what her husband could not. A man who, despite being enslaved, had something more than Thomas could ever offer—strength, dignity, and an unshakable resolve that had drawn her to him from the start.

His name was Elijah, and he worked the fields with a strength that commanded respect. He was a man who had endured more than most, a man who had seen his family torn apart and his life controlled by forces far beyond his control. And yet, he carried himself with a quiet dignity, his eyes filled with a wisdom that was both rare and dangerous. Elijah was everything Thomas was not—he was real, he was alive, and he was someone Charlotte had come to admire in ways that made her question everything she had been taught to believe.

Charlotte’s attraction to Elijah was not born out of weakness or desperation. It was born from a deep, primal need for something real, something human. She had spent her life in a world that demanded perfection, in a world that told her who to love, what to say, and what to do. But Elijah was different. In his presence, she felt seen—truly seen. And as the realization that she was trapped in a loveless marriage without the hope of heirs set in, Charlotte knew that there was only one path left for her.

She chose Elijah.

CITY DIRECTOR COL. MUARIP ON THE FILING OF CASES AGAINST FIRECRACKER BAN VIOLATORS 

The Davao City Police Office reiterates its unwavering and uncompromising enforcement of the Total Firecracker Ban as mandated by City Ordinance No. 060-02.

With the recent filing of a criminal case against two (2) firecracker ban violators in Barangay Sasa, the DCPO sends a clear, firm, and non-negotiable message to the public: there will be NO MERCY for violators of the firecracker ban in Davao City.

The case filed yesterday January 13, 2026, at the Office of the City Prosecutor, marks the sixth (6th) case lodged by the DCPO in line with the city’s sustained campaign against firecracker-related hazards. Five (5) earlier cases were filed for inquest proceedings last January 3, 2026, involving violators who were arrested in flagrante delicto. The latest case involves two additional individuals who chose to disregard the law despite repeated warnings and information drives.

Let this serve as a stern warning: firecracker use is not a harmless tradition—it endangers lives, causes injuries, and threatens public safety. The DCPO will relentlessly pursue legal action against anyone who violates this ordinance, regardless of status or circumstance.

We call on all residents to cooperate, comply, and protect one another by respecting the law. The DCPO remains steadfast in its duty to ensure a safe, injury-free, and peaceful community, and we will not hesitate to arrest, charge, and prosecute those who choose to defy this mandate.

The law will be enforced. Cases will be filed. Accountability will be exacted.

This whole “factory reset” thing on TikTok is not funny, it’s alarming. Full stop. Dressing up the idea of “resetting” people—especially queer people—as a joke is just recycled conversion-therapy language with a trend slapped on top. The implication is the same as it’s always been: that queerness is a mistake, a glitch, something that needs to be fixed or wiped away. That narrative has caused real harm, and seeing it casually normalized is unsettling.

And if you think you’re funny for saying it, you’re not. You’re not edgy, you’re not clever, you’re just repeating rhetoric that has been used for decades to shame, erase, and abuse queer people. Laughing at it doesn’t make it harmless—it just makes you complicit.

Let’s also clear something up because it always gets ignored in conversations like this: bisexuals exist. We are not confused. We are not indecisive. We are not “before” or “after” some imaginary reset. The idea that attraction has a default setting is exactly why bisexuality gets erased in the first place.

There is nothing to reset. Queer identities are not software bugs. They are not phases. They are not errors. If anything needs a reset, it’s the culture that keeps repackaging queerphobia as humor and expecting us to laugh along.

At 86-years-old, iconic civil rights activist, Claudette Colvin, passed away. 

On March 2nd, 1955, the 15-year-old Colvin was ordered to give up her seat for a while woman on a segregated bus. Being inspired by Harriet Tubman and Sojourner Truth, Claudette refused to move. She was arrested for her defiance. 9 months later, Rosa Parks would hake her historic stand and kickoff the Montgomery Bus Boycott. 

The local NAACP considered using Claudette's case to ignite the bus boycott, but the teenager was from a poor family and she later became pregnant; the NAACP feared that white Americans would not sympathize with her. Thus, Rosa Parks was chosen to lead the charge. 

It wasn't until much later that Claudette Colvin's contributions to the civil rights movement and the Montgomery Bus Boycott were recognized. 

She showed us that even small acts of defiance can have an incredible impact; that you are not too young to stand (or sit) for what is right; that cahnge is achieved by the massses acting, rather than only a few named leaders. 

It hurts to lose someone like Claudette, especially in times like these. But it is up to us to fill the ranks and fight against injustice in all of its forms.

Elago attended the promulgation of the decision to personally express solidarity and to underscore the call for the release of all political prisoners.
