If the latest anti-free speech law proposed by the Albanese Labor Government passes, you can be investigated, charged, and potentially imprisoned for speech that harms no one, threatens no one, and is lawful today.

Not for violence.
Not for incitement.
Not even for intimidation that anyone actually experienced.

For speech that a court later decides might have caused fear to a hypothetical person, judged through historical grievance and group identity.

That is not an exaggeration. That is what the Combatting Antisemitism, Hate and Extremism Bill 2026 does as drafted.

The Government says this Bill is a necessary response to rising hatred and extremism following the Bondi Beach terror attack of 14 December 2025. That attack was real. The suffering was real. But the legal justification collapses the moment you read the Bill itself. Australia already had extensive criminal laws covering terrorism, threats, violence, harassment, intimidation, and incitement. This legislation does not fill a gap. It builds a new structure, one that reaches far beyond violence and directly into lawful speech, belief, and political expression.

This is not a single bad clause that can be fixed with a tweak. It is a cumulative legal architecture. Expanded hate offences. Motive-based punishment. Speaker-based penalty escalation. Strict liability fear standards. Heightened penalties for offensive communications. Risk-based enforcement replacing harm-based law. Together, they create a system where speaking plainly about religion, culture, immigration, or national identity becomes legally hazardous.

One of the most dangerous features is the creation of aggravated offences targeting religious and spiritual leaders. Schedule 1 amends the Criminal Code so that multiple hate-related offences are aggravated where the conduct is engaged in by a religious official or spiritual leader (however described).

That phrase matters. “However described” is not narrow. It does not limit itself to radical Imams and crazy Sheiks. It can capture pastors, priests, rabbis, monks, nuns, church elders, lay preachers, chaplains, and informal community leaders who provide moral or spiritual guidance. Religious leadership itself becomes an aggravating factor.

The Explanatory Memorandum justifies this on the basis that leaders have influence. Influence is treated as inherently dangerous. The result is that the same words spoken by an ordinary citizen carry one level of risk, while the same words spoken from a pulpit can carry penalties of up to twelve years’ imprisonment.

This is not about coercion. It is not about violence. It is about controlling influential speech.

Layered on top of this is the Bill’s reliance on hate motivation as a punishment multiplier. Courts are instructed to treat motive as an aggravating feature across multiple offences. This shifts criminal law away from what a person did and toward why they believe what they believe.

Motive is inferred from expression, sermons, articles, social media posts, speeches, associations, and prior statements. Speech becomes evidence not just of opinion, but of a criminal mindset. Two people can engage in identical conduct, yet the one whose views are characterised as hostile faces harsher punishment.

In practice, this opens the door to belief-based punishment. Mainstream right-wing positions on immigration levels, multiculturalism, cultural compatibility, religious doctrine, gender ideology, or national identity can be reframed as hateful when assessed through a politicised lens. Once motive aggravation exists, punishment is no longer neutral between ideas.

The most liberty-destroying element of the Bill is that it abandons any requirement to prove actual harm. Proposed section 80.2BF establishes criminal liability where conduct would cause a reasonable person who is the target, or a member of the target group, to be intimidated, to fear harassment or violence, or to fear for their safety. Strict liability applies.

The Explanatory Memorandum is explicit. The prosecution does not need to prove that anyone actually felt fear. There does not need to be an identified victim. It is immaterial whether the conduct resulted in any person being intimidated at all.

Liability is triggered by speculation.

Worse still, the reasonable person is not an ordinary objective standard. Courts are directed to assess fear through the perspective of a person with the lived experience of the target group, including historical oppression and marginalisation. Judges must also consider the cumulative effect of conduct by others, not just the accused.

Your words are judged against historical grievance and third-party behaviour you did not commit and do not control. Individual responsibility is diluted. Context becomes elastic. Lawful speech can be reinterpreted as threatening simply because of who is discussed and what history is invoked.

The Bill also creates unequal speech protections. Quoting religious texts is categorically exempt if done for religious teaching or discussion. There is no equivalent exemption for secular critique, political commentary, policy analysis, or journalistic examination of the same texts.

Identical words can be lawful or criminal depending on who says them and why. That is not content neutrality. It is the state privileging certain forms of expression and punishing others based on framing.

Online speech is almost entirely captured. Penalties for using a carriage service to cause offence are increased from two years to five years’ imprisonment. Public conduct is defined broadly to include social media, blogs, videos, and online platforms. In modern Australia, this means virtually all political debate.

The situation can be aggravated if a court believes that the offence also threatened the “peace, order and good government of the Commonwealth” (whatever that means). The penalty could then by 10 years’ imprisonment.

Offence is the basis of all of this, but offence is not harm. Offence is an unavoidable feature of democratic life. This Bill converts that reality into criminal exposure.

The Government frames all of this as prevention, stopping risk, radicalisation, and future harm. This replaces harm-based criminal law with risk-based enforcement. Speech becomes punishable not for what it does, but for what authorities believe it might lead to.

There is no meaningful protection for political communication in the Bill. No explicit safeguard. No proportionality analysis. No serious engagement with the implied freedom of political communication recognised by the High Court. The burden is shifted onto individuals to become constitutional test cases after enforcement has already occurred.

Even without convictions, the process itself is punitive. Investigations, complaints, platform moderation, employment consequences, reputational damage, and institutional over-compliance occur long before any court rules. Churches pull sermon recordings. Publishers decline controversial pieces. Platforms over-moderate. Ordinary Australians choose silence over risk.

That is how free speech dies in a country like ours. With opaque censorship of certain undefined discourse, and breaches of that censorship regime punishable with severe jail sentences. That inspires fear, which leads people to remain silent instead of saying what they want to say.

To understand how far this Bill reaches, consider six illustrative hypotheticals that expose its outer limits.

A Christian pastor delivers a sermon stating, “Islam is an ideology that is destructive, incompatible with Western civilisation, and must be resisted if Australia is to survive.” There are no threats and no incitement. Because the speech is delivered by a religious leader, aggravated provisions apply. Prosecutors could argue the language is hostile, infer hate motivation from theology, and rely on hypothetical fear. Twelve-year penalties become possible.

A political activist posts online, “Mass immigration has destroyed social trust. Non-European cultures are fundamentally incompatible with ours, and continuing the policy of mass migration from the Middle East, Africa and China will fracture the nation.” This is classic political communication. No violence. No threats. Yet it can be reframed as hostility toward groups defined by ethnicity or national origin, triggering online communications offences.

A journalist writes an opinion piece stating, “This Islamic religious worldview produces intolerance, misogyny, and social division. Australia must stop accommodating it.” This is opinion journalism. Under the Bill, hostile framing combined with historical grievance analysis could justify investigation and prosecution, chilling public debate.

An activist at a rally says, “The wearing of full-face coverings like the burqa and niqab should be banned in Australia because they undermine our values and social order.” This is advocacy for law reform. Yet it may be reframed as targeting people rather than conduct, particularly if the speaker is an organiser or community figure.

A social media user posts crime statistics showing that crime in Melbourne comes from the African community is wildly disproportionate compared to other ethnic groups and adds, “Ignoring who is responsible for this crime wave is destroying our country.” The post relies on data and interpretation. Prosecutors could infer hate motivation and argue the post creates fear, despite no threats and no actual harm.

A policy paper by a think tank argues, “Australia should prioritise migrants from culturally compatible nations such as the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada and Europe to preserve social cohesion.” This is immigration policy debate at the core of political communication. And yet distinctions by national origin could be characterised as discriminatory hostility under this proposed law.

None of these scenarios involve violence, threats, or conduct criminal under existing law. Yet all could plausibly trigger enforcement under this Bill.

From a constitutional perspective, the problems compound. The Bill burdens political communication in its terms and effect. It criminalises speech without proof of harm, applies strict liability to fear, replaces objective standards with historically weighted ones, attributes third-party conduct to individual speakers, escalates penalties based on status, and expands offence-based online crimes.

Preventing violence is a legitimate aim. But criminalising hypothetical fear, belief, and offence fails necessity and proportionality. Less restrictive alternatives already exist. The balance struck is constitutionally fragile.

Individually, several provisions raise serious constitutional questions. Cumulatively, they present a profound threat to free political discourse.

The most bizarre and perverse thing about this proposed law, which has been crafted supposedly in response to the Bondi Beach terror attack, is that it will undoubtedly be used to clamp down on those who are critical of Islam and its anti-semitic and anti-Christian tendencies.

The Combatting Antisemitism, Hate and Extremism Bill 2026 does not abolish free speech outright. But it renders it conditional, unstable, and punishable by interpretation. Once that framework exists, the decisive question is no longer who uses those laws today, but whether any future government can resist using it against their political opponents.

If you value the right to speak openly about faith, culture, identity, and politics in Australia, this Bill must be confronted now. Read it. Share it. Challenge it. Because once speech is criminalised by perception rather than harm, reclaiming that freedom becomes extraordinarily difficult.

A PRAYER FOR DELIVERANCE FROM MAGA  
O Lord Jesus Christ, our only Savior and King,  
You commanded us to have no other gods before You (Exodus 20:3). Yet an ideology has risen among Your people, demanding allegiance above the gospel. We confess the sin of blending faith with earthly power and cry out:
Deliver us from MAGA!
Lord, deliver us from its “America First” nationalism that places country above neighbor, exalting borders over Your command to love without limit (Mark 12:31) and disciple all nations (Matthew 28:19).
Deliver us from its harsh rhetoric and policies that demonize immigrants and refugees, ignoring Your call to welcome the stranger (Leviticus 19:34; Deuteronomy 10:19) and see You in the foreigner (Matthew 25:35-40)—as Your own family once fled as refugees (Matthew 2:13-15).
Deliver us from its economic vision that enriches the wealthy through tariffs, deregulation, and tax cuts while neglecting the poor, defying warnings against greed (Luke 12:15) and exploitation (James 5:1-6).
Deliver us from its culture-war rhetoric that wields “traditional values” as a weapon, hardening hearts against the marginalized and outcast. Free us from fear-driven crusades that wound the very sinners You ate with and came to save with grace (Luke 15:1-2).
Deliver us from its distrust of institutions, misinformation, and division that violate truth (Ephesians 4:25), forbid slander (James 4:11), and command peace (Romans 12:18).
Above all, deliver us from MAGA’s exaltation of power, fear, and tribalism over Your gospel of humility, enemy-love (Matthew 5:44), and blessing on the meek (Matthew 5:3-12). Shatter its fusion of faith with political idolatry and Christian nationalism.
Spare Your church from the delusion You warned against (2 Thessalonians 2:11), lest we delight in deception and cruelty. Purge this ideology utterly—root and branch—so no remnant tempts future generations.
Make MAGA as odious to Your people as ancient syncretism with Baal and Asherah became after exile. Through whatever discipline is needed, awaken and free Your church.
Set Your people free, dear Lord.  
Deliver us from MAGA.
In the holy name of Jesus Christ, our true Lord and King,  
Amen.

Kennedy would have filled had he lived to see this precious day, creating a moment that would forever symbolize the unbreakable bonds of family love, protection, and continuity that defined the Kennedy clan through both their greatest joys and most devastating heartbreaks. Ted, who had already buried two of his brothers and watched his family endure unimaginable heartache, walked twenty-eight-year-old Caroline down that flower-filled aisle with such tenderness and pride, giving her away to the brilliant forty-one-year-old interactive designer who had captured her heart while they both worked at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and though the day belonged to the bride and groom, there was something profoundly moving about watching Ted fulfill this sacred duty for his late brother's only daughter, standing in for Jack Kennedy who would never see his little girl become a woman, never witness her graduate from Harvard, never walk her down any aisle, but whose presence was felt in every moment of that intimate Catholic ceremony attended by four hundred guests who understood they were witnessing not just a wedding but the continuation of a legacy despite all the forces that had tried to tear this family apart. Caroline and Edwin's wedding day was made even more special by the presence of Caroline's cousin Maria Shriver serving as matron of honor—having married Arnold Schwarzenegger just three months earlier—and Caroline's brother John F. Kennedy Jr. standing as Edwin's best man, and seated in the front pew was Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis dressed in an elegant pale green ensemble with long gloves and flower earrings, tears streaming down her face as she watched her only daughter marry, standing beside Ted who had been such a constant presence and support to both her children after their father's death, creating a tableau of family strength and love that spoke to everything the Kennedys had survived and everything they continued to represent to millions of Americans who had followed their journey through triumph and heartbreak. What makes the relationship between this family—Caroline, Edwin, Ted, and later their children—particularly beautiful is how it wove together different backgrounds and traditions into something stronger than any single thread could have been alone, with Edwin bringing his Orthodox Jewish heritage from a family of Ukrainian immigrants whose parents had come through Ellis Island, Caroline bringing her Irish Catholic Kennedy legacy and her mother's refined Bouvier elegance, and Ted representing the continuity of the Kennedy political dynasty and the unwavering family loyalty that had sustained them through decades of both glory and grief. Seven years after walking Caroline down the aisle, on January 19, 1993, when Caroline and Edwin welcomed their third child and only son into the world, they named him John Bouvier Kennedy Schlossberg—Jack for short—honoring both President Kennedy and Caroline's maternal great-grandfather, and they asked Ted to serve as the baby's godfather, cementing a relationship that would profoundly shape young Jack's understanding of what it meant to be a Kennedy, what it meant to serve the public good, and what it meant to carry forward a legacy while building your own identity and making your own mark on the world. Ted embraced his role as Jack's godfather with the same dedication he had shown to Caroline and John Jr. after their father's death, making regular trips from Washington to New York to spend time with his godson, taking him to Red Sox games, sharing stories about President Kennedy and the family's history, and modeling through his decades in the Senate what committed public service looked like even when it wasn't glamorous or easy or politically convenient. In 1970, after Robert Kennedy's death, Jacqueline had written Ted a letter asking him to become Caroline's godfather since she had been without one, and Ted had stepped into that role with such love and commitment, making those regular trips to see Caroline when she was in school, and now a generation later, he was doing the same for Caroline's son, creating an unbroken chain of mentorship, guidance, and family devotion that connected Jack directly to his grandfather's legacy through the living presence of his great-uncle who had known JFK intimately and who carried forward his brothers' visions for America through his own legislative work. Jack grew up hearing stories from Uncle Ted about his grandfather President Kennedy, learning about the New Frontier and the space program and the Peace Corps, understanding that being a Kennedy meant believing that government could be a force for good and that every individual had a responsibility to contribute to their community and their country, and these lessons—delivered not as abstract principles but through the warm, booming voice of a great-uncle who loved him and believed in him—shaped Jack's earliest understanding of politics and his eventual decision to enter public service himself. In 2007, when Jack was just fourteen years old, he experienced a moment that would stay with him forever and that he would later recount in interviews about what sparked his political engagement—Uncle Ted called him on the phone to ask what he thought about Senator Barack Obama, who Ted and Caroline were considering endorsing in the Democratic primary, and rather than dismissing Jack's opinions as those of a teenager, Ted genuinely listened to his thoughts and made him feel involved, heard, and excited about politics, showing Jack that political engagement wasn't something reserved for adults but something everyone could participate in and that even young voices mattered in shaping the future. Jack told Vogue years later that this conversation with Uncle Ted made him feel that anything could happen and he could make a difference, revealing how profoundly his godfather's respect and attention had impacted his understanding of civic participation and his own potential to contribute to important causes. Throughout Jack's childhood and teenage years, Ted remained a constant presence at family gatherings, holidays at the Kennedy Compound in Hyannis Port, and important family events, always making time for his godson despite his demanding Senate schedule, and Jack got to witness firsthand how Uncle Ted fought for healthcare reform, immigration rights, and labor protections—the same issues that his grandfather had cared about and that Jack himself would eventually champion as he developed his own political voice. The bond between Ted and the Schlossberg family extended beyond just Jack to include his sisters Rose and Tatiana, with Ted treating all three of Edwin and Caroline's children as his own grandchildren, taking them sailing, teaching them about Kennedy family history, and instilling in them the values of service, compassion, and commitment to making the world better that had defined the best of what the Kennedy family represented across generations. When Ted Kennedy passed away on August 25, 2009, after a long battle with brain cancer, sixteen-year-old Jack lost not just his godfather but one of his most important mentors and connections to his grandfather's legacy, and Caroline spoke at Ted's memorial service about how fortunate their family had been to witness his passion, self-discipline, and generosity of heart every single day, words that surely resonated with Jack as he mourned the great-uncle who had taken such personal interest in his development and who had modeled what it meant to dedicate your life to fighting for people who needed a voice in the halls of power. Years later, when Jack was studying at Harvard—his grandfather's alma mater and Uncle Ted's as well—he told the Boston Globe that his favorite restaurants were on JFK Street and that he noticed the Kennedy legacy everywhere but that it felt humbling rather than burdensome, and it was clear that the foundation Ted had helped build in young Jack—teaching him to honor the past while embracing the present, to carry the Kennedy name with dignity but not let it define his every choice—had given Jack the confidence to attend Harvard and walk those same streets his grandfather and great-uncle had walked without feeling overwhelmed by the weight of expectation. In 2016, Jack wrote a passionate essay for Politico responding to Senator Ted Cruz's claim that President Kennedy would be a Republican if alive today, and Jack wrote with the authority of someone who had learned about his grandfather not just from history books but from his Uncle Ted who had known JFK intimately, declaring that as Kennedy's grandson and as a student of his life and legacy, he found Cruz's assertion absurd, and noting that his grandfather would be excited about the progress America had made, would feel urgency about challenges ahead, and most certainly would not be a Republican—words that echoed arguments Uncle Ted himself had made throughout his Senate career and showing how deeply Ted's teachings about his brother's true values had taken root in his godson's understanding. When Jack speaks publicly about the Kennedy legacy today, he often mentions Uncle Ted alongside his grandfather, telling the New York Times that President Kennedy inspires him and that Uncle Teddy fought for healthcare, immigration, and labor, which are still the issues of our time, demonstrating how Ted's forty-seven years in the Senate fighting for these causes had become as much a part of Jack's political inheritance as his grandfather's brief but transformative presidency. The family that Ted helped unite on that July day in 1986—walking Caroline down the aisle to Edwin, later becoming godfather to their son Jack, spending decades as the patriarch who held the Kennedy clan together through continued heartbreak including the loss of John Jr. in 1999—created a foundation of love, mentorship, and shared values that continues to shape Jack's approach to public service today as he pursues his own congressional campaign in New York. Edwin, who came from his own immigrant family story of grandparents arriving at Ellis Island with almost nothing and building successful lives through hard work and creativity, found in Ted Kennedy and the broader Kennedy family not just in-laws but kindred spirits who believed in America's promise, in the power of education and innovation, and in the responsibility of those with privilege and platform to fight for those without, and these shared values helped create the stable, loving environment where Jack could grow up understanding both his Schlossberg heritage and his Kennedy legacy as sources of strength rather than burden. Caroline, who had lost her father at six years old and who had leaned so heavily on Uncle Ted throughout her childhood and adult life, must have felt profound gratitude watching Ted embrace his role as Jack's godfather with such devotion, giving her son the same kind of attention, guidance, and unconditional love that Ted had given to her and John Jr. when they needed it most, ensuring that even though Jack would never meet his grandfather President Kennedy, he would still have a direct connection to that generation through Ted's stories, values, and living example of what Kennedy service meant in practice. The photograph of Ted and Caroline at the church entrance on her wedding day—him gesturing for quiet, her smiling up at him with such trust and affection before they walked down the aisle together—captures something essential about the Kennedy family's greatest strength, which isn't their political achievements or their famous name but their ability to show up for each other in moments of both celebration and grief, to step into roles that need filling even when it's painful, to pass down values and stories from generation to generation, and to model through their daily choices that family loyalty, public service, and personal integrity matter more than fame or fortune or any individual ambition. As Jack continues building his own career in political journalism and public advocacy, potentially following in his great-uncle Ted's footsteps by running for Congress in New York, he carries forward not just the Kennedy name but the specific lessons Ted taught him about listening to people, fighting for working families, never giving up on important causes even when progress seems impossible, and understanding that real leadership means service rather than self-promotion, all values that Edwin and Caroline reinforced at home through their own examples of creativity, dedication, and commitment to making meaningful contributions to society. The story of this family—Ted walking Caroline down the aisle to Edwin, later becoming godfather to their son Jack, spending years mentoring and guiding his godson in the Kennedy tradition, and Jack now stepping forward to serve the public in his own way—reminds us that the most important legacies aren't written in history books or preserved in presidential libraries but are passed down through relationships, through uncles who make time for their godsons, through parents who blend different traditions into beautiful new combinations, through families who show up for each other decade after decade, and through young people who honor their ancestors not by trying to recreate the past but by taking the best values they inherited and applying them to the challenges and opportunities of their own time, carrying forward the torch not because they have to but because they've been loved and mentored and shown through living example that service to others is the most meaningful way to spend the precious time we have on this earth, and that family—however it's defined and whoever it includes—remains our greatest source of strength, identity, purpose, and hope for building a future worthy of those who came before us and those who will come after."

Australia's Biggest Battery Just Woke Up – And It's Already Smirking at Coal

Right on cue, with the sun barely up on 2026, Origin Energy has officially flicked the switch on the first chunk of the Eraring Big Battery. We're talking 460 MW of power and 1,770 MWh of storage straight out of the blocks, with ambitious plans to eventually hit 700 MW / 3,160 MWh when all four stages are humming. 

And where did they plonk this lithium giant? Smack-bang next to the soon-to-be-retired Eraring coal-fired power station. It's the energy world's equivalent of moving your cool new electric mate into the spare room while Grandpa Coal is still muttering about the good old days from his recliner.

The coal unit is over there wheezing away its final contracts, while this battery is already out here flexing like it just finished a 12-week program at the grid gym. "Yeah mate, I can slam 460 megawatts into the system faster than you can say 'system strength'." 

Then it calmly sips its electrolytes and keeps the lights on during the evening peak while the old fella is still trying to remember where he parked his pulverised-coal injection system.Origin's Greg Jarvis called the whole thing a "milestone" and – get this – they actually delivered it on time and under budget. 

In Australian infrastructure speak, that's basically an urban legend. Normally we get excited when something only blows out by 18 months and $400 million. So hats off, team. You've built something that can finally help stop the NEM from having a complete meltdown every time half the country decides to run the air-con, the pool pump, and the second Netflix account at 6:45 pm simultaneously.

Imagine solar farms out there all day pumping free sunshine like an over-caffeinated barista, only for the sun to clock off and prices to go full feral. Then in strolls the Eraring battery like the mate who shows up to the barbecue at sunset with a perfectly chilled esky and says, "Don't stress, I've got enough cold ones to get us through till bedtime." Except the cold ones are electrons, and bedtime is 4.5 hours of grid stability.

It's almost karmic. The battery is literally helping to "ease pressure on wholesale prices" while sitting on the same patch of dirt where coal used to be king. The ultimate glow-up: from black lung to big lithium, same postcode.

Of course this "Australia's Biggest Battery" belt comes with a very Australian asterisk. Queensland's Supernode is warming up in the bullpen (500 MW / 1,560 MWh and growing), and there's a whole queue of other monsters waiting to steal the title. But right now? Eraring is wearing the crown. Enjoy it while it lasts, big fella – probably about as long as a Tim Tam lasts in a house full of kids.

So cheers to you, Eraring Big Battery. May your round-trip efficiency stay high, your degradation stay low, and your ability to prevent the next "load-shedding o'clock" become the stuff of legends. Just don't get too comfortable on that throne. We Australians have a proud tradition of building something enormous, giving it a nickname, then immediately whinging that it's still not big enough the next time someone boils the kettle during a heatwave.

Welcome to the future. It's shiny, it's expensive, and it's currently giving coal-powered nostalgia a very polite side-eye.

Yesterday, I saw many mourning posts for Abdu Rahaman. Activists, youth, leaders, journalists, and teachers all shared their grief. I felt it too. His death feels personal, because when an intellectual dies, a community loses a voice, not just a person.

But a question keeps coming to my mind. What about the others who are suffering in the same way quietly without posts or attention?

Every time our people attend conferences or meetings, they speak about education, funding issues, and political stories. After that, there are selfies with delegates and long Facebook posts, as if those words alone have changed our reality.

The truth is simple and painful. Our healthcare system in the camps is very limited. Mismanagement is everywhere. Many people are living with serious illnesses, just as Abdu Rahaman did. Who has raised the healthcare issue in meetings or conferences? Even people in the camps are not receiving basic health services.

Breast cancer, blood cancer, heart disease, and other critical conditions are becoming common. If someone falls seriously ill, there is almost no option except death. Very few people can afford such treatment on their own at private hospitals.

Treatment for these diseases costs money that most families can never afford. Even Gaza, under constant attack, has better medical facilities than our camps in Bangladesh. People there can receive cancer treatment like chemotherapy, other cancer-related treatments, and basic surgical care. Here, we struggle to get even the minimum.

Basic medical tests are not properly available. Some facilities exist, but their services are very limited. Most reports are handwritten. Even after an X ray, patients are told there is no film because there is no printer.

Simple surgeries like gallbladder stones, appendicitis, kidney stones, or emergency care for accidents and fractures are not available.

The only service that is good in the camps is women’s delivery care. Beyond that, survival depends more on luck than on the system.

So the question remains. Who is responsible.

A Cry from Muhoroni
In Muhoroni the soil is rich with pain,
Voices cry beneath leadership in vain,
Those trusted to guard the people’s will,
Feast on power while the common folk stand still.
Resources meant for all are split by name,
Not need nor merit, but a clan’s acclaim,
The well runs dry where hope once grew,
While chosen circles drink what isn’t due.
Clanism walks our corridors of might,
Dividing neighbors, turning day to night,
A brother’s worth weighed by blood alone,
Justice buried beneath a tribal throne.
The CDF, meant to light a child’s way,
Now serves a few while others fade away,
One group’s children march through schoolhouse doors,
The rest are left to count broken dreams and floors.
Bright minds are dimmed by biased hands,
Opportunity ruled by hidden plans,
Education bends to favoritism’s rule,
When leadership forgets the meaning of a school.
Last-mile power snakes past willing homes,
Lighting allies’ roofs while darkness roams,
Poles stand tall where loyalty is sworn,
While others wait, ignored and torn.
Electric wires whisper of unfair play,
Progress sold to friends along the way,
Development delayed by selfish gain,
As villages drown in silent pain.
Our sugar factories, pride of the land,
Now bleed under misuse close at hand,
Machines rust where wealth should flow,
Because greed chose power over the poor man’s hoe.
Farmers sweat but reap no reward,
While leaders dine behind guarded boards,
The sweetness stolen from honest toil,
Leaves bitterness in Muhoroni soil.
Yet hope still stirs in the people’s cry,
A demand for truth that will not die,
For justice blooms when courage speaks,
And the oppressed refuse to remain weak.
Let fairness rise, let unity stand,
Let service guide the leader’s hand,
Till Muhoroni heals, renewed and free,
A home of equity and dignity.

When Family Becomes Foe: Nigeria’s Inheritance Wars and the Struggle Over Wills, Power and Legacy

By Kio Amachree

When my father died — Chief Godfrey Kio JaJa Amachree, Queen’s Counsel, statesman, and Prince of the Kalabari Kingdom — I became, as the eldest child and son, the sole executor of his will. In Nigeria, that role does not simply confer responsibility. It confers authority. And authority, in matters of inheritance, can be explosive.

In the days before his death, I spent three uninterrupted days with him in Port Harcourt. No lawyers. No relatives. Just father and son. He spoke openly about his life, his struggles, his achievements, and, with striking honesty, about his children. At one moment, overwhelmed by anger and disappointment, he told me there was one child he wanted me to give my gun to “deal with.” I did not comply. I understood his pain, but I also understood that inheritance is not a place for revenge.

My father was trained in the British legal tradition. A Queen’s Counsel to the core. His will reflected that discipline and restraint. He asked for no lavish funeral. He requested Psalm 25, the hymn Abide With Me, and a quiet burial without ceremony. But my father was not only a lawyer. He was a Kalabari chief, a pioneer, the first lawyer his people had ever produced. When the will was read, his people — my people — told me plainly that this Oyinbo simplicity was not going to happen.

And it did not.

What followed was a magnificent, deeply traditional Kalabari send-off. Days of ceremony, celebration, chiefs, elders, and history on full display. It was a farewell befitting a trailblazer, a man who had carried his people into modern Nigeria. In death, as in life, he belonged to more than one world.

Then came the real test.

I knew with absolute clarity that if I followed the will strictly, there would be trouble. I had seen it before in Nigeria’s great families — estates frozen in courtrooms, siblings turned enemies, eldest sons asserting dominance, outside children erased, and lawyers growing rich while families collapsed. Across Nigeria, the death of a loved one is too often not an end, but the beginning of a new kind of conflict: a bitter struggle over who gets what, who controls the narrative, and who is pushed aside.

In Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, and far beyond, Nigeria’s courts are clogged with inheritance and land disputes that drag on for years, sometimes decades. What should be an orderly transfer of assets becomes an identity war, where land, homes, and property transform into symbols of power and legacy. The courtroom becomes the final battlefield of family feuds.

One of the most public examples is the estate of Herbert Wigwe, the Access Bank co-founder who died in a helicopter crash in early 2024 alongside his wife and son. Despite a clear will that provided for his surviving children and elderly parents, tensions erupted among extended family members, trustees, and business interests. The dispute spilled into court, accompanied by online rumors and competing narratives, illustrating how modern inheritance wars are now fought simultaneously in legal filings and on social media timelines.

But these conflicts are not confined to billionaires. In Kaduna, the family of former Secretary to the Government of the Federation Alhaji Saidu Gidado Idris has been locked in years-long disputes over access to property and wills, with siblings accusing a stepmother of withholding documents and defying court orders. Appeals have been made not only to judges but to traditional rulers and public opinion, revealing how fragile enforcement can be even when the law is clear.

Some disputes spiral beyond courts entirely. Across Nigeria, inheritance battles have ignited violence, including cases where siblings have attacked — and even killed — one another over land and assets. These flashpoints often follow the absence of a clear will or bitter disagreements over ancestral land, a deeply emotive issue in a country where property is inseparable from heritage, livelihood, and identity.

The legal landscape only deepens the tension. In many communities, customary practices historically favored male primogeniture, excluding daughters from inheritance. Although landmark court rulings have challenged these norms, the clash between tradition and statutory law remains unresolved in practice. When no will exists, Nigeria’s Administration of Estates laws attempt to impose order, prioritizing spouses and children, yet ambiguity invites extended relatives into the fray, turning grief into litigation.

Standing at that crossroads, I made a decision.

I chose not to rule as executor. I chose not to punish, reward, or dominate. I shared my father’s estate equally among all nine of his children. No hierarchy. No exclusions. No favorites. I put my sister in charge of the process, boarded a plane, and returned to Sweden.

There were no fights.
No court cases.
No police.
No judges.

Just nine heirs to a big man.

This outcome is rare in Nigeria.

Behind every inheritance dispute lies an emotional cost that cannot be measured in property or money. Families fracture. Spouses are alienated. Children feel erased. Siblings sever ties. Ancestral homes, meant to anchor memory and identity, become symbols of betrayal rather than legacy.

In Nigeria’s inheritance wars, wealth is only one prize. The other is dignity. And in the struggle to claim both, families often lose far more than they will ever inherit.

I was given power.

I chose peace.

Monique Muller: From Influencer to Controversy Amid Gang Allegations in Cape Town

Monique Muller Back in the Headlines Amid Cape Town Arrest
Monique Muller, once celebrated for her social media presence and advocacy work, is now making headlines under far more serious circumstances. The Cape Town influencer was recently arrested in Ravensmead on charges of illegal firearm possession, with authorities linking the incident to alleged gang-related activities.

Reports suggest the firearm was discovered at a property connected to a known gang hitman, raising questions about the depth of Muller’s alleged involvement. She appeared before the Cape Town Magistrates’ Court on October 21, alongside several co-accused, and her case has been remanded to October 30.

From Public Figure to Public Scrutiny
Before this latest controversy, Muller had largely stepped back from public scrutiny. She first rose to prominence as the former girlfriend of award-winning TV presenter Katlego Maboe, sharing a son, Phoenix Katlego Maboe, with him.

Their highly publicised relationship ended in 2020 amid scandal. A viral video showed Maboe admitting to infidelity, leading Muller to publicly accuse him of abuse and seek a temporary protection order. She also alleged that Maboe transmitted an STD to her, impacting her fertility—a claim he denied.

The fallout affected Maboe’s career significantly: he was dismissed from the “Expresso Morning Show”, lost an OUTsurance endorsement deal, and was excluded from Saftas nominations. Over time, he has regained public trust and returned to television.

Who Is Monique Muller?
Born and raised in Cape Town, Muller built her career as a social media influencer and women’s rights advocate. She has worked with organisations like SA Women Fight Back and Women For Change, focusing on gender-based violence awareness. She participated in the 16 Days of Activism campaign in November 2020, further establishing her voice in the community.

Beyond activism, Muller has professional experience in marketing and business development, and previously worked as a flight attendant for Emirates. Her social media platforms once celebrated lifestyle, empowerment, and advocacy, making her arrest a striking contrast to her earlier public image.

Public Reaction and Social Media Buzz
Muller’s arrest has reignited public debate online. Supporters of her advocacy work expressed shock at the allegations, while critics questioned her associations and choices. On platforms like X and Instagram, the story has sparked discussions about the intersection of influencer culture, personal responsibility, and crime in South Africa.

A Complex Story Unfolding
Monique Muller’s journey, from influencer, activist, and public figure to facing serious criminal allegations—is a stark reminder of how quickly public perception can shift. With her court date set for October 30, South Africans are watching closely to see how this chapter unfolds, and what it means for both Muller and the broader conversation around public figures and accountability in Cape Town.

The only service that is good in the camps is women’s delivery care. Beyond that, survival depends more on luck than on the system.

So the question remains. Who is responsible.

Not only have I averted this evil out of fear, I have also engaged in spells that caused the death of my opponent. So now I must bear the fault of having taken the life of another!”

The great Vajrāsana replied, “It would have sufficed merely to wear the mantra I have spoken of on your body, but you have recited the mantra day and night without interruption! Thus you have accumulated the fault of killing. Now you must exert yourself in purifying this bad deed. Do not return to me until definite signs arise that it has been purified.”

For one whole year, then, the lotsawa exerted himself in purifying this evil, during which time he did not have a single opportunity to meet his guru, the great Vajrāsana. The close disciples of Vajrāsana, without any signs of pride, treated Baripa with great kindness, bringing him food and liquor when possible, along with anything else he needed, all without the guru’s knowing. When signs finally arose that Baripa had purified his evil deeds, and his guru’s command, his wish, had been accomplished and fulfilled, he was once again able to meet his guru.

From then onwards, Baripa requested many teachings and became both learned and faithful. When he returned to Tibet, he benefited beings on a vast scale. Later still, he journeyed to the glorious Sakya monastery and transmitted the pith instructions and related empowerments, sādhanas and activity liturgies to Sachen Kunga Nyingpo.

The instructions on Siṃhamukhā were then transmitted to the precious teacher Jetsün Drakpa Gyaltsen,the great Sakya Paṇḍita,the great Jetsün Phakpa, Nyene Rongpo Dorje, Rongpo Sangye Yeshe, and the precious teacher of Rongpo, the learned Yakde Paṇchen.

Thus the uncommon practice of the wisdom ḍākinī Siṃhamukhā was established. This led many to gain visionary experiences of the deity, while the practice itself brought a constant rain of blessings.

The heart-essence mantra also reached the accomplished lady Jetsünma Timudra; the eminent scholar, the precious Samten Pal Zangpo; the Mantra-holder of the degenerate time, the great Vajradhara, the realized Namkha Sangye Gönpo; Rechen Kunga Darpo, the heart-son Kunga Zangpo; and finally the learned and accomplished master, the kind teacher, speech of infinite teachings, Champa Chökyi Nyima.

The Uncommon Lineage

The uncommon lineage of the inner and secret empowerments and activity liturgies of the white, black and varied, is:

Dharmakāya Samantabhadra in union,
The wisdom ḍākinī Simḥamukhā,
The unequalled Guru of Uḍḍiyāna in union,
The realized Namkha Sangye Gönpo,
The destroyer of illusion, the great Repa Kunga Darpo,
The Mantra-holder Tsöndru Senge,
From whom my root teacher Chökyi Nyima received the teachings on Siṃhamukhā.

This concludes the history of the lineage of Siṃhamukhā that inspires faith."

"Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo was born on the first day of the sixth month of the iron dragon year, or July 11, 1820, in the village of Dilgo (dil mgo) in the Terlung (gter klung) valley to the southeast of the Derge capital. His father was Rinchen Namgyel (rin chen rnam rgyal), and his mother was named Sonam Tso (bsod nams 'tsho). His clan was Shingkhamga (shing khams sga) and his lineage was the Nyo (myos). A lama named Sharchen Rinchen Mingyur Gyeltsen (shar chen rin chen mi 'gyur rgyal mtshan, d.u.) named him Rinchen Wanggyel (rin chen dbang rgyal), and later his father gave him the name Tsering Dondrub (tshe ring don grub). He had at two older brothers, Kelzang Dorje (skal bzang rdo rje) and Gyurme Dondrub ('gyur med don grub), and five older sisters.

At the age of three the boy met Tartse Khenchen Jampa Kunga Tendzin (thar rtse mkhan chen byams pa kun dga' bstan 'dzin, 1776-1862), the head of Ngor Ewaṃ Choden Monastery (ngor e waM chos ldan) who was in Derge serving as court chaplain. The following year, or possibly the next, Tartse Khenchen gave him his lay vows. By the age of eight he had studied reading and writing with a lama named  Chaga Khenpo Pema Tashi (b' ga mkhan po pad+ma bkra shis), and medicine with the Derge court physician, Chodrak Gyatso (chos grags rgya mtsho).

In his youth he visited Dzongsar (rdzong sar dgon), an ancient Sakya monastery in the Mesho (sman shod) valley to the immediate west of Terlung, where his family had long-standing connections. He also visited Katok (kaH thog), a large Nyingma monastery to the south where he met his paternal uncle, the Second Moktsa Tulku, Choying Dorje (rmog rtsa sprul sku 02 chos dbying rdo rje, d.u.), an important incarnate lama of the monastery, who gave him the name Jigme Khyentse Dogar ('jigs med mkhyen brtse'i zlos gar). There he also received a blessing from Pema Chogyel Tulku Jangchub Chokyi Nyima (pad+ma chos rgyal sprul sku byang chub chos kyi nyi ma, d.u.), who prophesied that he would have a long life.

When the boy was twelve Tartse Khenpo identified him as the reincarnation of Tartse Khenchen Jampa Namkha Chime (thar rtse mkhan chen byams pa nam mkha' 'chi med, 1765-1820), and gave him the name Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo Kunga Tenpai Gyeltsen Pelzangpo ('jam dbyangs mkhyen brtse' dbang po kun dga' bstan pa'i rgyal mtshan dpal bzang po). Tartse Khenpo urged the boy's father to send him to Ngor in Tsang for training, but the father declined, refusing to trade his son for the silver then being offered. However, he said he was willing to allow his son to enter into the religious life should the boy later show interest. From then on Khyentse Wangpo was known as Tartse Tulku (thar rtse sprul sku) or simply Zhabdrung (zhabs drung). Later he came to be identified as the mind incarnation of the famous Nyingma treasure revealer Jigme Lingpa ('jigs med gling pa, c.1730-1798), but how late this identification was made -- whether it was during or after his life -- is not clear.

At the age of twenty Khyentse Wangpo left Kham for Tibet. At Ngor he received the Cakrasaṃvara and Hevajra from a brother of Tartse Khenpo Namkha Chime, among other transmissions of Sakya teachings. Despite his Sakya incarnation identification, he took ordination at age twenty-one at Mindroling Monastery (smin grol gling dgon), with Minling Khenchen Gyurme Rigdzin Zangpo (smin gling mkhan chen 'gyur med rig dzin bzang po, d.u.), from whom he received the name Kunga Tenpai Gyeltsen (kun dga' bstan pa'i rgyal mtshan). At Mindroling he received transmission of Yangdak Heruka in the So lineage (so lugs yang dag) and the Terdak Lingpa (gter bdag gling pa, 1646-1714) treasure cycle Rigdzin Tuktik (rig 'dzin thugs thig).

Khyentse Wangpo is well-known for having studied with many of the leading lamas of his day in both Tibet and Kham. Before leaving Kham he had gone to Shechen Monastery (zhe chen dgon) to give at long-life empowerment, at the request of the Derge King, Damtsik Dorje (dam tshig rdo rje, 1811-1852), to Shechen Wontrul Gyurme Tutob Namgyel (zhe chen dbon sprul 'gyur med mthu stobs rnam rgyal, 1787-1854), from whom he received Māyājāla teachings and empowerments in return. At the age of twenty he received transmission in the Longchen Nyingtik (klong chen snying thig) from Jigme Gyelwai Nyugu ('jigs med rgyal ba'i myu gu, 1765-1842), who was traveling through the Terlung Valley. Although the Longchen Nyingtik was not one of his primary practices, he figures large in the transmission history of the treasure cycle.

Other prominent lamas that he studied with include: Shechen Paṇḍita Jamyang Gyepai Lodro (zhe chen paNDita 'jam dbyangs dgyes pa'i blo gros, d.u.), the Second Dzogchen Khenrab Zhenpen Taye (rdzogs chen mkhan rabs 02 gzhan phan mtha' yas, 1800-1855), the Fourth Dzogchen Tulku Mingyur Namkhai Dorje (rdzogs chen 04 mi 'gyur nam mkha'i rdo rje, 1793-1870), the Thirty-fourth Sakya Trichen Pema Dundul Wangchuk (sa skya khri chen 34 pad+ma bdud 'dul dbang phyug, 1792-1853), the Thirty-fifth Sakya Trichen Dorje Rinchen (sa skya khri chen 35 rdo rje rin chen, 1819-1867), Zhalu Ribuk Tulku Losel Tenkyong (zhwa lu ri sbug sprul sku blo gsal bstan skyong, b. 1804), the Forty-seventh Ngor Khenchen Jampa Kunga Tendzin, and Pelyul Dongak Tendzin (dpal yul mdo sngags bstan 'dzin, 1830-1892).

At the age of twenty-four Khyentse Wangpo returned to Kham with the Fifty-first Ngor Khenchen, Jampel Zangpo (ngor mkhan chen 51 'jam dpal bzang po, 1789-1864), and took up residence at Dzongsar, in the Tashi Latse (bkra shis lha rtse) residence, which later came to be called the Khyentse Labrang (mkhyen brtse bla brang). For the next four years, in accordance with the Ngor custom, he practiced tantra, such as Hevajra, the three classes of Kriya tantra, and so forth.

At the age of twenty-nine, in 1848, Khyentse Wangpo traveled again to Tibet with the Ngor Khenchen, where he remained until the beginning of the 1850s.

Over the decade of the 1850s Khyentse Wangpo collaborated so closely with two men that the three continue to be referred to as the Khyen Kong Chok Desum (mkhyen kong mchog sde gsum), meaning “the triumvirate of Khyentse Wangpo, Jamgon Kongtrul Lodro Taye ('jam mgon kong sprul blo gros mtha' yas, 1813-1899), and Chokgyur Lingpa (mchog gyur gling pa, 1829-1870)." Jamgon Kongtrul was a prominent tulku at Pelpung (dpal spungs), the Karma Kagyu monastery a half a day's walk from Dzongsar. Chokgyur Lingpa  was an up-and-coming treasure revealer active in the Derge and Nangchen regions of Kham who relied on both Khyentse and Kongtrul for his initial affirmation of legitimacy.

Khyentse Wangpo met Jamgon Kongtrul at the end of 1840, when he went to Pelpung to receive teachings from the elder lama on Chandragomin's grammar. They met again before Jamyang Khyentse went to Tibet the second time. Khyentse Wangpo's beloved elder brother, Gyurme Dondrub had passed away in Tibet, and it appears that in his grief Khyentse Wangpo turned to his growing friendship with Jamgon Kongtrul for companionship. He went to Pelpung for an extensive transmission of Jonang teachings, including the complete works of Tāranātha and the Kālacakra. Jamgon Kongtrul continued his transmission of Jonang teachings to Khyentse Wangpo after the later returned from Tibet in the early 1850s, giving Tāranātha's Drubta Rinjung (sgrub thabs rin 'jung). At the time Khyentse Wangpo gave Jamgon Kongtrul a complete set of Tāranātha's writings.

Khyentse Wangpo appears to have first met Chokgyur Lingpa when Jamgon Kongtrul sent the young treasure revealer for evaluation sometime between the end of 1853 and the end of 1855. It was during this time that Khyentse Wangpo, by then a respected lama, gave his public approval to the struggling treasure revealer. There is reason to believe that Chokgyur Lingpa attended a public empowerment at Dzongsar prior to this meeting, but the accounts of these events by Jamgon Kongtrul and Khyentse Wangpo are muddled and it is impossible to determine the sequence of events. In any case, over the two years Khyentse Wangpo gave Chokgyur Lingpa three empowerments, the result of which was that the young treasure revealer's psychic knots were untied and he became capable – and, of equal importance, publicly authorized – to reveal treasure.

During the last of the empowerment rites Chokgyur Lingpa is said to have experienced a number of visions, including seeing Khyentse Wangpo as Vimalamitra, and also the Nyingma deity Ekajaṭī, who gave him the prophesy that he and Khyentse Wangpo would together discover a treasure cycle called the Dzogchen Desum (rdzogs chen sde gsum).

Two years later Khyentse Wangpo did indeed extract a treasure by that name, in collaboration with Chokgyur Lingpa. In January, 1857 the two lamas sanctified – “opened,” in Tibetan parlance – a new meditation site for Khyentse Wangpo, the cave known as Pema Shelpuk (padma shel phug), or Lotus Crystal Cave. This was in part a public ceremony, in which visitors were invited to witness the processes by which the cave and the surrounding hillside was mapped out as a supernatural site – they identified a spring of medicinal water, an overhang where Vimalamitra was said to have practiced, and so forth. Khyentse Wangpo also participated in the sanctification of Jamgon Kongtrul's hermitage above Pelpung, Tsadra Rinchen Drak (tsa 'dra rin chen brag) a month later.

Khyentse and Chokgyur Lingpa again collaborated on the sanctification of a site near Dzongsar, Rongme Karmo Taktsang (rong me dkar mo stag tshang), a cave site that became the hermitage for the monastery's college at the beginning of the twentieth century. Over a two week period in November 1866, the two identified caves, propitiated deities of the site, and extracted treasure, the Tukgrub Dorje Draktsel (thugs sgrub rdo rje drag rtsal) from a lake, Sengu Yumtso (seng rgod g.yu mtsho), the Wild Lion Turquoise Lake. The Rongme opening was a major ritual event in the region, attracting the presence not only of large crowds of people, but also the King of Derge, Chime Dakpai Dorje ('chi med rtag pa'i rdo rje, 1840-1898?). Rongme Karmo later offered Khyentse Wangpo's disciple, the famous Nyingma lama Ju Mipam Gyatso ('ju mi pham rgya mtsho, 1846-1912), a location for long-term practice; Mipam is said to have resided there for thirteen years.

When the group went up to the lake, a small body of water in the midst of a scree field more than 15,500 feet / 4,700 meters above sea level, Chokgyur Lingpa declared that a naga was guarding the treasure, and that everyone should be quiet so as to not offend him. Khyentse is said to have responded “What is there to fear in a naga? It is a worm! The so-called naga has no primordial existence. If he is there, I want to wake him up! I do not fear naga! If there is a naga, let it come here!” at which point he threw many stones into the lake. The others, obeying Chokgyur Lingpa's command, refrained from throwing stones. Chokgyur Lingpa then attempted to retrieve the treasure using his robe as a lasso; when the lake water suddenly churned violently, Chokgyur Lingpa shrieked and fell back. Khyentse Wangpo slapped him, scolding him that as Padmasambhava's representative he ought not be afraid. After the treasure was finally obtained, Khyentse Wangpo claimed that they succeeded because of the rocks he had thrown in, and on the way down the mountain he continued to throw rocks and people, claiming that everyone he struck was purified of their negative karma.

Khyentse Wangpo was a crucial player in the promotion of Chokgyur Lingpa's treasures. Following Chokgyur Lingpa's death in 1870, Khyentse Wangpo composed a brief biography of him in which his  complete treasures were categorized into thirty-seven separate revelations, or “caskets” (gter sgrom / gter kha). He also took it upon himself to be a co-revealer of several of Chokgyur Lingpa's treasures, most famously of the popular Barche Kunsel cycle (bar chad kun gsal), an assertion that should probably be taken as part of the elder lama's process of affirming the treasure revealer's legitimacy. Chokgyur Lingpa is said to have revealed this treasure in 1848; in 1855 the two worked together to decipher the treasure, an act which both Jamgon Kongtrul and Khyentse Wangpo describe as a merging of two separate revelations. Tradition has it that many of Chokgyur Lingpa's treasure were initially fated to be revealed by Khyentse Wangpo, who passed them instead to the younger revealer.

Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo also participated in the production of Jamgon Kongtrul's well-known “Five Treasuries” (mdzod lnga). According to traditional accounts, it was in a dream that Khyentse Wangpo had in 1861 in which he had a vision of a five-doored stupa, which signified to him that Jamgong Kongtrul ought to create “five treasuries.” Khyentse Wangpo proposed the Kagyu Ngakdzod (bka' brgyud sngags mdzod) in 1848, declaring that the available liturgies for the Ngok (rngog) maṇḍalas were inadequate, and he repeated the request from Tibet, where he received a prophesy that Jamgon Kongtrul should undertake the job of collecting ritual manuals for the Kagyu tantras. In 1855 Khyentse Wangpo suggested the organization of the Rinchen Terdzod (rin chen gter mdzod), and he advised which treasures to include. And, while it was the Kagyu lama Dabzang Tulku Karma Ngedon (zla bzang sprul sku kar+ma nges don, 1808-1867) who asked for the root text of the Sheja Kunjab (shes bya kun khyab), it was Khyentse Wangpo who insisted that Jamgon Kongtrul write a lengthy auto-comentary. Khyentse Wangpo also worked with Kongtrul on his Damngakdzod (gdams ngag mdzod), a collection of religious instructions (gdams ngag). Only the last of the five, Jamgon Kongtrul's collected miscellaneous writing, lacked input from Khyentse Wangpo.

Well before he put the idea to his colleague to create five great treasuries, Khyentse Wangpo had begun his own massive collection, the Drubtab Kundu (sgrub thabs kun btus), a compendium of Sakya sādhanas that he first began when he was staying at Sakya in the late 1840s. According to Jamgon Kongtrul, he gave the empowerment for the collection in 1852 at Pelpung for a group of about twenty prominent lamas. Khyentse Wangpo was the main inspiration and patron of Jamyang Loter Wangpo's ('jam dbyang blo gter dbang po, 1847-1914) Gyude Kuntu (rgyud sde kun btus) in thirty-two volumes, a collection of  initiations manuals for the 132 maṇḍalas of the Sakya tradition. According to Lodro Puntsok (blo gros phun tshogs) he also produced a collection of Lamdre Lobshe (lam 'bras slob bshad) teachings in seventeen volumes, and eight volumes of songs and instructions from the eight practrice lineages (sgrub brgyud shing rta brgyad kyi zhal gdam gsung mgur), although this later collection is not included in the works associated with Khyentse Wangpo on TBRC. In addition, thirteen addition volumes of material not included in the above which constitute his personal collected works (bka' 'bum), which runs to twenty-four volumes. Khyentse Wangpo also famously authored a pilgrimage guide to Tibet, the U-tsang Neyik (dbus gtsang gnas yig), which has been translated several times into English.

It was largely on the basis of these impressive compendiums of teachings that Khyentse Wangpo is often referred to as a member of a so-called “Rime Movement.”  It is more accurate to say that he embodied an ecumenical ideal (ris med) long cherished by Tibetan scholars, one of appreciating and exploring multiple traditions of Buddhism in Tibet. It is important to remember that Khyentse Wangpo was a Sakya lama whose primary ritual and literary activity was dedicated to that tradition, and while he worked closely with the Kagyu Jamgon Kongtrul and the Nyingma Chokgyur Lingpa, neither he nor his colleagues made any effort to merge traditions or initiate a new teaching institution.

Khyentse Wangpo served the Derge court for most of his career, both alone and together with Jamgon Kongtrul and Chokgyur Lingpa. He regularly went to the capital to perform rituals for the royal family and for the well-being of the realm. In 1859, for example, the three were in Derge to perform exorcism rites for the kingdom, at the request of the Queen, Choying Zangmo (chos dbying bzang mo, d. 1892) and her two sons, including the future king Chime Dagpai Dorje ('chi med rtag pa'i rdo rje, 1840-1898?), during which Jamgon Kontrul records that Khyentse Wangpo “gave the most amazing lecture.” Jamgon Kongtrul took the opportunity to give the Queen, her sons, and his two colleagues the empowerment of the entire Nyingma Kama.

Later that same year Khyentse Wangpo participated in rituals designed to consecrate the ground for a new temple to the northeast of Derge, the construction of Chokgyur Lingpa had predicted would prevent the coming onslaught of the Nyarong War; owing to sectarian conflicts in Derge (the Sakya ministers would not allow the construction of yet another Nyingma temple, it seems), it was never built. During the war Khyentse Wangpo ransomed the safety of Dzongsar, although some buildings were burned by the Nyarong (nyag rong) chieftain Gonpo Namgyel's (mgon po rnam rgyal, 1799-1863) forces. For the most part he seems to have avoided the sort of involvement in the war that befell Jamgon Kongtrul, who found himself ministering to both Gonpo Namgyel and to the Tibetan forces from Lhasa who arrived to defeat him.

Khyentse Wangpo also drafted legislation, writing, again with Chokgyur Lingpa, a law restricting the killing of wild animals in the kingdom.

According to Jamgon Kongtrul, Khyentse Wangpo received all seven of the “seven transmissions” (bka' babs bdun): Kama (bka' ma), earth treasure (sa gter), mind treasure (dgongs gter), re-concealed treasure (yang gter), visionary transmission (dag snang), recollection (rje dran) and hearing lineage (snyan brgyud). This classification of transmission vectors appears to have originated with Khyentse Wangpo, who used it in his biography of Chokgyur Lingpa, and it serves as an organizing structure for most hagiographies of him as well. Among his best known treasure revelations were the Semnyi Ngalso (sems nyid ngal gso) cycle of Avalokiteśvara, revealed as earth treasure at Drakmar Drinzang (brag dmar mgrin bzang). His Drubtob Tuktik (grub thob thugs tig) was classified as a mind treasure, which came to him in a vision of Tangtong Gyelpo (thang stong rgyal po, 1361- 1485). Jamgon Kongtrul also includes in his biography of Khyentse Wangpo an event in which Khyentse Wangpo revealed thirteen treasure at the great mountain of Khawa Karpo (kha ba dkar po) when he was sixteen, with the help of a consort.

Khyentse Wangpo also is said to have recovered, via vision or dream, treasure cycles that had been lost over the years, reestablishing the transmission and making them available for inclusion in Jamgon Kongtrul's Rinchen Terdzod. On the basis of his prodigious treasure-revealing activity, Jamgon Kongtrul counted Khyentse Wangpo as the last in a group of five kingly treasure revealers (gter ston rgyal po nga). His treasure name was Do-ngak Lingpa (mdo sngags gling pa).

Khyentse Wangpo is also remembered for greatly expanding Dzogsar Monastery. He built a fifty-pillar temple there, the Tashi Latse Utser Gonjang Lhakang (rdzong gsar bkra shis lha rtse'i dbu rtser mngon byang lha khang). He also built a small six-pillar temple, the Riksum Lhakang (rigs gsum lha khang) on the plain below Dzongsar Monastery, known in local dialect as Khamshetang (kham bye thang), in 1871. This temple was transformed by the second Khyentse, Chokyi Lodro ('jam dbyangs chos kyi blo gros, 1893-1959) in 1918 into the Khamshe Monastic College (kham bye bshad grwa).

Khyentse Wangpo died on March 19, 1892, the twenty-first day of the second month of the water dragon year. Jamgon Kongtrul presided over the funeral, washing his body and preparing them for cremation. He performed a five-day Vajrakila rite in his presence, and, with the aid of the Tartse Khenpo and Loter Wangpo, performed three weeks of additional rituals. Jamyang Khyentse's brother Kelzang Dorje, the head steward of Dzongsar, paid for much of the funeral. An elaborate reliquary was installed in Dzongsar, recently reconstructed together with much of the monastery.

At least eight reincarnations of Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo are known to have been identified at different monasteries across the Derge region. These included Dilgo Khyentse Tashi Peljor (dil mgo mkhyen brtse bkra shis dpal 1910-1991), based at Shechen, and Jamyang Khyentse Chokyi Wangpo (mkhyen brtse chos kyi dbang po, 1894-1909) who was based at Dzongsar; when he died young he was replaced at Dzongsar by Jamyang Khyentse Chokyi Lodro ('jam dbyangs mkhyen brtse chos kyi blo gros, 1893-1959), who had been based at Katok, and whose reincarnation is Dzongsar Khyentse Norbu (b. 1961); Jamyang Khyentse Chokyi Wangpo's reincarnation was identified as Jamyang Chokyi Wangchuk ('jam dbyangs chos kyi dbang phyug, 1910-1963) and was moved to Derge Gonchen (sde dge dgon chen). He was the uncle and teacher of Namkhai Norbu (1938-2018).

Karma Khyentse Wozer (karma mkhyen brtse'i 'od zer, 1896-1945), based at Pelpung, was known as the First Beru Khyentse (be ru mkhyen brtse). A fifth line was initiated with Ngawang Tutob Wangchuk (ngag dbang mthu stobs dbang phyug, 1900-1950) who served as the Fortieth Sakya Trizin, from 1937 to 1950; his grandson David Khon was recognized as his reincarnation. Kunzang Drodul (kun bzang 'gro 'dul, 1897-1945), based at Pelme Monastery (dpal me) and known as the Pelme Khyentse Kunzang Drodul (dpal me mkhyen brtse kun bzang 'gro bdul). The First Dzogchen Khyentse was Guru Tsewang (rdzog chen mkhyen brtse 01 gu ru tshe dbang, 1896-1935), whose reincarnation, the Second Dzogchen Khyentse, was named Zhonnu Lodro (rdzog chen mkhyen brtse 02 gzhon nu blo gros, 1937-1959). Another incarnation, Pakchok Dorje ('phags mchog rdo rje, 1893-1943) was the son of the famous Tokden Shākya Shrī (rtogs ldan shAkya shrI, 1853-1919) of Dzogchen Monastery (rdzogs chen dgon)."

Navigation with centimeter-level precision anywhere on Earth—no satellites required. Australian quantum positioning uses atomic clocks and inertial sensors so accurate they detect Earth's rotation. It's GPS that can't be jammed, spoofed, or denied by anyone. And the Pentagon is blocking civilian use.

Traditional GPS relies on satellites broadcasting timing signals. Quantum positioning uses ultra-precise atomic clocks and quantum accelerometers to track movement from a known starting point—essentially dead reckoning with physics-defying accuracy. The system detects motion at the sub-millimeter level and maintains position accuracy within centimeters indefinitely. It works underground, underwater, in buildings—anywhere satellites can't reach.

Australia developed it for civilian autonomous vehicles and surveying. But the US Defense Department classified quantum navigation as "strategically sensitive dual-use technology" and pressured allies to restrict exports. Why? GPS is controlled by the US military—they can degrade or disable civilian GPS during conflicts. Quantum positioning eliminates that leverage. Countries with quantum navigation can't be denied positioning access.

For American consumers, this means continuing to depend on satellite GPS that can be jammed (already happening in Ukraine and Taiwan Strait), while Australian mining companies use unhackable quantum positioning for autonomous trucks. The technology exists to make navigation infrastructure-independent. But strategic concerns override civilian benefits.

Our virtual journey takes us to North Macedonia, to Samuel's Fortress. “The Secrets of Samuel's Fortress: A Legendary Fortress Through the Centuries.” I wish you an exciting experience. Let's begin.

Samuel Fortress sits majestically on the hills of Ohrid in North Macedonia and bears witness to centuries of architectural mastery and historical significance. With roots dating back to antiquity and many stories hidden behind its stone walls, the fortress offers not only a panoramic view of Lake Ohrid, but also an extraordinary journey through time, encompassing myths, legends, and imperial ambitions.

Ancient origins and philhellenic mysticism - The history of Samuel's Fortress begins long before the era of Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria, dating back to the 4th century BC. Recent excavations led by Macedonian archaeologists suggest that the fortress stands on the remains of a structure believed to have been commissioned by the famous King Philip II of Macedon. Philip II, the father of Alexander the Great, was known for his military conquests and promotion of Hellenistic culture throughout his empire. The design and construction techniques of the original fortress are testament to the sophisticated architectural standards of the Macedonian kingdom, which was renowned for its strategic innovations.

The connection to Philip II lends the fortress an air of classical heroism and attracts curious visitors eager to walk the same ground once trodden by legendary warriors.
 
Local tour guides whisper that relics of ancient battles may lie hidden beneath the stones—the echoes of clashing shields and the cries of soldiers who dared to defy the course of history.

The Medieval Resurrection: Tsar Samuel's Vision - In the late 10th century, a new chapter began under the rule of Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria, who had the fortress rebuilt into an impressive stronghold of the First Bulgarian Empire. Samuel's reign was marked by a resurgence against Byzantine rule, and his decision to rebuild the fortress in Ohrid was both strategic and symbolic. Samuel made it his capital and fortified the walls with medieval improvements, creating an impressive citadel that could withstand sieges and signal Bulgarian sovereignty.

The architecture of this era reflected the need for robustness. Massive walls and watchtowers were built using the advances in masonry and defensive architecture that were crucial in the Middle Ages. This was not only for protection, but also to make a statement of power and autonomy.

Within these walls, Samuel orchestrated military campaigns and administered the affairs of government, shaping the course of history in the Balkans against the ambitions of Byzantium.

Restoration and today's tourist pilgrimage - By the beginning of the 21st century, Samuel's fortress had weathered the storms of time but needed extensive restoration to regain its former glory. In 2003, the fortress underwent a comprehensive restoration project, during which new battlements were installed, as the old ones had fallen victim to the relentless passage of time. Modern archaeologists and historians meticulously reconstructed parts of the fortress based on historical texts and preserved architectural traces, allowing the past and present to coexist harmoniously.

Today, Samuel's Fortress is more than just an archaeological site; it is a cultural attraction that draws thousands of tourists every year. Visitors can explore the extensive fortress walls, imagine the defensive strategies of past eras, and enjoy the sweeping views of the surrounding landscape. The restored parts provide insight into medieval building techniques, while ongoing excavations continue to uncover new finds that contribute to the fortress's historical heritage.

Timeless: Myths and legends surrounding Samuel's Fortress - In addition to the historical facts, Samuel's Fortress is also interwoven with folklore and mythical tales that spark the imagination. It is said that treasures left behind by fleeing rulers are buried in the depths of the fortress. However, these riches are supposedly guarded by the spirits of warriors who were loyal to Tsar Samuel and swore to protect the secrets until they are deemed worthy by the guardians of fate.

Another legend tells of a mysterious tunnel stretching from the fortress to the shores of Lake Ohrid – a hidden passageway used by envoys in times of siege or for secret missions.
 
According to local lore, this tunnel was enchanted by ancient sorcerers, so that anyone who enters it is lost forever unless guided by a chosen spirit.

There are also stories of enchanted springs within the fortress grounds, believed to impart wisdom or courage to those who drink from them. Pilgrims from the surrounding villages often came here secretly in the moonlight to seek the blessing of the water for their courageous and harmless endeavors.

A modern place of historical encounter - Samuel's Fortress stands for its mythical past, but is also a center for contemporary cultural engagement. The fortress regularly hosts festivals, historical reenactments, and educational tours that bring its rich history to life. Scholars and historians gather to discuss newly discovered artifacts and add new chapters to the saga of the fortress.

Furthermore, digital technology has transformed the way the stories of Samuel's Fortress are told. Virtual reality experiences allow a global audience to immerse themselves in its splendor and admire this Balkan gem across geographical boundaries.

In summary, Samuel's Fortress is a remarkable fusion of history and legend, an architectural marvel that connects ancient Macedonia with medieval Bulgaria and the modern world. Il design e le tecniche di costruzione della fortezza originale testimoniano gli standard architettonici altamente sviluppati del regno macedone, noto per le sue innovazioni strategiche.

Il legame con Filippo II conferisce alla fortezza un tocco di eroismo classico e attira visitatori curiosi, desiderosi di calpestare lo stesso suolo che un tempo calpestarono guerrieri leggendari. L'islam n'est pas contre, et ne nous interdit pas de conserver nos cultures et nos traditions. Il n'est pas venu nous les arracher. D'ailleurs, il y a des règles de la charia qu'on applique ou pas en fonction du contexte culturel du peuple.

Ce que l'islam ne nous autorise pas en tant que musulmans, c'est de placer des croyances, des rites et des célébrations culturels et traditionnels au-dessus de l'Unicité Absolue d'Allah (Tawhid ), interdisant ainsi tout acte de polythéisme, d'idôlatrie et d'associationnisme(Shirk).

On ne peut pas se dire croyant et musulman, et rester quand même attaché(e) à une culture et à des traditions dont les fondements et l'exécution impliquent de croire, d'invoquer, de consulter et/ou de vénérer des "divinités" autres qu'Allah. De chanter et de danser pour elles. Même si c'est pour le fun, il faut s'en éloigner. 

Par ailleurs, tant que ce qu'elles impliquent ne piétinent pas les bases du Tawhid, il n'y a aucun problème. Tant qu'elles ne vont pas dans le sens de ce que l'islam interdit, il n'y a également aucun problème.

Bref. Au regard de plusieurs faits, je pense que la question du Tawhid doit réellement être abordée autant de fois que possible pendant les sermonts.

Tribute to the amboseli national park
To the amboseli,
I grew up watching you closely, walking beside you, breathing you in, blessed and proud to have been born within you. I speak with deep pride and  joy whenever I say "I am from the amboseli".
You are a land where the roars of  lions and the triumphant calls of elephants echo every day. A land that carries the stories of generations and speaks for itself. The sacred home of the amboseli Indigenous people. This is my home, my forever empire.
Our fathers sat with us and told stories of the ancient paths they walked. In our culture, animals were not just wildlife; they were family. They were given names and became clan totems. For my clan, , the  elephant is our totem, honored as a sister or brother. , the Hyena holds that sacred place of ilaitayiok. Through this bond, the amboseli protected every life.
Then conservation came. Songs were sung, poems recited, and land was surrendered with hope, without knowing the cost.
Today, the amboseli is no longer the endless open land it once was. The plains are shrinking, land grabbing is swallowing its soul, and politicians have become brokers. The savannah is slowly turning into mini-city.
This is not the amboseli that raised us.
Still, I hold onto hope that the land will remember us, the ancestors will speak, and the lion’s roar will outlive greed.
Amboseli, you are wounded, but still sacred. 🥺💔
